practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the caravel that made long ocean voyages possible.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students may describe: lateen (triangular) sails that allowed the ship to sail closer to the wind / a sturdy hull capable of surviving Atlantic conditions / a shallow enough draught to navigate coastal waters. One mark for identifying the feature; two marks for a developed explanation of why it mattered for ocean voyages.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Treaty of Tordesillas, 1494.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It divided the non-Christian world between Spain and Portugal along a north-south line through the Atlantic (approximately 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands).
• It allocated territories east of the line to Portugal (Africa and Asia) and west of the line to Spain (the Americas).
• It was brokered by the Pope (Pope Alexander VI), giving it religious authority.
• It gave Spain the right to explore westward, enabling Columbus’s voyages and later the conquest of the Americas.
[2 marks per feature: 1 mark for identification, 2 marks for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of European voyages of exploration in the late fifteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Secure: Identifies and explains a cause with supporting evidence (e.g. economic motive: Ottoman control of overland routes raised the cost of Asian goods, pushing Portugal and Spain to seek sea routes; or technological: caravel and astrolabe made ocean navigation viable for the first time).
Mastering: Develops the cause fully, linking it to specific evidence and explaining the connection (e.g. the Reconquista completing in 1492 left Spanish crusading energy and military resources free for overseas expansion; Ferdinand and Isabella saw exploration as continuation of their mission to spread Christianity).
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: States a cause without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the fall of Constantinople in 1453 for European exploration.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that Ottoman control of the eastern Mediterranean disrupted or blocked trade and raised prices for spices and silk, creating an urgent economic incentive for both Portugal and Spain to find alternative sea routes; links this to specific voyages (e.g. Dias 1488, Columbus 1492).
Secure: Identifies the consequence with relevant supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Describes the fall without explaining consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Prince Henry the Navigator for the age of exploration.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (sponsored systematic Portuguese voyages down African coast; established infrastructure of navigational knowledge; reached Sierra Leone by 1460; gave Portugal a decades-long lead) AND over time (his programme made da Gama’s 1498 voyage to India possible; established the model of state-sponsored exploration copied by Spain). Developed argument with evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with supporting evidence; may lack the over-time dimension fully.
Developing: Describes what Henry did without fully analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Technology was the most important reason why European voyages of discovery became possible in the late fifteenth century.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• The caravel’s lateen sails allowed sailing against the wind, making return journeys along the African coast possible for the first time.
• The magnetic compass and astrolabe allowed open-ocean navigation by latitude even when stars were obscured.
• Improved cartography (rediscovery of Ptolemy’s Geography) gave navigators a theoretical framework.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• Economic motive (Ottoman blockade, spice trade profits) drove investment in exploration; technology was the means, not the motive.
• State sponsorship — Ferdinand and Isabella, the Portuguese crown — provided capital that technology alone could not supply.
• Religious motivation (Reconquista ethos, desire to spread Christianity) gave explorers and their backers ideological justification.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some points on both sides, limited judgement.
Emerging: Simple description of technology or motives without evaluating the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of food rationing in Britain in the early 1950s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Food rationing continued until 1954, the last product being meat (July 1954); weekly allowances were very limited, e.g. 13 oz of meat and 6 oz of butter per adult.
- Ration books with coupons were required for shopping at designated shops; buying beyond one's allowance was illegal and a black market existed.
- Bread, never rationed during the war, was placed on ration between 1946 and 1948 due to post-war grain shortages.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature: 1 for feature identified, 2 for feature + developed detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the housing crisis in Britain after 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple identification of a cause with limited explanation.
Secure: Clear cause identified with developed explanation and some specific factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation with precise supporting evidence, explaining how/why this factor led to the housing crisis.

Causes may include:
- Wartime bombing destroying or damaging an estimated three million homes, creating immediate shortfall.
- Population growth and returning servicemen creating demand that the wartime suspension of house-building could not quickly address.
- Slow pace of post-war construction despite prefab programme (156,000 prefabs built) because permanent housing took years to plan and build.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the creation of the National Health Service in 1948.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple consequence identified with limited explanation.
Secure: Clear consequence with developed explanation and factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation of consequence, supported by precise evidence and showing wider significance.

Consequences may include:
- NHS spending far exceeded projections (reaching £400 million in its first year against an estimate of £132 million), forcing the introduction of charges for spectacles and dental treatment by 1951.
- Millions of people accessed medical care for the first time, improving public health but also creating enormous unexpected demand.
- Political controversy as costs became apparent, with Labour split over charges (Bevan resigned over them) and Conservatives questioning the affordability of welfare.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was the housing shortage in shaping life in Britain in the early 1950s? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points about housing, limited or no evidence.
Developing: Some explanation of significance at the time, basic evidence used.
Secure: Clear explanation of significance at the time and over time, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of significance at the time AND over time, precise evidence, sustained argument.

Points may include:
At the time: families in overcrowded lodgings, long waiting lists for council housing (5+ years), prefabs as emergency measure, emotional and social stress of homelessness.
Over time: housing remained a major political issue into the 1960s; Harold Macmillan's success in hitting the 300,000 homes target boosted Conservative popularity; the council house programme created communities that shaped British society for decades.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The welfare state was the most important cause of Britain's economic difficulties in the early 1950s.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation using limited factual knowledge; may address only one side.
Secure: Clear evaluation, addresses both agreement and disagreement, uses factual knowledge effectively.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation with precise evidence; sustained argument weighing welfare costs against wartime debt, nationalisation, and other factors; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: NHS cost far exceeded projections; welfare commitments required high taxation constraining business investment; charges introduced as early as 1951 show costs were unmanageable.

Disagreement: wartime debt (£3 billion; American loan conditions) was a more fundamental cause; nationalised industries were often loss-making; global post-war scarcity affected all European economies; the welfare state also supported workforce health and productivity.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the prefab housing programme in post-war Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Prefabs were prefabricated, quickly assembled single-storey homes; approximately 156,000 were built between 1945 and 1949 as an emergency response to the housing shortage.
- They were intended as temporary accommodation lasting about ten years, but many were still occupied into the 1970s because permanent housing was so slow to follow.
- Prefabs offered self-contained modern amenities (bathroom, fitted kitchen) that were often superior to the shared facilities in older, damaged housing stock.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

before.exam_tip_html: For a ‘4 marks — Describe Two Features’ question on post-war austerity, give two distinct features with specific supporting detail for each. For example: “One feature was food rationing, which continued until 1954 and included restrictions on meat, butter, and sugar. A second feature was the housing shortage, with an estimated three million homes needing repair and families waiting years for council housing.” Avoid vague answers such as “life was hard” — examiners reward precise factual knowledge. For 8-mark significance questions, address both significance at the time and significance over time: the welfare state mattered immediately for ordinary people’s health and security, and its long-term significance lies in establishing principles of universal entitlement that shaped British politics for decades.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Boers' military tactics in the early phase of the Second Boer War.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: The Boers used guerrilla tactics (1), attacking British supply lines with small mobile commando units before retreating into the countryside (1). Mastering: accurate feature with precise supporting detail. Developing: feature stated but not developed.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the British concentration camps set up during the Boer War.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail). Feature 1 examples: overcrowding; inadequate food rations; poor sanitation; high disease rates (measles, typhoid). Feature 2 examples: held mainly women and children; approximately 26,000 Boer civilian deaths; Black Africans held in separate camps. Mastering: two precise features, each with accurate supporting detail. Secure: two features with some supporting detail. Developing: one or two features, limited detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Second Boer War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Developed explanation of one cause linked to outcome, supported by accurate contextual knowledge. E.g. the discovery of gold in the Transvaal in 1886 made the republic hugely valuable; British mine owners and financiers pressed the government to extend control; Boer resistance to British domination led to diplomatic breakdown and war in October 1899. Secure (3–4): Clear cause with some development. Developing (1–2): Simple identification with limited development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Emily Hobhouse's 1901 report on the concentration camps.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Developed consequence with precise supporting knowledge. E.g. Hobhouse's report triggered a public outcry that divided opinion in Britain; the government responded by commissioning the Fawcett Commission, which broadly confirmed her findings and recommended improvements; the pro-Boer movement grew, with Liberal politicians like Lloyd George using the scandal to attack the government's conduct of the war. Secure (3–4): Clear consequence with some development. Developing (1–2): Simple statement of a consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Boer War for attitudes to the British Empire.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): Significance at the time AND over time, both substantiated. At the time: the Khaki Election showed public support; concentration camps created the first widespread anti-imperial movement; Emily Hobhouse's revelations damaged the moral image of empire. Over time: the war raised questions about whether military force alone could maintain empire; it contributed to the reform debates of the Liberal government after 1906; influenced later critiques of empire and independence movements. Secure (5–6): Significance at the time and over time, with some development of each. Developing (3–4): Significance mainly at the time, or over time, not both. Emerging (1–2): Simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'The concentration camps were the most significant consequence of the Second Boer War for Britain.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Agrees and disagrees using own contextual knowledge, reaches substantiated overall judgement. Agree: camps caused massive civilian deaths; Hobhouse's report created a humanitarian crisis debate; Fawcett Commission forced policy change; 'pro-Boer' movement fed into Liberal reform thinking. Disagree: military cost (~22,000 British lives) and financial cost (~£220 million) were also transformative; diplomatic isolation (Splendid Isolation) had wider consequences; Khaki Election showed pro-empire sentiment remained strong. Secure (7–9): Clear agreement and disagreement, some development, some conclusion. Developing (4–6): Mainly one-sided with limited development. Emerging (1–3): Simple agreement or disagreement only.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Crusades as a religiously motivated conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks. Students should identify a feature and support it:
• The Crusades were launched by the Pope (Pope Urban II called the First Crusade in 1095) with the aim of capturing Jerusalem from Muslim rule [1 mark for feature, 1 mark for supporting detail].
• Crusaders were offered spiritual rewards, including absolution from sins, as an incentive to fight [1+1 as above].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the English Civil War as a politically caused conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail):
• Feature 1: The war arose from a constitutional crisis over the power of Parliament versus the Crown — Charles I had attempted to rule without Parliament during his ‘Personal Rule’ of 1629–1640 [1+1].
• Feature 2: Charles I’s belief in the divine right of kings meant he refused to accept limits on his authority, bringing him into direct conflict with Parliament’s demands [1+1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains a cause with precise supporting evidence and analysis of how it led to war. E.g., German nationalism under Hitler — the desire to reverse the Treaty of Versailles and expand into Eastern Europe (Lebensraum) — directly caused the invasion of Poland in September 1939, triggering Britain's declaration of war.
Secure: Clear explanation with supporting evidence but less analytical depth.
Developing: Identifies a cause with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement with little or no evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of ideology as a cause of the Cold War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues the significance of ideology both at the time (shaped NATO formation, nuclear deterrence, proxy wars) and over time (defined British foreign and military policy for four decades). Reaches a substantiated conclusion about why ideology was uniquely significant compared to previous causes of war.
Secure: Explains significance at the time and over time with relevant evidence.
Developing: Explains significance at the time only, or gives thin evidence.
Emerging: Describes the Cold War without analysing significance.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that religion was the most important cause of war in the medieval period? Use your knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues convincingly for and against, with precise evidence from the Crusades (Pope Urban II, 1095; Richard I, Third Crusade 1189–1192) and awareness of other medieval factors (land, political power, dynastic ambition). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument for and against with relevant evidence and a conclusion.
Developing: Some argument, limited evidence, conclusion not fully justified.
Emerging: Describes rather than evaluates; little or no evidence.

practice_questions.text: How far did the causes of British involvement in war change between c.500 and the present day? In your answer, refer to religion, politics, nationalism and ideology as causes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces causes across all three eras (medieval: religion — Crusades; early modern: politics — Civil War; modern: nationalism/ideology — World War Two, Cold War). Weighs change against continuity (e.g., economic interest as a persistent background factor). Reaches a sophisticated, substantiated overall judgement on the extent and nature of change.
Secure: Covers all three eras with relevant evidence and some analysis of change vs continuity. Concludes.
Developing: Covers two eras adequately; limited change/continuity analysis.
Emerging: Describes one or two events; no analytical framework.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the manorial system in fourteenth-century England.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. One mark for a simple identification, two marks for a developed feature. Example: Villeins owed their lord a set number of days of labour each week on the demesne land [1], and in return received strips of land to farm for their own subsistence [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Church's role in medieval English society.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature (1 for a simple point, 2 for a developed point). Feature 1: The Church was the centre of community life, marking births, marriages and deaths through the parish system [1] and providing charity and the rhythm of the agricultural year through religious festivals [1]. Feature 2: The Church was enormously wealthy, owning roughly a third of all English land by the fourteenth century [1] and collecting tithes — a tenth of each parishioner's produce — as compulsory income [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the tension between rich and poor in fourteenth-century England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (e.g. serfdom, the Church's landholding, labour obligations) and explains it in depth, linking it to broader inequalities in medieval society with precise factual support. Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with some factual detail. Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference to inequality without a specific cause identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of England's dependence on the wool trade in the 1330s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific consequence (e.g. Crown reliance on wool customs for war finance, diplomatic ties to Flemish towns, growth of a merchant class) and explains it in depth with factual support, showing how it shaped Edward III's decisions. Secure: Identifies a consequence and explains it with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague point without specific factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of serfdom to an understanding of the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance both at the time (serfdom created resentment, bound people to land, restricted freedom and wages) and over time (the revolt accelerated serfdom's decline; the issue of bound labour remained contested into the fifteenth century). Precise factual knowledge integrated throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some reference to longer-term impact. Developing: Describes features of serfdom without clearly linking to its significance. Emerging: Limited factual knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The position of the Church was the most important feature of English society in 1337.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with the interpretation using precise factual knowledge. Agrees: Church owned ~one third of land, collected tithes, shaped daily life through parishes and festivals, held political power via bishops in the Lords. Disagrees: The manorial system and serfdom were arguably more important to most people's lives; the wool trade drove royal policy and shaped alliances. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence; judgement present but may lack full development. Developing: Describes features without clearly evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple descriptive response; no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Emergency Quota Act of 1921.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: The Emergency Quota Act introduced national origin quotas [1], capping annual immigration of each nationality at 3 per cent of that nationality's population in America as recorded by the 1910 census [1].
Other acceptable features: it reduced annual immigration to approximately 357,000; it was the first time the US government had used a quota system for immigration.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Palmer Raids.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature: one for the feature, one for supporting detail.
Feature 1: The Palmer Raids arrested large numbers of suspected radicals — approximately 10,000 people across 33 cities, many detained without warrants. [2]
Feature 2: Those arrested were frequently deported without trial — the most prominent deportee was the anarchist Emma Goldman, sent to Russia in December 1919. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growing demand for immigration restrictions in the United States after the First World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains a specific cause with precise factual support and clear causal reasoning, addressing both the cause and its link to the outcome.
Secure: Identifies a valid cause with some supporting evidence and a clear explanatory link.
Developing: Names a cause but explanation is limited or generic.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.
Valid causes: nativist racial ideology (e.g. Madison Grant); economic competition for jobs after the war; fear of communism and anarchism linking immigrants to radicalism; the Red Scare linking foreignness to political threat.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Red Scare for immigrants living in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces a consequence with precise evidence and clear reasoning about how the Red Scare produced that outcome.
Secure: Identifies a valid consequence with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a consequence but the causal link is vague.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid consequences: thousands of immigrants arrested and deported without trial during the Palmer Raids; immigrants associated with radicalism regardless of individual beliefs; increased public support for immigration restriction laws; climate of fear for immigrant communities.

practice_questions.text:
How significant was the Sacco and Vanzetti case in revealing the treatment of immigrants in the United States in the 1920s?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance both at the time and in the longer term, with precise evidence and sustained analysis.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant detail; may address only one timeframe fully.
Developing: Some explanation of significance but limited evidence.
Emerging: Simple points.
At the time: exposed racial and political prejudice in the justice system; provoked international protests; made immigrants afraid; discredited anti-immigrant hysteria.
Over time: became a symbol of nativism; Massachusetts acknowledged in 1977 that they had not received a fair trial; shaped later debates about justice and immigration.

practice_questions.text:
'The Immigration Act of 1924 was the most important turning point in US immigration policy in the years 1910 to 1929.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence; judgement present but may be underdeveloped.
Developing: Some relevant points but response is unbalanced or lacks a clear judgement.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Agreement: The 1924 act introduced the most restrictive quotas using the 1890 baseline, effectively ended mass immigration from southern and eastern Europe, imposed near-total Asian exclusion, and set the template for US immigration policy until 1965.
Disagreement: The 1921 Quota Act introduced the quota principle first; the Red Scare and Palmer Raids shaped anti-immigrant attitudes before either act; Sacco and Vanzetti showed that prejudice already existed in the system.

practice_questions.text: Describe one reason why poverty caused crime in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students should identify a specific mechanism: e.g. harvest failure drove people to steal food or livestock; famine years such as 1315-1322 created widespread desperation; warfare disrupted food supply and pushed communities into survival crime. A simple identification (1 mark); development with context or example (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of religious change on crime in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail). Feature 1: Religious legislation created new crimes — Catholics who refused to attend Protestant services were guilty of recusancy, and priests risked execution. Feature 2: Witchcraft fears produced prosecution waves — the Witchcraft Act of 1563 made witchcraft a capital offence, and during the 1640s Matthew Hopkins prosecuted hundreds in East Anglia. Other valid features: Protestant heretics burned under Mary I; possession of forbidden devotional materials became criminal.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the increase in crime during the Industrial Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names a cause (e.g. urbanisation) without explanation. Developing: Identifies urbanisation and notes it created overcrowded cities. Secure: Explains how anonymity of city life broke down traditional community controls, making crime easier to commit and harder to detect; may add specific detail (Manchester population growth, pick-pocketing and street robbery rising). Mastering: Sustains analytical explanation linking rapid urbanisation to the breakdown of parish-based enforcement, uses specific evidence (population figures, types of crime), and connects to the wider context of industrialisation displacing rural workers.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Luddite movement (1811-1813) as evidence of a cause of crime.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Identifies Luddites smashed machinery. Developing: Explains economic threat to framework knitters from mechanisation. Secure: Analyses significance at the time (collective response to livelihood destruction; treated as capital crime by the state) and connects to a wider cause (industrial displacement as a driver of disorder). Mastering: Sustains analysis of significance both at the time and over time; evaluates whether collective industrial crime represents continuity with earlier survival crime or a new phenomenon unique to industrialisation; reaches a substantiated judgement.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that poverty was the main cause of crime in Britain between c.500 and the present day?
Give reasons for your answer. You should refer to different periods in your response.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments supporting poverty as the main cause: medieval famine-theft; Tudor inflation and displacement; urban destitution driving pick-pocketing and prostitution; twentieth-century drug crime linked to deprivation. Arguments for other causes: religious change (Reformation, witchcraft) creating entirely new categories of crime; industrialisation and mechanisation producing collective protest crime; twentieth-century technology enabling cybercrime regardless of poverty. Emerging: One-sided or superficial. Developing: Both sides noted but not sustained. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from at least two eras; some weighing. Mastering: Sustained argument across all three eras, weighs poverty against other causes with specific evidence, reaches a justified overall conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of twentieth-century causes of crime that were not present in earlier centuries.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Motor vehicles created new crime categories — speeding, drink-driving and car theft emerged only after the spread of the motor car from the early twentieth century. Feature 2: Cybercrime (fraud, identity theft, hacking) emerged from the late twentieth century as internet use became universal, enabling crime on a global scale impossible in earlier eras. Other valid features: drug-related crime growing from the 1960s; terrorism by organisations using modern communications.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Treaty of Versailles (1919) and its impact on Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• The War Guilt Clause (Article 231) forced Germany to accept sole responsibility for the First World War. This caused widespread anger among Germans, who felt the clause was unjust and used it to label the Weimar politicians who signed the treaty as ‘November criminals’. [2 marks]
• Germany was required to pay reparations, eventually set at 132 billion gold marks in 1921 (about £6.6 billion at the time). This placed a severe burden on the German economy and contributed to the financial crises of the early 1920s. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for a simple identification with no development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the crisis year 1923 in Weimar Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple identification of two features with basic description.
Secure: Each feature is described with relevant context, e.g.:
• The French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr in January 1923, following Germany’s failure to deliver reparations goods, led the government to call for passive resistance, which was funded by printing money and triggered hyperinflation. [2 marks]
• Hitler’s Munich Putsch in November 1923 was an attempt to seize power during the economic crisis. It failed when police opened fire; sixteen Nazis were killed and Hitler was arrested and imprisoned. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the rise of the Nazi Party between 1929 and 1932.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: A simple statement of a cause with little explanation.
Developing: Cause identified with some explanation of the mechanism.
Secure: Clear explanation of how the cause led to Nazi growth, with specific evidence.
Mastering: Analytical explanation that considers the mechanism in depth, using precise data (e.g. unemployment figures, election percentages).
Example content: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 caused American banks to recall loans to Germany, leading to rapid industrial collapse and mass unemployment. By early 1932 approximately six million Germans were out of work. This created desperation and resentment that the Nazis exploited, offering scapegoats (Jews, communists, the Weimar government) and promises of strong leadership. Nazi support rose from under 3% in 1928 to 37.4% in July 1932.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the hyperinflation crisis of 1923 for the Weimar Republic.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification of a consequence.
Developing: Consequence described with some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses the long-term significance of the consequence beyond 1923.
Example content: Hyperinflation wiped out the savings of the German middle class — pensioners and civil servants on fixed incomes lost everything overnight. This created lasting hostility towards the Weimar Republic, as many blamed democratic politicians for the crisis. Even after Stresemann stabilised the currency, the memory of 1923 left many middle-class Germans distrustful of democracy and susceptible to extremist parties that promised stability and strong government.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Stresemann’s policies for the Weimar Republic in the years 1923–1929.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description of what Stresemann did.
Developing: Some assessment of importance with limited analysis.
Secure: Explains significance at the time AND over time, using evidence.
Mastering: Weighs immediate recovery against the underlying fragility; argues how far Stresemann’s achievements masked structural weaknesses.
Content to use: Stresemann ended passive resistance, introduced the Rentenmark, negotiated the Dawes Plan (1924) and Locarno Pact (1925), and secured League of Nations membership (1926). At the time these restored economic confidence and international respectability. Over time, however, the recovery rested on short-term US loans, meaning Germany’s prosperity was fragile and dependent on continued American investment — exposed when the Depression struck in 1929.

practice_questions.text:
'The Weimar Republic was doomed to fail from the start because of the Treaty of Versailles.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
In your answer, consider both reasons to agree and reasons to disagree, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Limited points, mostly descriptive, no overall judgement.
Developing: Some argument for and against, limited use of evidence, weak conclusion.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence for both sides, clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Sophisticated argument that weighs the relative importance of Versailles against other factors (structural flaws of the constitution, Depression, political miscalculations), reaches a substantiated conclusion.

Arguments to agree: War guilt caused immediate resentment; reparations destabilised the economy; the ‘November criminals’ myth delegitimised the republic; territorial losses fuelled nationalism.
Arguments to disagree: The republic survived Versailles and the crises of 1919–1923; Stresemann’s era (1924–1929) showed democracy could work; it was the contingent factor of the Depression combined with poor political decisions in 1930–1933 that actually destroyed the republic.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• The treaty created the Irish Free State as a self-governing dominion covering 26 southern counties.
• It allowed Northern Ireland (six counties) to opt out and remain part of the United Kingdom, which it promptly did.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the General Strike of 1926.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• The strike was called by the TUC in support of coal miners who faced pay cuts and longer hours.
• Around 1.75 million workers from key industries joined the strike.
• The strike lasted nine days in May 1926 before the TUC called it off.
• The government used emergency powers, volunteers and the military to keep essential supplies moving.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the General Strike of 1926.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. coal mine owners demanding pay cuts and longer hours) and explains the mechanism in detail — showing how economic decline in the coal industry after post-war boom ended, combined with owners refusing to subsidise wages, forced the miners to resist and the TUC to act in solidarity. Reaches a developed explanation of the causal chain.
Secure: Names the cause and offers a clear explanation with some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference to the cause without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the defeat of the General Strike of 1926.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. weakening of the trade union movement) and develops a detailed chain of consequences — miners forced to accept pay cuts, trade union membership fell, the 1927 Trade Disputes Act further restricted union power, and working-class confidence in industrial action declined.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation of a consequence with some development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Representation of the People Act 1918 for women in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains significance at the time (gave approximately 8.4 million women over 30 the vote for the first time, recognising their wartime contributions) AND over time (paved the way for the Equal Franchise Act 1928 giving all women over 21 the vote; represented a fundamental shift in who counted as a political citizen). Weighs the limits of the Act (property qualification, age restriction) against its long-term importance.
Secure: Addresses significance at the time and over time with clear explanation.
Developing: Addresses significance at the time only, or over time only, with some explanation.
Emerging: Simple descriptive points about the Act with no real analysis of significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The most important challenge facing Britain in the 1920s was economic instability.' How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing economic instability alongside other key challenges (Ireland, industrial relations, women's rights). Weighs the relative importance of factors with clear evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement that goes beyond simply listing both sides.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on two or more challenges. Some weighing of factors. Structured overall judgement.
Developing: Some relevant evidence on the challenges but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account of events without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Stalin's role as General Secretary of the Communist Party.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: Stalin used the role to control party appointments and promotions, placing loyal supporters throughout the party organisation. Any one valid feature clearly described scores 2 marks; a feature without description scores 1 mark.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Stalin's defeat of Trotsky between 1924 and 1927.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: Stalin allied with Zinoviev and Kamenev to isolate Trotsky in 1924–25; Trotsky's doctrine of Permanent Revolution was attacked as reckless; Trotsky was stripped of his role as War Commissar in January 1925; by 1927 Trotsky was expelled from the party and by 1929 exiled from the USSR.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed, or one developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Stalin's rise to power by 1929.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates should identify a cause and explain why it led to Stalin's consolidation of power. Strong answers will show causal reasoning, not just description.

Possible causes: Stalin's control of the General Secretaryship; suppression of Lenin's Testament; the Lenin Enrolment; Stalin's Socialism in One Country policy; the divisions among his rivals.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise cause identified, causal chain clearly explained, supported with specific knowledge.
Secure: cause identified and explained with relevant knowledge.
Developing: cause identified but explanation is descriptive rather than causal.
Emerging: simple point with no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Lenin's Testament for the leadership struggle after 1924.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: the Testament warned against Stalin but the Central Committee voted to suppress it, removing the most credible institutional check on his power. Over time: by remaining in post as General Secretary, Stalin was able to build the machine that defeated all rivals.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance explained at two points or in two ways, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point, partial knowledge.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of Stalin's rise to power:

“Stalin won the leadership struggle primarily because his rivals underestimated him and made political mistakes.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge of Soviet history between 1924 and 1929 in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: Trotsky dismissed the Secretaryship as 'administrative'; he failed to attend Lenin's funeral (Stalin told him the wrong date according to some accounts); Zinoviev and Kamenev helped Stalin destroy Trotsky then tried to form a belated opposition when it was too late; rivals failed to unite until 1926, by which point Stalin had packed party congresses.

Disagreement: Stalin's own actions were decisive — he built a genuine power base through the Secretaryship; his Socialism in One Country doctrine appealed ideologically; the Lenin Enrolment brought in new members whose loyalty he cultivated; he was a skilled political operator, not merely a beneficiary of others' errors.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence for both sides, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered with relevant evidence, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement with interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Was Stalin's control of the party machine the most important reason for his rise to power by 1929? Use your knowledge of Soviet history in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires substantiated overall judgement, not just both sides listed.

For the argument: the General Secretaryship gave Stalin control over appointments across the entire party; he could promote loyalists and marginalise opponents; the Lenin Enrolment expanded membership under his watch.

Alternative factors: rivals' ideological divisions and tactical errors; Stalin's Socialism in One Country ideology appealing to party members; suppression of Lenin's Testament removing an institutional check; Stalin's personal political skill in allying with different factions.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing multiple factors, clear overall judgement with supporting evidence.
Secure: two or more factors explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: factors listed or described, limited weighing.
Emerging: one factor or descriptive throughout.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of medieval beliefs about the causes of disease.
practice_questions.marks: One feature, supported with accurate detail. Example: People believed disease was caused by miasma (bad air), thought to rise from rotting matter and sewage. This led them to burn herbs or light fires to purify the air. [2 marks: 1 for identifying a feature, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of industrialisation on disease in nineteenth-century Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: Rapid urbanisation created overcrowded slums with contaminated water supplies, enabling diseases like cholera and typhoid to spread quickly. Feature 2: Poor sewage disposal in industrial towns meant waste polluted rivers and drinking water, leading to multiple cholera epidemics (1831, 1848, 1853). [2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the persistence of the miasma theory in Britain into the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: Clear identification of a cause (e.g. lack of microscopes / no awareness of microorganisms) with sustained explanation of why this allowed miasma to go unchallenged. Developing: A cause is identified but explanation is limited. Emerging: A simple statement about miasma without explanation of why it persisted. [6 marks — Mastering: sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and clear link to change; Secure: clear cause with relevant evidence; Developing: some explanation, limited evidence; Emerging: simple points, little evidence]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of germ theory for understanding disease in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (overturned miasma, gave basis for targeted treatments, enabled public health reform) AND over time (antibiotics, vaccines, modern epidemiology). Secure: Significance at the time covered with relevant evidence; some reference to longer-term impact. Developing: One aspect of significance with limited evidence. Emerging: Simple statement about Pasteur or Koch without analysis. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Miasma theory was the most important reason why disease was difficult to control in Britain before 1900.'
How far do you agree with this statement? Use your knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument evaluating miasma alongside other factors (poverty, lack of government action, rapid urbanisation, religious beliefs) with a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Both sides addressed with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion. Developing: Some discussion of miasma and one other factor, limited judgement. Emerging: Description of miasma only, no weighing of factors. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How has the understanding of the causes of disease changed between the medieval period and the present day? Use evidence across all three eras to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change across all three eras (medieval: miasma/humours/God; early modern: miasma persists through 1665; modern: germ theory to virology), weighs change against continuity, reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: All three eras covered with evidence, clear line of argument. Developing: Two eras covered; limited weighing of change vs continuity. Emerging: Single-era narrative, no comparative judgement. [16 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: On questions asking you to explain a cause or consequence, be specific about the time period — the examiner wants to see you distinguish between medieval, early modern and modern explanations. Don’t just say ‘people believed in miasma’: say when, give an example of how it shaped behaviour (such as the beaked masks in 1665), and explain why this view persisted. For 8-mark ‘Explain Change’ questions, you must show the change over time and link it to a factor such as science, technology or government action.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Treaty of Versailles that affected Germany's military strength.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific military clause (e.g. army limited to 100,000 men) AND adds precise detail (no tanks, no aircraft, navy stripped). Secure: identifies a military clause with some supporting detail. Developing: names a clause without detail. Emerging: vague reference to military restrictions.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Weimar Constitution that made it difficult to govern Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each developed with precise detail — e.g. proportional representation led to coalition governments that were frequently unstable (20 cabinets 1919–1933); Article 48 allowed presidential rule by emergency decree, used 136 times 1930–1932, undermining parliament. Secure (3): two features with some development. Developing (2): two features briefly identified. Emerging (1): one feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Spartacist Rising of January 1919.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): identifies a clear cause (e.g. revolutionary socialism inspired by the Bolshevik revolution of 1917; workers' suffering under wartime conditions; anger at the new SPD government's moderate policies) AND develops it with specific supporting detail AND shows how it led directly to the uprising. Secure (3–4): clear cause with development but limited linkage to consequence. Developing (2): cause identified with brief explanation. Emerging (1): simple, undeveloped point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Kapp Putsch for the Weimar Republic.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): identifies a precise consequence (e.g. the putsch revealed the army's disloyalty — it refused to fire on the Freikorps; the republic was saved by trade-union general strike, not its own forces; this exposed the weakness of Weimar's security apparatus) AND develops the consequence with specific evidence AND shows further effects. Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): consequence identified with limited explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention of consequences.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 'stab-in-the-back' myth for the development of German politics in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): addresses significance at the time (immediate political impact — delegitimising the republic, fuelling right-wing violence, targeting democratic politicians) AND over time (Hitler's use of the myth to justify overthrowing Weimar in the 1930s) with specific evidence throughout. Secure (5–6): significance addressed with development; may focus more on one time period. Developing (3–4): some analysis of significance but limited to description or one time period. Emerging (1–2): simple points about the myth without analytical development.

practice_questions.text: 'The Treaty of Versailles was the main reason why the Weimar Republic faced serious problems in its early years.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): sustained argument agreeing AND disagreeing — agrees: Versailles created economic hardship, war-guilt resentment, stab-in-the-back myth, right-wing anger; disagrees: structural weaknesses (proportional representation, Article 48), political extremism (Spartacists, Freikorps), economic disruption pre-dated Versailles. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both perspectives developed with evidence; judgement present. Developing (4–6): one side developed more than the other; limited overall judgement. Emerging (1–3): descriptive with little analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Cluniac reform movement.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students may describe: Cluny was founded in 910 and placed directly under papal authority (bypassing local lords); it followed the Rule of Saint Benedict strictly; its network spread to hundreds of monasteries across Europe; it targeted simony and clerical marriage. 1 mark for a simple identification; 2 marks for a developed description with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Investiture Contest.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should identify two features with supporting detail.
Feature 1: The Investiture Contest was a power struggle over who had the right to appoint bishops and abbots — kings argued they needed loyal clerics to govern; popes argued only Rome could confer spiritual office.
Feature 2: Pope Gregory VII excommunicated Henry IV in 1076, and Henry was forced to walk barefoot to Canossa in 1077 to beg for the excommunication to be lifted.
2 marks per feature: 1 mark for a simple point, 2 marks for a developed point with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growing importance of the papacy in the eleventh century.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (e.g. Cluniac reform, conflict with emperors, control of pilgrimage) and explains it with precise detail and links the cause to the outcome (increased papal authority). Sustains a clear line of reasoning throughout.
Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with some detail; some link to the outcome.
Developing: Identifies a cause but explanation is brief or not fully developed.
Emerging: Simple statement of a cause with little or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Walk to Canossa (1077) for the power of the medieval papacy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains significance both at the time (Henry IV humiliated, excommunication shown to be a real political weapon, papal authority over emperors demonstrated) and over time (set precedent for papal supremacy, influenced later relations between Church and state, shaped the ideological context for the Crusades). Sustains a clear judgement throughout.
Secure: Covers significance at the time and over time with some evidence; clear explanation.
Developing: Covers significance mainly at the time or in one dimension; limited detail.
Emerging: Simple description of the event; little sense of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Cluniac reform movement for the relationship between the papacy and secular rulers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific consequence (e.g. papacy gained independent clergy loyal to Rome rather than local lords; simony reduced, reducing royal control of Church appointments; Cluniac monks became papal advisors undermining royal influence) and explains it with precise detail. Sustains a clear line of reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a consequence and explains it with some detail.
Developing: Identifies a consequence but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: 'Pilgrimage was the most important reason why the medieval papacy gained power in the eleventh century.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues both in support of and against the interpretation using own knowledge. Support: Jerusalem pilgrimage gave the papacy emotional authority; controlling access to sacred sites was a source of spiritual power. Against: Cluniac reform was more structurally significant (built papal network across Europe); the Investiture Contest demonstrated coercive power over rulers. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Argues for and against with relevant evidence; reaches a conclusion.
Developing: Mainly one-sided argument; limited evidence.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement with little justification.

before.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about why the Crusades happened, examiners want you to connect the power of the papacy to the call for crusade. Don’t just describe Cluniac reform in isolation — explain how it strengthened papal authority, which then made Urban II’s appeal possible. For 8-mark significance questions, remember to address significance at the time (e.g. Canossa immediately weakened Henry IV) and over time (e.g. papal supremacy shaped European politics for centuries).

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Hoovervilles that appeared across the USA during the Great Depression.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names the feature (makeshift shanty towns housing homeless/unemployed Americans) AND explains one specific aspect (e.g. built from scrap materials; named sarcastically after Hoover; located on the outskirts of cities). Developing: Identifies the feature without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Roosevelt's 'Hundred Days' legislation in 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Mastering: Two fully developed features, e.g. (1) It was a period of intense legislative activity March-June 1933 in which Congress passed a large number of emergency measures; (2) It produced key agencies such as the CCC and NRA designed to bring immediate relief and economic recovery. Developing: Identifies features without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Hoover's defeat in the 1932 presidential election.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. Hoover's refusal to provide direct federal relief; his handling of the Bonus Army; his belief in rugged individualism) AND explains how this cause led to electoral defeat through a developed chain of reasoning, linking public perception to the scale of unemployment and homelessness. Secure: Cause identified with some development. Developing: Simple cause stated without explanation. Emerging: Vague or asserted response.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Social Security Act of 1935.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. creation of a federal unemployment insurance scheme; introduction of old-age pensions) AND explains how this changed the relationship between citizens and the federal government, with a developed chain of reasoning. Secure: Consequence identified with some development. Developing: Simple consequence without explanation. Emerging: Vague response.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) for the development of the USA in the 1930s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (jobs created, rural electrification, flood control across seven states) AND over time (model for federal intervention in the economy; lasting infrastructure; transformation of the South's economy). Secure: Addresses significance at the time with limited coverage of longer-term impact. Developing: Describes the TVA without analysing significance. Emerging: Vague or narrative only.

practice_questions.text: 'The New Deal successfully ended the Great Depression.' How far do you agree with this view? Use your knowledge of the period 1929-1939 to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs evidence on both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Should consider: evidence FOR (unemployment fell from ~25% to ~15% by 1937; alphabet agencies provided relief and infrastructure; Social Security Act created safety net) AGAINST (full recovery only came with wartime production 1941-42; 1937-38 recession when Roosevelt cut spending; Supreme Court struck down key agencies; African Americans largely excluded from benefits). Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument, evidence limited to one side. Emerging: Narrative description without argument.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Privy Council in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Candidates may describe: the Privy Council comprised around nineteen members including nobles, lawyers and churchmen; it met several times a week; it could issue proclamations and direct local officials; William Cecil was its most influential figure. Mastering: a precise feature with supporting detail (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature without specific detail (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of Justices of the Peace in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: a precise feature with accurate supporting detail (2 marks). Emerging: a simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: JPs were unpaid local gentry appointed by the Crown; they enforced the law at quarter sessions; they collected taxes; they oversaw poor relief; they enforced royal proclamations in the counties; approximately 50–60 JPs served in each county by the end of the reign. Maximum 4 marks (2 marks per feature).

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of tensions between Elizabeth I and Parliament.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a detailed causal chain linking evidence to outcome, e.g. Elizabeth restricted parliamentary free speech because she considered her marriage, succession and religion to be royal prerogatives — this led to confrontations such as Peter Wentworth's imprisonment in 1576 when he pressed for unrestricted debate. Secure: a clear cause with some supporting evidence. Developing: a relevant cause with limited development. Emerging: a simple statement with minimal support. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of William Cecil to the government of Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (almost forty years of loyal service, managing foreign policy, intelligence networks, and the succession question) AND over time (securing Protestant England's survival as a stable state). Secure: clear explanation of significance with specific examples. Developing: some explanation with limited range of evidence. Emerging: simple descriptive points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a portrait of Elizabeth I at her coronation in 1559 for understanding how she projected royal authority in the early years of her reign? Use the source and your own knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (what the source shows), provenance (a formal royal commission, designed to project power) and contextual knowledge (Elizabeth used imagery deliberately — crowns, orbs, ermine — to emphasise legitimacy) to make a substantiated judgement about utility and limitations. Secure: addresses two of the three elements. Developing: mainly describes source content. Emerging: simple comment on one element. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'Elizabeth I was successful in governing England in the years 1558–1603 because of the effectiveness of the Privy Council.' How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your own knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: agrees with evidence (Cecil's management of plots and foreign policy; the Council's role in proclamations and administration) AND disagrees with evidence (Elizabeth's personal skill in court management and patronage; the JP system; Parliament's role in taxation) before reaching a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: both sides covered with some supporting detail; clear conclusion. Developing: one-sided or limited evidence. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement. Maximum 12 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of medieval village sport.
practice_questions.marks: One feature clearly described, such as: games were played on feast days / games tested physical strength or endurance / football was violent with few rules and could involve whole communities / wrestling and stone-lifting were common [2 marks: 1 for identifying a feature, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of jousting tournaments in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks: Two features, each developed: e.g. two armoured knights charged on horseback with lances trying to unhorse each other (feature + detail); tournaments trained knights for real combat and allowed nobles to display martial skill and seek prize money (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identifying, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Crown tried to restrict popular sports such as football in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A precisely developed explanation linking village sport to military readiness, with named evidence (e.g. Edward III’s 1363 proclamation banning ‘useless sports’) and an explanation of why men were needed for archery. Secure: A clear explanation with some supporting detail about archery or the Crown’s military concerns. Developing: A simple reason given with limited development. Emerging: A basic point with little support. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Forest Laws introduced by the Norman kings after 1066.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation of how Forest Laws created exclusive royal hunting grounds, criminalised poaching and reinforced social inequality in leisure, with evidence. Secure: Clear consequence explained with some supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence with limited development. Emerging: Basic point, little support. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was social class in shaping sport and leisure in medieval and early modern England? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analysis of how class shaped both access and purpose of sport at the time AND over time (e.g. class divisions in sport persisted into the nineteenth century). Uses specific evidence from at least two social groups across the period. Secure: Clear analysis of class significance with relevant examples. Developing: Some points about class with limited use of evidence. Emerging: Simple statement that class mattered, little support. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The main purpose of upper-class sport in medieval and early modern England was to display social status.' How far do you agree with this view? Explain your answer, considering sport from across the period c.500 to c.1800.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates the statement across medieval, early modern and early industrial eras. Agrees with evidence (jousting, falconry, real tennis as status displays) but challenges it (tournaments also trained for war; hunting provided food; real tennis was also genuine recreation). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Addresses the statement with evidence from at least two eras, some weighing of agreement vs disagreement. Developing: Some argument with limited range of evidence. Emerging: Simple agree/disagree with little support. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Saxon shield wall as a battle tactic.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks. Students should identify a feature and support it:
• The shield wall involved warriors locking their shields together to form a continuous defensive line [1], making it very difficult for attacking infantry or cavalry to break through without disrupting the formation [1].
• Professional huscarls formed the core of the shield wall, providing the discipline needed to hold the formation [1+1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the New Model Army created in 1645.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail):
• Feature 1: It was a professional, paid standing army [1], unlike the feudal levies that preceded it, which ensured consistent training and discipline [1].
• Feature 2: It had a clear command structure and uniform regimental system [1], which allowed coordinated manoeuvres and contributed to decisive victories at Naseby and Langport in 1645 [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Battle of Hastings (1066) was significant for the development of medieval tactics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains the significance in depth — the Norman use of combined arms (archers, infantry, cavalry) and the feigned retreat broke the Saxon shield wall and demonstrated the vulnerability of infantry-only formations to disciplined cavalry. Analyses the longer-term consequence: Norman cavalry dominance replaced Saxon infantry as the core of English armies.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant supporting evidence.
Developing: Identifies significance with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement with little evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the change in English tactics between c.1000 and c.1500.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces change from Saxon shield wall → Norman cavalry → longbow tactics (Crécy 1346, Agincourt 1415). Explains the reasons for each shift and weighs which was most significant. Reaches a substantiated conclusion.
Secure: Covers at least two tactical changes with relevant evidence and an explanation of cause.
Developing: Describes changes but analysis is limited.
Emerging: Simple description of one tactic; no analysis of change.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the longbow in changing English tactics in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries? Use specific evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues significance at the time (Crécy 1346, Poitiers 1356, Agincourt 1415 — all decisive English victories against larger forces) and over time (established the principle that missile power and discipline can defeat armoured shock troops; influenced subsequent firearms development). Concludes on degree of significance.
Secure: Explains significance with battle evidence and some analysis.
Developing: Identifies battles but analysis is thin.
Emerging: Describes the longbow without evaluating its significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did tactics change in Britain between c.500 and the mid nineteenth century? In your answer, cover at least two eras.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces change across medieval (shield wall → cavalry → longbow) and early modern (firearms → linear tactics → New Model Army) eras. Identifies continuity (discipline as constant; combined arms as recurring theme). Weighs change against continuity and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on how far and why tactics changed.
Secure: Covers both eras with evidence, some analysis of change/continuity, and a conclusion.
Developing: Covers one era well; limited analysis.
Emerging: Describes events without analysing change.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of vagrancy as a crime in Tudor England.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Students should note that vagrancy was the offence of wandering homeless without work or support, created by Tudor legislation responding to enclosure and population growth. The Vagabonds Act 1531 authorised whipping; repeat offenders faced branding or mutilation. Simple identification (1 mark); developed with legislation or consequence (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the witch trials in England during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: The Witchcraft Act of 1563, passed under Elizabeth I, transferred witchcraft from church courts to secular law and imposed the death penalty where the victim died — though not all witchcraft became a capital offence. Feature 2: Matthew Hopkins operated as Witchfinder General in East Anglia during the 1640s, using coercive methods to extract confessions and responsible for over 100 executions. Other valid features: trials targeted poor, elderly women; accusations arose from local disputes; Civil War chaos enabled persecution.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why heresy became such a serious crime in Tudor England.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States heresy was a religious offence. Developing: Notes the Reformation changed which beliefs were criminal. Secure: Explains how the Reformation politicised religious belief — denying royal supremacy or practising the wrong faith became threats to state authority; uses the example of Mary I burning 287 Protestants. Mastering: Sustains analysis of how heresy law served as political control, linking the Treason Act of 1534 (making verbal denial of royal supremacy treasonous) to the broader pattern of the Tudor state using crime definitions to police loyalty and belief.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the wergild system in Anglo-Saxon England.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Describes wergild as a payment for crimes. Developing: Explains that payments depended on the victim's rank. Secure: Analyses how wergild embedded social hierarchy into justice — a nobleman's life was valued more than a peasant's, and wealth could effectively buy immunity from criminal liability. Mastering: Evaluates significance at the time (it reduced blood feuds; it reflected a community-based rather than state-based justice system) and over time (it represented a continuity of wealth-based justice that persisted in various forms; its absence marks a genuine shift when the Norman state began to assert royal courts over local custom).

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that the nature of crime changed significantly between the medieval era and the seventeenth century?
Give reasons for your answer. Refer to specific examples in your response.
practice_questions.marks: For change: heresy and treason became major new crimes after the Reformation; the Witchcraft Act 1563 criminalised a new category; vagrancy legislation made poverty itself criminal. Against (continuity): petty theft remained the most common offence throughout; assault and violence persisted; the underlying driver of poverty did not change. Emerging: Simple list of changes. Developing: Notes change and continuity without sustained argument. Secure: Argues a position, uses specific evidence from both eras. Mastering: Evaluates the degree of change, weighing new categories (politically-driven crime: heresy, treason, witchcraft) against continuity (poverty-driven petty crime), and reaches a justified conclusion about how significant the change was.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of treason as a crime in Tudor England.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: The Treason Act of 1534 dramatically expanded the definition to include verbal denial of royal supremacy, not just physical acts against the king. Feature 2: High-profile cases such as Sir Thomas More (executed 1535) showed that treason could be used against respected individuals who merely refused to swear loyalty to new religious settlements. Other valid features: execution was the standard punishment; treason charges could be politically motivated; it was used to silence opposition.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of medieval attempts to prevent the spread of plague.
practice_questions.marks: One feature supported with accurate detail. Example: Towns quarantined infected houses, sealing them shut to stop plague victims moving around and spreading disease to others. [2 marks: 1 for identifying a feature, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Edward Jenner's work on vaccination.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: Jenner vaccinated James Phipps in 1796 using cowpox matter, demonstrating that exposure to cowpox could protect against the more dangerous smallpox. Feature 2: Jenner published his findings in 1798, and his work eventually led to compulsory smallpox vaccination for infants in Britain by 1853. [2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why it took time for Jenner's vaccination to become widely accepted in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation with multiple linked reasons (medical scepticism, religious objections, satirical/cultural opposition) demonstrating why acceptance was slow. Secure: A clear reason with relevant explanation and evidence. Developing: A reason identified but explanation limited. Emerging: Simple statement that people were against it, no explanation. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of inoculation and vaccination in the prevention of disease in Britain between 1700 and 1900.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (reducing smallpox deaths, replacing dangerous inoculation, enabling compulsory vaccination 1853) AND over time (foundation of all modern immunisation programmes, eradication of smallpox 1980). Secure: Significance at the time with evidence; some longer-term reference. Developing: One aspect of significance with limited evidence. Emerging: Basic description without significance analysis. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The work of Edward Jenner was the most important turning point in the prevention of disease in Britain.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
