practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees with evidence (safer than inoculation, led to compulsory vaccination, smallpox eradication) AND disagrees by weighing other turning points (germ theory enabling vaccines for other diseases; antibody discovery; public health legislation). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Both sides addressed with evidence, clear conclusion. Developing: One-sided argument with some evidence. Emerging: Descriptive with no evaluation. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How did the approach to preventing disease change between c.1350 and c.1900? Use evidence from across the period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change across all three eras (medieval: miasma/prayer/flagellants; early modern: inoculation introduced c.1721; modern: Jenner's vaccination 1796, compulsory vaccination 1853, antibody discovery 1890), weighs change against continuity (quarantine throughout all periods), reaches substantiated judgement. Secure: All three eras covered with evidence. Developing: Two eras, limited weighing. Emerging: Single era, descriptive only. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Harold Macmillan's government's approach to improving living standards in the 1950s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Wage rises and tax cuts (e.g. 1955 and 1959 budgets) put more money in people's pockets, contributing to a consumer boom.
- Motorway investment (Preston bypass 1958; M1 opened November 1959) modernised transport infrastructure.
- House-building programme continued: new towns and council housing expanded.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Beeching cuts of 1963.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple cause identified, limited explanation.
Secure: Clear cause explained with factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation with precise evidence, showing the chain of reasoning from cause to decision.

Causes may include:
- Many rural branch lines were loss-making; the report showed that the railways as a whole were running a deficit; closing unprofitable lines was seen as economically necessary.
- Growing car ownership (doubled 1955-1965) meant fewer passengers on rural lines, reducing revenue further.
- Government policy favoured road investment over rail; the motorway programme signalled a belief that the future lay in road transport.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the introduction of comprehensive schools in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple consequence, limited development.
Secure: Clear consequence with explanation and specific evidence.
Mastering: Detailed consequence, precise evidence, wider significance addressed.

Consequences may include:
- Removal of the eleven-plus in many areas ended early selection, giving all children access to the same school; supporters argued this improved equality of opportunity.
- Some grammar schools closed, removing a path for academically able children from working-class backgrounds; critics argued standards fell.
- By the late 1970s the majority of secondary pupils attended comprehensives, fundamentally reshaping British education.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was Harold Wilson's 'white heat of technology' vision for changing Britain in the 1960s? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence.
Developing: Some significance explained, basic evidence used.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time addressed, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of significance at the time and over time, precise evidence, sustained argument.

At the time: created new Ministry of Technology; promoted university expansion (Robbins Report 1963 recommended expanding higher education places from approximately 216,000 to 558,000 by 1980/81); Wilson won 1964 and 1966 elections partly on modernisation appeal.
Over time: raised expectations about technology-driven growth that were not always met; university expansion created a larger graduate class that shaped later political and cultural life.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Rising living standards in the 1950s benefited all sections of British society equally.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple one-sided response, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation, addresses limited range of evidence.
Secure: Clear evaluation, both agreement and disagreement, factual knowledge used.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation, precise evidence, sustained weighing of factors, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: real wages rose for most workers; consumer goods became widely affordable through hire purchase; unemployment under 2%; housing improved.

Disagreement: prosperity was regionally uneven — older industrial areas in the North, Wales, and Scotland saw little improvement; hire purchase created debt problems for some; women's economic position remained limited; immigrant communities faced discrimination.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the motorway construction programme in Britain in the late 1950s and early 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Britain's first motorway, the Preston bypass, opened in December 1958; the M1 connecting London to the Midlands followed in November 1959.
- The programme reflected the rapid growth of car ownership (which doubled between 1955 and 1965) and represented confidence in a motoring future.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of David Lloyd George's People's Budget of 1909.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: The budget introduced a new super-tax on high incomes (1), targeting wealthy landowners and top earners to pay for welfare reforms and naval rearmament (1). Mastering: accurate feature with supporting detail. Developing: feature stated but undeveloped.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Parliament Act of 1911.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature examples: Lords could not block money bills; Lords could only delay other legislation by two years; maximum term of a parliament reduced to five years. Mastering: two precise features with accurate supporting detail. Developing: features without adequate development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the House of Lords rejected the People's Budget in 1909.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Developed explanation with accurate contextual knowledge. E.g. the budget proposed land-value taxes that would directly hit aristocratic landowners who dominated the Lords; Lloyd George's provocative language framing the budget as a class war inflamed opposition; Conservative peers saw the budget as an attack on the propertied classes and felt justified in using their blocking power. Secure (3–4): clear cause with some development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Taff Vale case of 1901 for the Labour Party.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Consequence developed with supporting knowledge. The ruling that unions could be sued for strike losses threatened union funds; this pushed trade unions to fund independent Labour candidates in 1906 to obtain parliamentary protection; the Liberal government responded with the Trade Disputes Act 1906 restoring union immunity, but the episode had cemented the union–Labour alliance. Secure (3–4): clear consequence with some development. Developing (1–2): simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Parliament Act 1911 for British democracy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): Significance at the time AND over time. At the time: removed Lords’ absolute veto, enabling Liberal welfare and constitutional reforms to pass; established elected Commons’ supremacy. Over time: set the precedent for later Lords reform (1949 Parliament Act); made the Lords a revising rather than blocking chamber; foundation of modern constitutional balance. Secure (5–6): both dimensions, some development of each. Developing (3–4): one dimension only. Emerging (1–2): simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'The Lords crisis of 1909–1911 was caused mainly by Lloyd George's confrontational style.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Agrees and disagrees, substantiated, reaches an overall judgement. Agree: Lloyd George’s rhetoric, 'fully equipped duke' speeches, land taxes directly targeting Lords’ wealth provoked an avoidable confrontation. Disagree: structural causes were deeper — Lords had blocked Liberal bills before 1909; the Conservatives lost two elections and still used the Lords to obstruct; the constitutional convention barring Lords from blocking money bills already existed. Own-knowledge synthesis: Asquith’s plan to flood Lords with new peers was the mechanism that resolved it. Secure (7–9): reasoned argument both ways. Developing (4–6): limited development. Emerging (1–3): one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the wartime economy in the USA after 1941.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names a feature (e.g. rapid conversion of factories to war production) AND develops it (e.g. car plants began making tanks and aircraft; by 1944 the USA produced more war material than all Axis powers combined). Developing: Identifies feature without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of American suburban life in the 1950s.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) Mass-produced housing communities like Levittown made home ownership affordable for veterans using GI Bill mortgages; (2) Consumer goods such as televisions and cars became widespread, with TV ownership rising from 9% to nearly 90% of homes in the decade. Developing: Identifies features without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growth of American suburbs in the 1950s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (GI Bill mortgages; Levittown-style mass building; car ownership enabling commuting; wartime savings) AND explains through a developed chain of reasoning how this cause led to suburban expansion. Secure: Cause with some development. Developing: Simple statement. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Michael Harrington publishing The Other America in 1962.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (influenced Kennedy and then Johnson's War on Poverty; drew public attention to hidden poverty; challenged the myth that 1950s prosperity was universal) AND explains the chain of effects with development. Secure: Consequence identified with some development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the GI Bill (1944) for the development of post-war America.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (enabled veterans to buy homes, attend college, start businesses; fuelled suburban growth; created better-educated workforce) AND over time (reinforced racial inequalities as Black veterans were largely excluded; shaped American middle-class identity; contributed to 1950s prosperity). Secure: One time frame covered. Developing: Describes the GI Bill without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: 'The post-war economic boom of the 1950s benefited all Americans equally.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge of the period 1944-1965.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing evidence for and against with a substantiated judgement. FOR: GDP growth; TV/car ownership rising; suburban expansion; GI Bill opportunities. AGAINST: GI Bill discriminatory in practice; Levittown initially refused Black residents; Harrington's 40-50 million in poverty; Appalachian poor; elderly on fixed incomes; African Americans excluded from union jobs. Overall judgement must be argued, not listed. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Limited evidence, one-sided. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the growth of spectator sport in Victorian Britain.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with supporting detail, such as: railway travel allowed fans to attend away fixtures / enclosed grounds allowed clubs to charge admission / the FA Cup (1872) attracted growing crowds / the Saturday half-holiday gave workers free time for sport. [2 marks: 1 for feature, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Football League, founded in 1888.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. it provided regular competitive fixtures between twelve founding clubs (feature + detail); it supported the growth of enclosed grounds and admission charges, creating a commercial basis for professional football (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why professional football was legalised in 1885.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking covert payments in the north, northern clubs’ threat to break away, and the FA’s decision to legalise rather than lose those clubs, with evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with supporting detail about class or geography. Developing: Simple reason with limited development. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the formation of the Premier League and the 1992 Sky Sports deal for English football.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed consequence (e.g. massive wage inflation, influx of overseas players, football becoming a global brand) linked to the specific financial scale of the deal (£304 million). Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was the class divide in shaping the development of sport in Britain between 1860 and 1995?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses class significance at the time (professionalism debate, rugby split) AND over time (amateur ideal persisted until 1995 in rugby union, still shapes access to sport). Secure: Clear analysis with evidence from at least two sports. Developing: Some points about class, limited evidence. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The growth of television and sponsorship was the most important factor in the development of spectator sport in Britain after 1950.' How far do you agree? Use evidence from across the modern period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substantiated judgement weighing TV/sponsorship against other factors (rising wages, leisure time, transport, health consciousness). Traces change across the modern period with specific evidence. Challenges the claim by noting that earlier forces (codification, railways, Saturday half-holiday) built the foundations. Secure: Addresses both sides with relevant evidence, some overall judgement. Developing: Some argument, limited range. Emerging: Simple agree/disagree. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Moscow show trials of 1936–1938.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: defendants confessed to fabricated crimes such as plotting against Stalin or sabotaging industry; confessions were extracted through coercion by the NKVD; prominent Old Bolsheviks such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin were tried and executed.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the gulag system under Stalin.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: a vast network of forced labour camps across Siberia and the Far North; prisoners carried out dangerous work such as mining and logging in extreme cold; the gulag population numbered over a million by the late 1930s; conditions were deliberately harsh with minimal food and clothing.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed, or one developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the purge of the Red Army between 1937 and 1938.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates should identify a consequence and explain why it followed from the purge. Strong answers trace causal chains. Top response: the purge removed the most experienced senior commanders, leaving the Red Army without effective leadership; when Germany invaded in June 1941, the USSR suffered catastrophic early defeats that might have been avoided with a more experienced officer corps.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise consequence identified, causal chain explained, supported with specific knowledge.
Secure: consequence identified and explained with relevant knowledge.
Developing: consequence identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point with no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the murder of Kirov in 1934 for the development of Stalinist terror.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: Stalin immediately passed emergency laws allowing executions without full trial and used the assassination to justify mass arrests in Leningrad. Over time: the Kirov murder was the trigger for the Great Terror of 1936–38, which killed hundreds of thousands and fundamentally reshaped Soviet political culture through fear.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways or at two time points, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point, partial knowledge.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of the Great Terror:

“The Great Terror was caused primarily by Stalin’s personal paranoia rather than any genuine threat to his regime.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge of Soviet history in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree, then reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: the confessions were fabricated; the accused including Bukharin had shown loyalty to the party; the show trials targeted people who posed no realistic threat; Yezhov himself was purged in 1938 suggesting the terror had a self-perpetuating logic fed by Stalin's suspicion.

Disagreement: the USSR faced genuine external threats from Nazi Germany and Japan; there was a history of internal factional opposition from Left and Right; fear of a 'fifth column' had some historical basis in the Civil War era; some historians argue Stalin had rational political goals including eliminating potential rivals and creating a compliant population.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence for both sides, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: Was the use of terror the most important way in which Stalin maintained control of the Soviet Union? Use your knowledge of Soviet history in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement.

For the argument: the show trials eliminated potential rivals; mass arrests created a culture of fear that prevented organised opposition; the NKVD surveilled the entire population; the gulag removed dissidents from society.

Alternative methods: propaganda and the Cult of Stalin built genuine loyalty; economic successes of the Five Year Plans gave Stalin legitimacy; censorship controlled information; the party structure rewarded loyalty.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing multiple methods, clear judgement with supporting evidence.
Secure: two or more methods explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: methods listed or described, limited weighing.
Emerging: one method or descriptive throughout.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Edward III's claim to the French throne.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: Edward III was the grandson of Philip IV of France through his mother Isabella [1], giving him what he claimed was the strongest dynastic right to the French throne when Charles IV died without a male heir in 1328 [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Auld Alliance between France and Scotland.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: The Auld Alliance was a long-standing treaty first formalised in 1295 [1] under which France and Scotland agreed to support each other against their shared enemy England [1]. Feature 2: The alliance created a two-front strategic threat for English kings [1] — whenever England attacked France, Scotland could raid northern England, forcing Edward III to divide his military resources [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the outbreak of the Hundred Years' War in 1337.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (dynastic rivalry over the French throne, the confiscation of Aquitaine, the Franco-Scottish alliance, or Philip VI's provocations) and explains it in depth with precise factual knowledge, showing how this cause connected to wider context. Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with relevant factual support. Developing: States a cause with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference to conflict without a specific cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Philip VI's confiscation of Aquitaine in 1337.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains a consequence in depth with factual support — e.g. Edward III formally declared himself king of France and launched military campaigns, triggering the war that would last until 1453. Secure: Explains a consequence with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Isabella of France to the causes of the Hundred Years' War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance both at the time (her bloodline gave Edward III his dynastic claim; her role in the deposition of Edward II shaped English politics) and in the longer term (the dynastic claim became a recurring justification for English military intervention in France throughout the war's duration). Accurate factual knowledge integrated throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes Isabella without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The most important cause of the Hundred Years' War was Edward III's desire to claim the French throne.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees using precise factual knowledge. Agrees: the dynastic claim gave the war its ideological justification; Edward formally adopted the title King of France in 1337; the claim shaped English war aims throughout. Disagrees: the confiscation of Aquitaine was the immediate trigger and arguably more important economically; the Auld Alliance forced England's hand strategically; Philip VI's aggression was equally provocative. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement weighing the relative importance of causes. Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence; judgement present but may lack full development. Developing: Describes causes without evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple response; no judgement reached.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: The Klan reached a peak membership of approximately 4-5 million in the mid-1920s [1], attracting members not only in the South but also across northern and mid-western states, targeting Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Jim Crow system in the southern United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature: one for the feature, one for supporting detail.
Feature 1: Jim Crow laws enforced racial segregation in public life — schools, transport, restaurants and hospitals were separated, legally justified by the Supreme Court's 1896 'separate but equal' ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson. [2]
Feature 2: Voting rights for Black Americans were suppressed through poll taxes, literacy tests and the threat of violence — lynching was used as a weapon of terror, with approximately 3,446 Black Americans lynched between 1882 and 1968 according to NAACP records. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Ku Klux Klan grew so rapidly in the early 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains a precise cause with specific factual support and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Valid cause with supporting evidence and a developed explanatory link.
Developing: Names a cause but explanation is brief or generic.
Emerging: Simple statement.
Valid causes: fear of immigration and urban change among white Protestants; economic competition from Black workers migrating north; the 1915 film 'The Birth of a Nation' romanticising the original Klan; nativist and anti-Catholic sentiment; weak law enforcement response to Klan violence.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Great Migration for African Americans in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces a consequence with precise evidence and clear analysis of how migration produced that outcome.
Secure: Valid consequence with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a consequence without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid consequences: creation of vibrant Black urban communities in Chicago, Detroit and New York; escape from Jim Crow segregation and lynching; basis for the Harlem Renaissance; increased political visibility of Black communities; continued discrimination in northern cities (housing, work).

practice_questions.text:
How significant was the 1925 Scopes Trial in revealing tensions within American society in the 1920s?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time and over time with precise evidence and sustained analysis.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Some explanation; may address only one dimension.
Emerging: Simple points without developed analysis.
At the time: broadcast on radio to millions, exposing fundamentalism to national ridicule; revealed a deep rural-urban, religious-secular divide; Bryan's embarrassment under cross-examination; Scopes convicted but fine later overturned.
Over time: fundamentalist political influence weakened nationally; demonstrated the tension between religious tradition and scientific modernity that persisted in American culture.

practice_questions.text:
'Marcus Garvey's UNIA was a more effective response to racism in the 1920s than the NAACP.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or lacks a clear judgement.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.
Agreement (Garvey more effective): attracted hundreds of thousands of followers quickly; promoted positive Black identity and economic self-sufficiency; gave African Americans pride and a vision for the future.
Disagreement (NAACP more effective): used legal channels to challenge discrimination; sustained campaign over decades; kept anti-lynching legislation in public debate; Garvey imprisoned 1925 and deported 1927, leaving UNIA weakened.
Judgement: NAACP had longer-lasting institutional impact; Garvey's movement collapsed with his imprisonment.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the 1492 Capitulations of Santa Fe.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (Columbus was promised the title Admiral of the Ocean Sea / governorship of discovered lands / a share of profits). Two marks for a developed explanation of its significance.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Columbus’s treatment of the Tainos during his governorship of Hispaniola.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• He imposed a gold tribute requiring every Taino adult to deliver a set quota of gold or cotton; those who failed had a hand cut off.
• He authorised enslaved Tainos to be shipped to Spain (later stopped by Ferdinand and Isabella).
• He established the encomienda system, granting Spanish settlers the right to Taino labour.
• His policies contributed to a catastrophic collapse in the Taino population.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the decline of the Taino population of Hispaniola after 1492.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and fully develops a cause with evidence — e.g. the gold tribute system created impossible quotas; terror, violence and overwork undermined Taino society; disease introduced by Europeans killed those with no prior immunity; links cause to specific evidence from Columbus’s governorship.
Secure: Identifies a cause with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Columbus’s first voyage (1492) for Spain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that Columbus’s return to Spain in March 1493 created a claim to a vast new territory, triggered a second much larger expedition (1493, seventeen ships, ~1,200 settlers), and began the process of Caribbean colonisation that would eventually deliver huge wealth to Spain — links to specific evidence and explains the chain of consequences.
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Columbus’s voyages for the Taino people.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (immediate violence, tribute, enslavement, forced labour) AND over time (collapse of Taino population within decades; encomienda system applied across the Americas; loss of culture, religion and way of life). Develops argument with specific evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with relevant evidence; may lack full over-time analysis.
Developing: Describes impacts without fully analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Columbus’s primary motive for the 1492 voyage was personal glory rather than service to Spain.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• Columbus negotiated aggressively for the title Admiral of the Ocean Sea, governorship and a share of profits — personal rewards, not national service.
• He continued to claim he had reached Asia even when evidence suggested otherwise — protecting his status.
• He resisted sharing credit and authority with others in the colony.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• Spain had a clear national interest in finding an alternative route to Asia after Portugal monopolised the African route.
• Ferdinand and Isabella framed the expedition in religious terms — spreading Christianity — and Columbus shared this stated motive.
• The economic rationale (spice trade, trade routes) was a national as well as personal driver.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive response without evaluating the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Means Test introduced in 1931.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• Officials visited homes to assess all sources of household income, including earnings of other family members.
• Families might be required to sell possessions before qualifying for benefit.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Jarrow Crusade of 1936.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• Approximately 200 unemployed men marched 300 miles from Jarrow to London to petition Parliament.
• The marchers were disciplined and non-violent, deliberately distancing themselves from communist-led marches.
• MP Ellen Wilkinson helped organise and lead the march.
• The government refused to receive the petition officially, and the Prime Minister declined to meet the marchers.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of mass unemployment in Britain in the early 1930s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. the Wall Street Crash 1929 triggering the global depression) and traces the mechanism in detail — American banking collapse reduced world trade, demand for British exports collapsed, staple industries already struggling with structural decline faced catastrophic falls in orders, triggering mass lay-offs concentrated in the north and Wales.
Secure: Names a clear cause and provides a linked explanation with some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference to economic difficulty without identifying a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the uneven economic recovery of the 1930s in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. internal migration from north to south, or deepening regional inequality) and develops a chain — new light industries grew in the Midlands/south, workers moved south for jobs, northern communities hollowed out, Special Areas Act 1934 failed to bridge the gap, creating a lasting north-south divide.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation of a consequence with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Jarrow Crusade for attitudes towards unemployment in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (drew national sympathy, highlighted human cost of depression and government indifference) AND over time (became a defining memory for the Labour movement, influenced arguments for a welfare state, referenced in later debates about regional inequality). Weighs limits — government did not act directly — against longer-term cultural significance.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions of significance with clear explanation.
Developing: Addresses one dimension only.
Emerging: Describes the march without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The Means Test was the most significant way in which the Depression affected ordinary British people in the 1930s.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges the Means Test's impact (humiliation, family division, poverty) alongside other significant effects (mass unemployment, regional blight, internal migration, impact on health and housing). Weighs factors with evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on the Means Test and other factors. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the hyperinflation of 1923 that affected ordinary German people.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific impact (e.g. savings wiped out, prices rising so fast workers were paid twice daily, pensioners unable to afford food) with supporting detail. Secure (1–2): identifies an impact with some development. Developing (1): vague reference to people suffering. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr in 1923.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise detail — e.g. France and Belgium sent troops in January 1923 to seize coal and steel as reparations payment in kind; German workers responded with government-backed passive resistance (general strike) that spread across the occupied zone. Secure (3): two features with some development. Developing (2): two features briefly stated. Emerging (1): one feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the hyperinflation crisis of 1923.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): identifies a clear cause (e.g. the government printed money to fund passive resistance; underlying inflation from First World War spending) AND develops it with specific evidence AND shows how it led to hyperinflation. Secure (3–4): cause identified and developed but linkage limited. Developing (2): cause stated with brief explanation. Emerging (1): simple, undeveloped point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the hyperinflation of 1923 for German society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): identifies a clear consequence (e.g. middle-class savings destroyed, fuelling resentment against Weimar; debtors benefited while creditors suffered; social instability made extremist politics more attractive) AND develops it with specific detail AND traces further effects. Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): consequence stated briefly. Emerging (1): vague mention of suffering.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Munich Putsch for the development of the Nazi Party in the years 1923 to 1929.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): significance at the time (failed putsch, 16 Nazis killed, Hitler arrested) AND over time (trial gave national publicity, light sentence, Mein Kampf written in prison, Hitler switched to legal electoral strategy). Secure (5–6): both time frames addressed with development; may be uneven. Developing (3–4): focused mainly on immediate failure or on longer term, not both. Emerging (1–2): description without analysis.

practice_questions.text: 'Hyperinflation was more damaging to the Weimar Republic than the Munich Putsch.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): sustained argument with agreement (hyperinflation: wiped out middle-class savings, caused social chaos, undermined faith in the government, made extremism more attractive) AND disagreement (Munich Putsch: gave Hitler national platform, revealed judiciary's sympathy with the right, forced tactical shift to legal strategy that ultimately succeeded in 1933). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both sides developed with evidence; judgement present. Developing (4–6): one side more developed; limited judgement. Emerging (1–3): mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Battle of Manzikert (1071).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students may describe: it was a Byzantine defeat against the Seljuk Turks; Emperor Romanos IV was captured; it opened Anatolia to Seljuk settlement; it threatened Constantinople. 1 mark for a simple point; 2 marks for a developed point with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Pope Urban II's speech at the Council of Clermont in 1095.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should identify two features with supporting detail.
Feature 1: Urban II called on Western knights to stop fighting each other and march to liberate Jerusalem and the Holy Sepulchre from Muslim (Seljuk) control.
Feature 2: Urban II promised a plenary indulgence — full remission of all sins — to those who died on the expedition, an enormously powerful spiritual incentive.
2 marks per feature: 1 mark for a simple point, 2 marks for a developed point with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the enormous popular response to Urban II's call for a crusade in 1095.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific cause and explains it with precise detail, linking it clearly to the scale of the response. E.g. the plenary indulgence addressed the deepest medieval spiritual fear (purgatory), making participation spiritually irresistible; or the tradition of Jerusalem pilgrimage meant crusaders saw themselves as armed pilgrims doing a holy duty. Sustains a clear line of reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a cause with some explanation and some link to outcome.
Developing: Identifies a cause but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Council of Clermont (1095) for the history of the Crusades.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Covers significance at the time (immediate surge in recruitment, nobles and peasants taking the cross, launch of both the People's Crusade and the official crusade) and over time (established papacy as organiser of holy war, set precedent for future crusades, fundamentally changed Western-Muslim relations). Sustained judgement throughout.
Secure: Covers both dimensions with evidence; clear explanation.
Developing: Mainly one dimension, limited evidence.
Emerging: Describes Clermont with little sense of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Seljuk conquest of Anatolia for the Byzantine Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific consequence (e.g. loss of Anatolia removed the main source of Byzantine military recruits; Seljuks positioned at Nicaea threatened Constantinople; forced Alexios to appeal to the West, inadvertently starting the Crusades) and explains it with precise detail. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a consequence with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a consequence but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: 'Religious devotion was the main reason why so many people responded to Urban II's call for a crusade.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues for (plenary indulgence addressed profound spiritual fear; pilgrimage tradition made Jerusalem sacred; growing ideology of holy war; many crusaders made financial sacrifice) and against (younger sons sought land and wealth; adventure and glory; loyalty to crusading lords; political ambitions of noble leaders). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence; conclusion reached.
Developing: Mainly one-sided, limited evidence.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.

before.exam_tip_html: For questions on the causes of the First Crusade, you must connect the political context (Seljuk expansion, Byzantine appeal) with the ideological context (Cluniac reform, holy war, pilgrimage) and Urban II’s specific actions at Clermont. Examiners want you to weigh these factors — don’t just list them. For the 10-mark “Why do interpretations differ?” question type, be ready to explain why historians debate whether religious faith or material motives were more important for crusaders.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the lives of wealthy Elizabethans.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with supporting detail, e.g. wealthy Elizabethans built great houses with large glass windows as a mark of status, such as Hardwick Hall (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature without specific detail (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 1601 Poor Law.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: a precise feature with accurate supporting detail (2 marks). Emerging: a simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: it created a compulsory poor rate levied on householders; it appointed Overseers of the Poor in every parish; it distinguished between the impotent poor (to be helped), the able-bodied unemployed (to be set to work) and idle vagrants (to be punished). Maximum 4 marks (2 per feature).

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growth of vagrancy in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a detailed causal chain with evidence, e.g. population growth increased the supply of labour faster than demand, driving wages down and leaving labourers unable to find steady work. Secure: a clear cause with some supporting evidence. Developing: a relevant cause with limited development. Emerging: a simple statement. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1601 Poor Law for Elizabethan England and beyond.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (first national compulsory system of poor relief; parish-based structure; attempted to categorise and manage the poor) AND over time (remained the basis of English poor law until 1834). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation with limited range. Emerging: simple descriptive points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a contemporary pamphlet describing vagrants as dangerous 'sturdy beggars' for understanding attitudes to poverty in Elizabethan England? Use the source and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (what the pamphlet says about vagrants), provenance (written from an elite/government perspective to justify harsh treatment) and contextual knowledge (the Tudor distinction between the impotent poor and sturdy beggars; the 1601 Act reflecting this attitude) to make a substantiated judgement. Secure: addresses two of the three elements. Developing: mainly describes the source. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'The government of Elizabeth I dealt effectively with the problem of poverty.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: argues for (the 1601 Poor Law created a national compulsory system; it categorised the poor; it remained in force until 1834) AND against (enforcement was uneven; root causes of inflation and enclosure were not addressed; the law was as much about controlling the poor as relieving them) before reaching a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: both sides with some evidence; clear conclusion. Developing: one-sided response. Emerging: simple agreement. Maximum 12 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Enabling Act (1933).
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• The Enabling Act gave Hitler the power to make laws without consulting the Reichstag for four years. This meant he could govern by decree and bypass all parliamentary checks, effectively ending democratic government in Germany. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for a simple identification with no development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Hitler's consolidation of power between January 1933 and August 1934.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two features identified with basic description.
Secure: Each feature described with relevant context, e.g.:
• The Reichstag Fire Decree (28 February 1933) suspended civil liberties and allowed the Nazis to arrest communist opponents before the March 1933 elections. [2 marks]
• The Night of the Long Knives (June 1934) saw Hitler order the murder of SA leader Ernst Röhm and others, reassuring the army and eliminating a potential rival power base. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement of a reason.
Developing: Reason identified with some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Deep analysis of the mechanism, relating the cause to the broader context of Depression and democratic failure.
Example content: The Great Depression caused mass unemployment — approximately six million unemployed by early 1932. Weimar's coalition governments appeared unable to tackle the crisis, rotating chancellors through emergency decrees. This collapse of faith in mainstream parties drove voters towards the Nazis, making them the largest Reichstag party in July 1932 with 37.4% of votes. This electoral strength, combined with Papen's persuasion of Hindenburg that Hitler could be 'tamed', led to the appointment.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Enabling Act (1933) for Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores the longer-term consequences and links to later developments.
Example content: The Enabling Act gave Hitler the legal authority to govern without the Reichstag for four years. As a direct consequence, the Nazis used this power to ban all other political parties by July 1933 and to pass laws attacking Jews, trade unions and political opponents — all without parliamentary scrutiny. The Act also set the precedent that Hitler's will, not constitutional law, was the supreme source of authority in Germany.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Night of the Long Knives (June 1934) for Hitler's consolidation of power.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description of what happened.
Developing: Some assessment of importance.
Secure: Explains significance at the time and over time.
Mastering: Weighs significance against other consolidation steps; argues the Night of the Long Knives was decisive or contextualises it within the overall process.
At the time: Eliminated the SA leadership as a rival power base; secured the loyalty of the German army, which Hitler needed for rearmament.
Over time: Demonstrated the regime's willingness to use extrajudicial murder; the SS and Gestapo became the dominant instruments of control, foreshadowing the terror state.

practice_questions.text:
'Hitler's appointment as chancellor in January 1933 was the most important step in his consolidation of power.' How far do you agree?
In your answer, consider the importance of January 1933 alongside other key steps, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, limited or no judgement.
Developing: Some argument on both sides, limited evidence, weak conclusion.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Weighs each step (January 1933, Reichstag Fire Decree, Enabling Act, Gleichschaltung, Night of the Long Knives, August 1934 merger of roles) against each other and reaches a nuanced conclusion.

Arguments for: Without becoming chancellor Hitler had no access to state power; all other steps depended on being in that position.
Arguments against: Appointment alone was limited — the Enabling Act (March 1933) gave genuine legislative power; the Night of the Long Knives secured army loyalty; the August 1934 merger of president and chancellor gave Hitler supreme authority.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Nuremberg Laws (1935).
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• The Nuremberg Laws (1935) stripped Jews of German citizenship, making them stateless in their own country and denying them the rights of German citizens such as voting. [2 marks]
• The Nuremberg Laws banned marriage and sexual relationships between Jews and non-Jews, framed as preventing 'racial pollution', a concept central to Nazi racial ideology. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for a simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Nazi policy towards women in the years 1933–1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two features identified with basic description.
Secure: Each feature described with relevant context, e.g.:
• The 'Three Ks' (Kinder, Küche, Kirche) policy encouraged women to leave paid work and focus on bearing children; marriage loans of 1,000 Reichsmarks were offered as financial incentive. [2 marks]
• Women were removed from professional positions — female doctors, lawyers and civil servants were pushed out in 1933–1935. However, labour shortages from the late 1930s meant women were increasingly drawn back into the workforce. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the worsening treatment of Jews in Germany between 1933 and 1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement.
Developing: Some explanation of the cause.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses the mechanism and links cause to wider Nazi ideology or policy escalation.
Example: Nazi racial ideology, which defined Jews as an inferior racial threat to the German 'Volksgemeinschaft' (people's community), provided the ideological justification for escalating persecution. Each piece of legislation built on the last: dismissal from jobs (1933) was followed by legal exclusion (Nuremberg Laws, 1935) and then physical violence (Kristallnacht, 1938). The regime also responded to opportunities — the assassination of a German diplomat in Paris in November 1938 was used as a pretext for Kristallnacht.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Kristallnacht (November 1938) for Germany's Jewish community.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores long-term consequences and links to later persecution.
Example: Kristallnacht dramatically accelerated Jewish emigration. Approximately 30,000 Jewish men were sent to concentration camps after the pogrom, and property losses were severe. The regime also fined the Jewish community one billion Reichsmarks for the damage. In the months after November 1938, emigration rates increased sharply. However, many of those who wanted to leave faced difficulty finding countries willing to accept refugees, leaving them trapped in Germany.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Hitler Youth for Nazi control of Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description of what the Hitler Youth did.
Developing: Some assessment.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time.
Mastering: Weighs the Hitler Youth against other means of control (SS, propaganda, economic policy) and assesses how far it achieved its aims.
At the time: Built loyalty among young Germans; trained boys for military service; inculcated Nazi ideology from an early age.
Over time: Created a generation of soldiers and party members committed to Hitler; however, resistance groups (Edelweiss Pirates, Swing Youth) show the limits of the indoctrination.

practice_questions.text:
'Nazi economic policy was more successful than Nazi social policy in winning German support between 1933 and 1939.' How far do you agree?
In your answer consider economic and social policy and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, no judgement.
Developing: Some points on both sides, limited evidence.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Nuanced analysis weighing the range and depth of support generated by different policies; distinguishes genuine enthusiasm from coerced compliance.

For economic: Unemployment nearly eliminated by 1938; 'Strength through Joy' leisure benefits; visible public works created sense of national purpose.
For social: Many women resented removal from careers; Jewish persecution alienated some Germans; youth indoctrination generated both loyalty and resistance.
Judgement might argue economic recovery generated broader and more genuine support, while social policies divided opinion — though fear of the police state made dissent dangerous to express.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Dawes Plan of 1924.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific feature with precise detail (e.g. restructured reparations into manageable annual instalments; arranged approximately 800 million gold marks in American loans). Secure (1–2): identifies a feature with some detail. Developing (1): vague reference to American money or reparations. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Germany's foreign policy successes under Stresemann.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise supporting detail — e.g. the Locarno Pact (1925) committed Germany to accept western borders permanently; joining the League of Nations (1926) with a permanent Council seat restored Germany's international status. Secure (3): two features with some development. Developing (2): two features briefly stated. Emerging (1): one feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Germany's economic recovery between 1924 and 1929.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear cause (e.g. the Dawes Plan unlocked American loans, restructured reparations, allowed France to withdraw from Ruhr, enabled industrial modernisation) developed with specific evidence and linked to recovery outcome. Secure (3–4): cause identified and developed but linkage limited. Developing (2): cause stated briefly. Emerging (1): simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Germany joining the League of Nations in 1926.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear consequence (e.g. Germany gained a permanent Council seat equal to Britain, France, Italy and Japan, restoring international prestige; encouraged further foreign investment; undermined the argument that Versailles had permanently excluded Germany from international affairs) developed with evidence and further effects. Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Stresemann's economic and diplomatic achievements for Germany in the years 1923 to 1929.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): significance at the time (economic recovery, falling unemployment, international rehabilitation, Locarno, League membership) AND over time (demonstrated vulnerability — entire recovery dependent on US loans; Stresemann's death October 1929 removed Germany's best statesman just as Wall Street Crash ended US lending). Secure (5–6): both time periods addressed. Developing (3–4): mainly descriptive of achievements without analytical weight on significance. Emerging (1–2): lists achievements without analysis.

practice_questions.text: 'The Stresemann years were a genuine golden age for the Weimar Republic.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): sustained agreement (real economic gains, Dawes/Young Plans, falling unemployment, Locarno, League membership, cultural flourishing) AND disagreement (agricultural depression even in good times, US-loan dependency, unstable coalition governments, Nazi/communist parties survived, cultural changes controversial to conservatives). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both sides developed; judgement present. Developing (4–6): one side stronger. Emerging (1–3): mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the bootlegging trade during Prohibition.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: Bootlegging involved the illegal manufacture and distribution of alcohol [1], generating enormous profits that bankrolled organised crime syndicates such as Al Capone's Chicago Outfit, which earned an estimated $60 million per year at its peak [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Teapot Dome Scandal.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature: one for the feature, one for supporting detail.
Feature 1: Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly leased government oil reserves at Teapot Dome, Wyoming, to private oil companies [1] in exchange for cash bribes totalling approximately $400,000. [1]
Feature 2: Fall became the first US Cabinet member to be convicted of a crime committed while in office [1] — the scandal severely damaged the reputation of President Harding's administration, already associated with the corrupt 'Ohio Gang'. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Prohibition failed to stop the consumption of alcohol in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise cause with specific evidence and a clear causal chain explaining how that factor led to Prohibition's failure.
Secure: Valid cause with supporting detail and a developed link.
Developing: Names a cause but explanation is thin.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid causes: too few federal Prohibition agents (around 1,500 for the whole country); agents were poorly paid and easily bribed; speakeasies easy to run and hard to police; bootlegging profits so high that criminals could afford bribes at every level; public attitude shifted against the ban.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Prohibition for law and order in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear consequence traced with specific evidence; explains how Prohibition produced that outcome.
Secure: Valid consequence with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a consequence without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid consequences: rise of organised crime syndicates; Al Capone's gang earning $60 million annually; the St Valentine's Day Massacre (1929); widespread bribery of police and judges; public disrespect for law enforcement; Teapot Dome-type political corruption.

practice_questions.text:
How significant was Al Capone in revealing the weaknesses of Prohibition?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time and over time with precise evidence and sustained analysis.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation but limited in scope.
Emerging: Simple points.
At the time: embodied the scale of organised crime; corrupted police, judges and politicians; St Valentine's Day Massacre showed limits of law enforcement; earned an estimated $60 million per year.
Over time: became the iconic symbol of Prohibition's failure; helped turn public opinion; his eventual conviction for tax evasion (1931) showed that indirect methods were needed; legacy shaped anti-organised-crime legislation.

practice_questions.text:
'The failure of Prohibition was mainly caused by the weakness of federal enforcement.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Points for and against with relevant evidence; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or underdeveloped judgement.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.
Agreement: only 1,500 federal agents; poorly paid, easily bribed; no national police force; inconsistent enforcement between rural and urban areas.
Disagreement: public demand for alcohol made enforcement impossible regardless of resources; profits of organised crime too great to overcome with policing alone; widespread cultural acceptance of drinking in cities; political corruption at local and federal level made enforcement from above ineffective too.
Judgement: enforcement weakness was significant but insufficient on its own — social and economic factors made Prohibition inherently unenforceable.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the work of barber surgeons in medieval Britain.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with supporting detail. Example: Barber surgeons performed amputations and wound-setting without anaesthetics, meaning patients had to be physically held down and pain and shock frequently caused death. [2 marks: 1 for feature, 1 for detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of James Simpson's introduction of anaesthetics.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: Simpson first used chloroform in November 1847 after experimenting on himself and colleagues; it caused unconsciousness, removing the pain of surgery. Feature 2: Despite initial religious opposition, Queen Victoria's use of chloroform during the birth of Prince Leopold in 1853 gave royal approval and helped overcome resistance. [2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Joseph Lister's introduction of antiseptic surgery in 1865.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of the consequence (dramatic fall in post-operative infection deaths, enabling complex surgery, transformation of hospital mortality rates) with embedded evidence. Secure: Clear consequence with relevant evidence. Developing: Consequence identified, limited explanation. Emerging: Simple statement that fewer people died. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the discovery of anaesthetics and antiseptic surgery for the development of medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (pain-free, infection-reduced surgery) AND over time (foundation of modern surgical practice, enabling increasingly complex operations by 1900 and beyond). Secure: Both dimensions of significance with evidence. Developing: One dimension, limited evidence. Emerging: Description only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Lister's use of antiseptics was more significant than Simpson's use of anaesthetics in improving treatment.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates both sides with evidence — anaesthetics removed pain and fear, made complex surgery possible; antiseptics addressed the greater killer (post-operative infection) and made the surgery survivable. Acknowledges the two developments worked together. Reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: Both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: One side argued with limited evidence. Emerging: Descriptive. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How far did the treatment of disease change between the medieval period and 1900? Use evidence across all three eras to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change across medieval (bloodletting, herbal, barber surgeons), early modern (pharmacopoeia, gradual improvement but no major break), modern (anaesthetics 1847, antiseptics 1865, aseptic surgery 1890s). Weighs change against continuity (herbal remedies still used; bloodletting persisted into 19th century). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Three eras with evidence. Developing: Two eras. Emerging: Single era. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Bartolomeu Dias’s 1488 voyage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (e.g. rounded the southern tip of Africa / named the Cape of Good Hope / crew mutinied and forced a return before reaching India). Two marks for a developed explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Magellan’s circumnavigation of the globe, 1519–1522.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• He navigated the Strait of Magellan (southern tip of South America) in November 1520, providing the first European passage between the Atlantic and Pacific.
• He named the Pacific Ocean after its apparent calmness after the storms of the strait.
• He was killed at the Battle of Mactan in the Philippines on 27 April 1521; Elcano completed the voyage.
• Only eighteen of the original ~270 crew survived, arriving back in Seville on 6 September 1522.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Lisbon becoming Europe’s leading commercial city by the early sixteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and develops a cause with evidence — e.g. da Gama’s opening of a direct sea route to India allowed Portuguese traders to buy spices at source and sell in Europe without paying Ottoman or Arab intermediaries; spice prices fell; wealth concentrated in Lisbon; links specifically to the 1497–1499 voyage and the displacement of Venice as the spice hub.
Secure: Identifies a cause with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Magellan’s circumnavigation for European geographical knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the circumnavigation proved definitively that the Earth was a sphere and that the Americas were entirely separate from Asia; links to the specific evidence of the 1519–1522 voyage; explains how this changed European understanding of the globe and enabled more accurate cartography.
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Vasco da Gama’s voyage to India (1497–1499).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (first European sea voyage to India; cargo of spices repaid the cost many times over; undermined Arab and Ottoman trade monopoly; made Lisbon the centre of European trade) AND over time (established the Portuguese maritime empire from Brazil to the Spice Islands; transformed the global spice trade; reduced prices in Europe). Developed with evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with evidence; may not fully develop the over-time dimension.
Developing: Describes what da Gama did without analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Amerigo Vespucci’s contribution to the age of exploration was more significant than Bartolomeu Dias’s.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• Vespucci’s “Mundus Novus” letter (c.1502) established that the Americas were a new continent — the intellectual breakthrough that reframed the entire European understanding of the globe.
• The Americas were named after him, ensuring a lasting legacy in geographical knowledge.
• His recognition of a “New World” directly influenced subsequent expeditions and colonisation strategies.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• Dias’s rounding of the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 was the crucial practical breakthrough that made da Gama’s voyage and Portugal’s trading empire possible.
• Without Dias, the sea route to Asia might have remained theoretical; his voyage directly enabled the transformation of European trade.
• Vespucci’s exact role and the authenticity of some letters attributed to him have been questioned by historians.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, reaches a substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive, no evaluation of the interpretation.

before.exam_tip_html: Questions about the explorers often test the 8-mark “Explain Change” type: here you must explain what changed as a result of these voyages, not just describe what happened. Think about what changed for European trade routes (Lisbon replaced Venice), for geographical knowledge (confirmation that America was a separate continent; the Earth’s circumference confirmed by Magellan), and for indigenous populations. For 6-mark cause/consequence questions, always link your evidence directly to the specific cause or consequence you are explaining — examiners reward explicit causal links, not just description.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the teddy boy subculture in 1950s Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Teddy boys wore distinctive Edwardian-style clothing: drape jackets, drainpipe trousers, crepe-soled shoes, and quiff hairstyles, marking them out as a deliberately provocative youth group.
- They were Britain's first distinctive youth subculture, emerging in working-class areas of London in the early 1950s; press coverage linked them to violence and created a moral panic.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growth of youth culture in Britain in the 1950s.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple cause identified, limited explanation.
Secure: Clear cause with developed explanation and factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation, precise evidence, chain of causation clear.

Causes may include:
- Rising wages for young workers gave teenagers disposable income for the first time, creating a market for records, fashion, and entertainment aimed specifically at the young.
- American rock 'n' roll (Bill Haley, Elvis Presley) arrived in Britain from 1955, providing an exciting new music that appealed to youth and alarmed older generations.
- The ending of austerity (rationing ended 1954) and growth of hire purchase made consumer goods accessible, enabling a commercial youth culture to develop.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the coronation television broadcast of 1953 for British society.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple consequence, limited development.
Secure: Clear consequence with explanation and evidence.
Mastering: Detailed consequence, precise evidence, wider significance addressed.

Consequences may include:
- An estimated 20 million people watched the coronation, dramatically accelerating television set ownership; by 1959 two-thirds of households had a TV.
- Television became the dominant form of home entertainment, transforming how people spent their evenings and creating a shared national culture.
- The BBC's monopoly ended as ITV launched in 1955 to meet growing demand for popular programming.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was American culture in shaping British popular culture in the period 1951–1979? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence.
Developing: Some significance explained, basic evidence.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time addressed, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis, precise evidence, sustained argument weighing American influence against homegrown British developments.

At the time: rock 'n' roll transformed British music from the mid-1950s; American fashion (jeans), film, and TV shows heavily consumed by British youth.
Over time: British artists (Beatles, Rolling Stones) reinvented American music and exported it globally; Britain became a cultural producer, not just consumer.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Punk was the most important development in British popular culture in the period 1951–1979.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation, limited range of evidence.
Secure: Clear evaluation, addresses agreement and disagreement, factual knowledge used.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation, precise evidence, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: punk expressed genuine social frustration about unemployment and economic decline; the Sex Pistols' 'God Save the Queen' (1977) was a genuinely provocative cultural moment; punk's DIY ethic influenced later music and fashion.

Disagreement: the Beatles had far greater cultural reach (globally, not just domestically); television's introduction transformed mass culture more fundamentally; the mini-skirt and Swinging Sixties fashion had wider social impact on gender norms; punk appealed to a minority compared to the mainstream pop and rock of the period.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Mods and Rockers conflict in 1964.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Mods and Rockers clashed at coastal resorts including Brighton, Margate, and Clacton in 1964; the press covered the violence extensively, creating a moral panic about youth gangs.
- Mods and Rockers represented different subcultural identities: Mods rode Italian scooters and wore tailored suits; Rockers preferred leather jackets, motorbikes, and older American rock 'n' roll.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of smuggling as a crime in eighteenth-century Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Feature may include: high customs duties made it profitable; organised gangs (e.g. Hawkhurst Gang) operated openly; local communities sympathised and participated; coastline was difficult to police. Simple identification (1 mark); developed with specific detail (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Luddite movement (1811-1813).
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Luddites were skilled framework knitters and textile workers who smashed industrial machinery threatening their livelihoods; the movement was concentrated in the Midlands and North of England. Feature 2: The government responded with extreme severity — the Frame Breaking Act of 1812 made machine-breaking a capital offence and troops were deployed in greater numbers than Wellington had in the Peninsular War at the time.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why new types of crime emerged in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names a new crime category. Developing: Links it to a new technology or social change. Secure: Explains how the motor car created entirely new crime categories impossible before its invention; uses specific examples (drink-driving, vehicle theft); notes the volume of new offences it generated. Mastering: Sustains analysis of how technological change (motor car, internet) consistently generates new crime categories; may compare with how eighteenth-century trade routes generated smuggling and highwaymen in the same way — technology creating both opportunity and crime.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Swing Riots of 1830 as evidence about crime and punishment in early nineteenth-century Britain.
