practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Describes what happened. Developing: Notes government used severe punishment. Secure: Analyses significance at the time: the government's use of execution and transportation showed that it treated collective protest as a threat to social order; the riots revealed the gap between legal definitions of crime and popular views of justice. Mastering: Evaluates significance over time: the Swing Riots represent a pattern of criminalising collective protest that continued into the nineteenth century (trade union activity was criminalised by the Combination Acts); they also demonstrate continuity with earlier agrarian disorder driven by poverty.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that the nature of crime in Britain changed significantly between the eighteenth and twenty-first centuries?
Give reasons for your answer and refer to different periods in your response.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments for significant change: entirely new categories emerged (car crime, cybercrime, terrorism); organised crime became more sophisticated; the scale of fraud expanded with the internet; terrorism by non-state actors is a modern phenomenon. Arguments for continuity: property crime and theft have remained dominant throughout; violence has always been present; collective protest crime (Luddites-to-miners' strike) shows a recurring pattern. Emerging: one-sided or superficial. Developing: notes changes but without sustained argument. Secure: argues a clear position with evidence from at least two periods. Mastering: evaluates the degree of change against continuity, uses specific evidence from multiple periods, reaches a justified overall conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of terrorism as a crime in the late twentieth century in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: The Provisional IRA conducted a sustained bombing campaign in Britain from the 1970s; major attacks included the Birmingham pub bombings (1974) and Brighton hotel bombing (1984). Feature 2: Islamist terrorism became the dominant concern after 2001; the 7 July 2005 bombings in London killed 52 people and reshaped counter-terrorism legislation and policing priorities.

before.exam_tip_html: The 16-mark thematic change essay is likely to ask how far the nature of crime changed across all three eras. To reach the top band, cover the medieval era (petty theft, violence), the early modern era (vagrancy, heresy, collective protest), and the modern era (car crime, terrorism, cybercrime). A common mistake is treating the nineteenth century as ‘modern’ — examiners want you to reach the twentieth or twenty-first century for full credit. Show continuity too: poverty-driven crime and property crime persist in every era even as new categories emerge.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Double V Campaign launched by African Americans in 1942.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names the feature (demanded victory against fascism abroad AND racial discrimination at home) AND develops it (popularised by the Pittsburgh Courier; showed Black Americans linked wartime service to demands for equality). Developing: Identifies feature without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-1956).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) It lasted 381 days and involved the vast majority of Black Montgomerians refusing to use the buses, walking or carpooling instead; (2) It was organised using non-violent tactics by the Montgomery Improvement Association and established Martin Luther King Jr. as a civil rights leader. Developing: Identifies features without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Supreme Court's ruling in Brown v Board of Education (1954).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (NAACP legal campaign; the obvious inequality between Black and white schools; growing post-war pressure for civil rights reform) AND explains through a developed chain of reasoning how this cause led to the ruling. Secure: Cause with some development. Developing: Simple statement. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the murder of Emmett Till in 1955.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (energised civil rights movement; brought racial violence to national attention through open-casket funeral photographs; demonstrated inadequacy of Southern justice for Black Americans) AND explains the chain of effects with development. Secure: Consequence with some development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Brown v Board of Education ruling (1954) for the civil rights movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (struck down legal basis for school segregation; overturned Plessy v Ferguson; gave NAACP powerful legal precedent) AND over time (inspired further legal challenges; provoked white resistance that radicalised movement; Little Rock crisis showed limits of legal change without enforcement). Secure: One time frame covered well. Developing: Describes Brown without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: 'The most important factor in advancing civil rights before 1955 was the legal strategy of the NAACP.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing NAACP legal strategy (Brown v Board; Browder v Gayle) against other factors (wartime service and Double V Campaign; Truman's 1948 executive order desegregating the army; grassroots protest demonstrated by Montgomery). Substantiated overall judgement on relative importance. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes NAACP without weighing against other factors. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the chevauchée as a military tactic.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: The chevauchée involved mounted raiders burning crops and towns across French territory [1], undermining the French king's prestige by demonstrating he could not protect his subjects [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the English victory at the Battle of Crécy in 1346.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: Edward III positioned his army on a ridge with longbowmen on the flanks [1]; the massed archers repulsed approximately fifteen or sixteen French cavalry charges with devastating arrow fire [1]. Feature 2: The longbow's rate of fire — up to twelve arrows per minute — created a density of missiles that French armour could not withstand [1], and even Genoese crossbowmen deployed by France were outmatched and abandoned [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of English military success in the early Hundred Years' War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (longbow, chevauchée tactics, defensive positioning at Crécy/Poitiers, experienced commanders such as the Black Prince) and explains it in depth with precise factual knowledge, showing how it led to English victories. Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with relevant factual support. Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference without specific factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Battle of Poitiers (1356) for the French Crown.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains a consequence in depth — the capture of King John II and the subsequent ransom of three million gold crowns, which strained French finances; or the humiliation to French royal prestige; or the Treaty of Brétigny (1360) in which France ceded Aquitaine. Secure: Explains a consequence with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the longbow to England's military success in the Hundred Years' War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (decisive at Crécy and Poitiers; gave England tactical advantage over French heavy cavalry; enabled much smaller English armies to defeat larger French forces) and over time (shaped English military identity; longbow archers remained central to English armies for decades; influenced how medieval warfare developed). Precise factual knowledge throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes the longbow without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The Battle of Crécy was the most important English military achievement of the early Hundred Years' War.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with precise factual knowledge. Agrees: Crécy was the first great longbow victory, established English tactical superiority, and led directly to the capture of Calais (1347). Disagrees: Poitiers (1356) was arguably more significant — capturing King John II gave England enormous diplomatic leverage and led to the Treaty of Brétigny (1360) with its massive territorial and financial gains. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence. Developing: Describes events without evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple response; no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of trench warfare on the Western Front.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks. Students should identify a feature and support it:
• The trench system involved parallel lines of fortified dugouts [1], which meant neither side could easily advance because machine guns and artillery covered any open ground between the lines [1].
• No Man's Land separated the opposing trenches [1], and was filled with barbed wire and shell craters to prevent easy crossing [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of guerrilla warfare as a military tactic.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature:
• Feature 1: Guerrilla forces avoid pitched battles with larger conventional armies [1], instead using hit-and-run attacks, ambushes and raids on supply lines [1].
• Feature 2: Guerrilla forces rely on local knowledge and support from the civilian population [1], which makes them difficult for conventional armies to identify and destroy [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the creeping barrage was an important tactical development in the First World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains how the creeping barrage addressed the specific problem of trench warfare — keeping defenders' heads down as infantry advanced, reducing the time men were exposed to machine gun fire. Links to specific battles (Arras 1917, Hundred Days Offensive 1918) and explains why this was a significant improvement over earlier tactics.
Secure: Clear explanation with supporting evidence.
Developing: Identifies the creeping barrage with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement about artillery.

practice_questions.text: Explain the consequences of the Boer War (1899–1902) for British military tactics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses multiple consequences — the immediate failure of conventional tactics against Boer commandos, the British adoption of concentration camps (with their humanitarian consequences), and the longer-term lesson that conventional armies needed counter-insurgency doctrine to deal with guerrilla tactics.
Secure: Identifies two consequences with relevant evidence.
Developing: One consequence, limited development.
Emerging: Describes the Boer War without analysing consequences.

practice_questions.text: How significant were guerrilla tactics as a challenge to the British armed forces in the twentieth century?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues significance at the time (Boer War, Kenya, Northern Ireland each required major adaptations) and over time (shaped British counter-insurgency doctrine, influenced army training and operations in Afghanistan and Iraq). Reaches a substantiated conclusion about the degree of significance.
Secure: Explains significance with evidence from two or more conflicts.
Developing: One conflict discussed with limited analysis.
Emerging: Describes guerrilla warfare without evaluating significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did the tactics used by British forces change between c.1900 and the present day? In your answer, refer to the First World War and at least one later conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces change from trench warfare (1914–18: static, linear, firepower-dominated) through combined arms developments (1918 Hundred Days), to post-1945 guerrilla and counter-insurgency challenges (Boer War, Kenya, Northern Ireland, Falklands). Weighs change (tactics became more flexible, combined arms became standard) against continuity (discipline, logistics, leadership remain constant factors). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Covers at least two periods with evidence and some analysis.
Developing: Two events described, limited analysis of change.
Emerging: One event described, no analytical framework.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of feast days as a form of holiday in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with detail: e.g. feast days were provided by the Church calendar, giving ordinary workers around forty leisure days per year / they were occasions for sport, dancing and communal feasting, not only religious observance. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of the railway on British holidays after the 1840s.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. the railway made seaside resorts accessible to industrial cities — Blackpool became reachable from Manchester in hours (feature + detail); resorts invested in piers, towers and entertainment to meet the new demand from day-trippers (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why British seaside resorts went into decline after the 1960s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed causal explanation linking the growth of cheap air travel and Mediterranean package holidays (guaranteed sunshine, modern hotels, cheap wine) to falling visitor numbers at resorts like Blackpool. Specific evidence (e.g. Ryanair, easyJet, 1970s decline). Secure: Clear cause with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Holidays with Pay Act of 1938 for British workers.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed consequence explaining how guaranteed paid leave expanded the holiday market, enabled more workers to take week-long seaside holidays, and supported the growth of the holiday camp industry. Evidence-based. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was technology in changing British holiday patterns between 1840 and the present day?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses technological significance at the time (railway → seaside) AND over time (jet aircraft → package holidays → budget airlines). Weighs technology against other factors (legislation, rising wages). Secure: Clear analysis of technology’s role with named examples. Developing: Some points, limited range. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The most important change in British holiday patterns was the move from domestic to foreign holidays after 1960.' How far do you agree? Use evidence from across the full period c.500 to the present.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substantiated judgement. Agrees with strong evidence (package holidays, cheap airlines, decline of British resorts). Challenges by noting earlier turning points were also transformative (railway/seaside democratisation; Holidays with Pay Act enabling mass holidays). Traces all three eras. Overall conclusion weighs relative importance. Secure: Addresses both sides with evidence across two or more eras. Developing: Some argument, limited range. Emerging: Simple agree/disagree. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of bear-baiting as a form of Elizabethan entertainment.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with supporting detail, e.g. bear-baiting took place in purpose-built bear gardens on London's south bank, where a chained bear was attacked by dogs (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature without specific detail (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the design of an Elizabethan playhouse.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: precise feature with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: circular or polygonal wooden structure with an open central yard; covered galleries on three levels for wealthier patrons; a thrust stage projecting into the yard; groundlings stood in the yard for a penny; performances in daylight with no artificial scenery. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Puritan opposition to the Elizabethan theatre.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a detailed causal chain with evidence, e.g. Puritans believed theatre performances on Sundays competed directly with church attendance — audiences who went to see a play on a Sunday afternoon were not attending worship, undermining religious observance and giving the devil a foothold in everyday life. Secure: a clear cause with some supporting evidence. Developing: a relevant cause with limited development. Emerging: a simple statement. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the building of the first permanent playhouses in the 1570s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (created a commercial theatre industry; enabled regular professional performances; attracted playwrights like Marlowe and Shakespeare) AND over time (established a tradition of English theatre; Southwark as a cultural hub; the Globe). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation with limited range. Emerging: simple descriptive points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a Puritan pamphlet attacking theatres as 'dens of vice' for understanding attitudes towards the theatre in Elizabethan England?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (what the pamphlet argues), provenance (a Puritan author — one-sided, religious perspective) and contextual knowledge (Puritan opposition real and consistent; but theatres also had royal patronage and noble sponsors) to give a substantiated judgement about utility and limitations. Secure: addresses two of three elements. Developing: mainly describes the source. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'The Elizabethan theatre was the most important form of popular entertainment in Elizabethan England.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: argues for (professional playhouses drew large cross-class audiences; associated with Shakespeare; protected by royal and noble patronage; new cultural form) AND against (cruel sports drew larger daily audiences; court entertainment was more socially significant for the elite; theatre was concentrated in London) before a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: both sides with evidence and a conclusion. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: simple agreement. Maximum 12 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Seebohm Rowntree's survey of York, published in 1901.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: Rowntree introduced a scientific poverty line (1), calculating the minimum income needed for basic food, clothing and shelter, and found that 28 per cent of York's population lived below it (1). Mastering: accurate feature with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the National Insurance Act 1911.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature examples: Part 1 provided sickness benefit for about 10 million workers; Part 2 provided unemployment insurance for some 2.25 million workers in volatile trades; funding was contributory — worker, employer and government each contributed ('ninepence for fourpence'); Part 1 paid 10 shillings per week for the first 13 weeks, then 5 shillings per week for the next 13 weeks of illness. Mastering: two precise features with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Charles Booth's survey was important in bringing about social reform.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Developed explanation with accurate contextual knowledge. Booth's survey proved scientifically that around 30 per cent of Londoners lived in poverty; his identification of structural causes (low wages, old age, irregular work rather than personal failings) directly challenged the Victorian moral case against state intervention; his findings were widely read by politicians and helped shift public and political opinion towards the need for state action. Secure (3–4): clear cause with some development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Old Age Pensions Act 1908 for the elderly poor in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Around 650,000 people received pensions from January 1909; for the first time the state provided a direct income to elderly people without requiring them to enter the workhouse; it transformed the lives of the poorest elderly, who called the payments 'God bless Lloyd George money.' This was significant because it established the principle that the state had a duty to support citizens who could no longer support themselves. Secure (3–4): clear consequence with some development. Developing (1–2): simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Rowntree's concept of the 'poverty line' for British social policy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): At the time: gave reformers a scientific measurement to prove poverty was structural and gave journalists and politicians concrete evidence to use in debate; made it harder to dismiss poverty as a personal failing; directly influenced Liberal reform arguments. Over time: the poverty line concept became fundamental to all twentieth-century welfare policy; it was used by Rowntree in his 1941 survey and by Beveridge in designing the post-war welfare state. Secure (5–6): both dimensions with some development. Developing (3–4): mainly one dimension. Emerging (1–2): simple statement.

practice_questions.text: 'The Liberal reforms of 1906–1911 successfully tackled poverty in Britain.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Agrees and disagrees, substantiated, overall judgement. Agree: Old Age Pensions Act helped ~650,000; National Insurance Act covered 10 million sick workers; School Meals Act and medical inspections helped children; established the principle of state responsibility. Disagree: pension only for those over 70 (most working-class men didn't reach this age); National Insurance didn't cover families or all workers; school meals not universal; contributory element placed burden on low-paid workers; limited unemployment cover (selected trades only). Overall: reforms were significant beginnings but left major groups unprotected — foundations of a welfare state rather than a complete solution. Secure (7–9): argument both ways with some development. Developing (4–6): limited. Emerging (1–3): one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the evacuation programme that began in September 1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• Approximately 1.5 million children were moved from cities to rural areas in the first three days.
• Children were separated from their families and billeted with strangers in the countryside.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the government's rationing policy introduced from 1940.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• Rationing began in January 1940, initially covering butter, sugar and bacon, and expanded to most foods by 1942.
• Every person received a ration book stamped when the weekly allowance was used.
• Rationing improved nutrition among poorer families who had been underfed during the Depression.
• Food rationing did not fully end until 1954.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the introduction of rationing in Britain from 1940.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the cause (threat to supply chains from German U-boat attacks on Atlantic convoys, or simply the need to ensure fair distribution of scarce goods during wartime) and develops the mechanism — imports reduced, government needed to ensure the whole population had a guaranteed minimum, prevent hoarding, and maintain morale.
Secure: Names a clear cause and provides a linked explanation with some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference to wartime shortages without identifying a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Blitz for the people of Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. approximately 43,000 civilian deaths and one million made homeless, or the growth of community solidarity and the “Blitz spirit”) and develops a chain — the scale of civilian casualties transformed the war into a people’s conflict, forced the government to address working-class grievances, contributed to demand for post-war social reform.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the role of women on the Home Front during the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (conscription from 1941, 7.75 million women in work/auxiliary services by 1943, demonstrated capability in factory and military support roles) AND over time (contributed to changing expectations, fuelled later demands for equal pay, influenced post-war women's roles and eventually legislation). Weighs limits — lower pay than men, many returned to domestic roles post-1945.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions with clear explanation.
Developing: One dimension only with some explanation.
Emerging: Describes women's roles without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Propaganda was the most important way the government kept up morale during the Second World War.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing propaganda (Ministry of Information, BBC, poster campaigns) alongside other factors (genuine community solidarity, rationing fairness, Churchill's leadership, shared sacrifice). Weighs factors with evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on propaganda and other factors. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Siege of Antioch (1097–1098).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students may describe: the siege lasted eight months; the crusaders suffered from famine and disease; it ended when a garrison commander (Firouz) allowed Bohemond's men to scale the walls; a Seljuk relief army under Kerbogha then trapped the crusaders inside the city. 1 mark for a simple point; 2 marks for a developed point with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the capture of Jerusalem in 1099.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should identify two features with supporting detail.
Feature 1: Jerusalem was captured on 15 July 1099 after the crusaders built timber siege towers that allowed them to breach the north wall; this followed a period of extreme hardship including intense summer heat and lack of water.
Feature 2: The capture was followed by a massacre of the Muslim and Jewish inhabitants; Godfrey de Bouillon entered the city but refused the title of King, taking instead the title 'Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre'.
2 marks per feature: 1 mark for simple point, 2 marks for developed point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the crusaders were able to capture Antioch in June 1098.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific reason (treachery of Firouz; the role of Bohemond; the failure of earlier assaults making the infiltration necessary) and explains it with precise detail, linking cause to outcome. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a reason with explanation and some link to outcome.
Developing: Identifies a reason but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Holy Lance for the outcome of the First Crusade.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Significance at the time — the discovery restored morale when the crusade was on the verge of collapse inside Antioch; it contributed to the victory over Kerbogha's army on 28 June 1098. Over time — it became a symbol of divine support for the crusade; debates over its authenticity reflected wider questions about the nature of crusading motivation and the role of religious belief. Sustained judgement.
Secure: Covers both dimensions with evidence; clear explanation.
Developing: Mainly describes the discovery with limited significance analysis.
Emerging: Describes the Holy Lance with little sense of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the fall of Jerusalem in 1099.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific consequence (establishment of the Latin Kingdom; massacre of Muslim and Jewish inhabitants; the crusade became the model for all future crusades; fundamentally altered Christian-Muslim relations in the eastern Mediterranean) and explains it with precise detail. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a consequence with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a consequence but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: 'The lack of a single commander was the main reason the First Crusade nearly failed.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues in support (disputes over Antioch almost broke the crusade; Bohemond's refusal to honour his oath damaged relations with Byzantium; lack of unified supply chain caused famine) and against (the coalition structure allowed the crusade to survive individual failures; religious motivation and the indulgence compensated for poor organisation; the Holy Lance incident showed morale could be rescued). Substantiated judgement.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence; conclusion reached.
Developing: Mainly one-sided, limited evidence.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Soviet collectivisation in the early 1930s.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: peasant farms were forcibly merged into state-controlled collective farms (kolkhozy); resistance by kulaks was met with deportation or execution; grain was requisitioned by the state even when harvests failed.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Five Year Plans introduced from 1928.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: ambitious state targets for heavy industries such as steel, coal and electricity; new industrial cities like Magnitogorsk were built from nothing; workers faced pressure through the Stakhanovite movement; women entered industrial work in large numbers.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Ukrainian Holodomor famine of 1932–33.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates should identify a cause and explain why it led to the famine. Strong answers show causal reasoning. Key cause: the state maintained grain requisition quotas even as harvests collapsed; peasants who hid food were arrested; the destruction of kulak farmers through dekulakisation removed the most experienced producers.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise cause identified, causal chain explained, specific knowledge.
Secure: cause identified and explained with relevant knowledge.
Developing: cause identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point with no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Stakhanovite movement for Soviet industrial development.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: the movement created competitive pressure, raised production targets across industries and provided a mechanism for motivating workers without relying purely on coercion. Over time: it became a model for Soviet propaganda showing the 'new Soviet worker'; however, raising quotas increased resentment and may have encouraged falsification of production statistics.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways or at two points, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of Stalinist economic policy:

“The suffering caused by collectivisation and the Five Year Plans was an unavoidable price to pay for transforming the Soviet Union into an industrial power.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge of Soviet history in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: the USSR was transformed from an agricultural backwater into the world's second largest industrial economy within a decade; the industrial base built in the 1930s proved vital in defeating Germany after 1941; without collectivisation the state could not have fed urban industrial workers.

Disagreement: the Holodomor killed millions unnecessarily — the terror-famine was a policy choice, not an inevitability; dekulakisation destroyed experienced farmers, reducing long-term agricultural productivity; other paths to industrialisation (such as the NEP) existed; living standards for many workers remained very low.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: Was collectivisation more important than the Five Year Plans in transforming the Soviet economy under Stalin? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement weighing the two factors.

For collectivisation: provided the food surplus and labour force needed for industrialisation; but caused enormous human suffering and long-term damage to Soviet agriculture.

For the Five Year Plans: directly produced the industrial growth that made the USSR a major power; transformed specific sectors (steel, coal, electricity) with measurable results.

Strongest answers note that the two policies were interdependent: collectivisation was intended to supply the industrial plans.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing both factors, clear judgement with evidence.
Secure: two factors explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: factors listed, limited weighing.
Emerging: one factor or descriptive throughout.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the tithing system in Anglo-Saxon England.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Students may note: a tithing was a group of roughly ten households; members were collectively responsible for producing wrongdoers before a court; if a member could not be produced, all were fined; the system created social pressure on communities to police their own members. Simple identification (1 mark); developed with how it worked or its effect (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the parish constable system in the Tudor and Stuart periods.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: The parish constable was an unpaid post held by rotation among local men, usually for one year, alongside their normal occupation — most had no training, no uniform and little enthusiasm for the role. Feature 2: The constable's powers were limited to serving warrants and escorting prisoners to court — they could not investigate crime or maintain a regular patrol, making the system poorly suited to larger towns.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Justice of the Peace became so important in Tudor England.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States JPs maintained law and order. Developing: Notes JPs were from the gentry and unpaid. Secure: Explains that the Tudor state could not afford a paid professional administration, so it delegated local government and law enforcement to the gentry through the JP; by the Tudor period JPs were responsible for hearings, licensing, wage-setting, Poor Law administration and militias. Mastering: Sustains analysis of how the JP system embedded law enforcement in the hands of property-owning classes who had a direct economic interest in maintaining order; evaluates whether this was effective governance or a structural bias favouring the wealthy.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Statute of Winchester (1285) for law enforcement in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States it set up a watch system. Developing: Notes it required towns to provide watchmen. Secure: Analyses significance at the time: it formalised community responsibility in a statutory framework, required town watches and constables; it represented an attempt to extend royal oversight over local law enforcement. Mastering: Evaluates significance over time: it established the principle of unpaid community policing that persisted until the nineteenth century; its limitations were exposed by urbanisation — the same system that served rural villages proved wholly inadequate for nineteenth-century cities, directly provoking the demand for a professional police force.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that community-based law enforcement was effective in medieval and early modern England?
Give reasons for your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments for effectiveness: tithing and hue and cry worked well in stable rural communities where everyone knew each other; the JP system maintained local order in the countryside until the nineteenth century; manorial and church courts handled the bulk of everyday disputes. Arguments against: the system broke down in towns (anonymous populations; constables overwhelmed); the unpaid, part-time nature of all roles was a fundamental weakness; JPs enforced the law in the interests of property-owners; no mechanism for investigating crime. Emerging: superficial. Developing: notes strengths and weaknesses. Secure: argues a position with specific evidence. Mastering: weighs effectiveness in context (rural vs urban; early vs late period), reaches a justified conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the court system in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Manorial courts were held by lords to deal with local disputes and petty crimes on their estates — lords could fine, imprison and sometimes execute depending on royal privileges granted. Feature 2: Church courts operated alongside secular courts, dealing with adultery, defamation, tithes and clergy offences; clergy could claim benefit of clergy to be tried in church rather than royal courts.

before.exam_tip_html: For questions about law enforcement before 1829, examiners want you to understand why the system was so weak — not just describe it. The key points are: it was unpaid, part-time and community-based; it worked in small rural communities but broke down in larger towns; it depended on property-owners enforcing laws that protected their own interests. For the 8-mark ‘Explain Change’ question comparing medieval to early modern enforcement, focus on the shift from pure community responsibility (tithing, hue and cry) to a more formalised but still amateur system (constable, JP).

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the March on Washington in August 1963.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names feature (approximately 250,000 people gathered; it was the largest civil rights march in US history to that point; Martin Luther King Jr. delivered a speech at the Lincoln Memorial) AND develops it. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) It outlawed discrimination based on race, colour, religion, sex or national origin in public places such as hotels and restaurants; (2) It banned racial discrimination in employment, giving Black Americans legal protection from being refused work on grounds of race. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the passage of the Voting Rights Act in 1965.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (Selma marches and Bloody Sunday; televised police violence; continuing disenfranchisement of Black Southern voters through literacy tests; LBJ's political skill) AND develops the chain of reasoning to explain how it led to the Act. Secure: Cause with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the growth of Black Power after 1966.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (shift away from integrationist strategy; formation of Black Panther Party; increased FBI surveillance and COINTELPRO; concerned moderate white allies; demonstrated limits of legislative gains for Northern Black communities) AND develops the chain of effects. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Martin Luther King Jr. for the civil rights movement in the USA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (organised Birmingham campaign and March on Washington; key figure in passing Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act; gave movement moral authority through non-violence) AND over time (his assassination in 1968 triggered Fair Housing Act; his legacy shapes memory of civil rights movement; became symbol of non-violent change worldwide). Secure: One time frame well-covered. Developing: Describes King without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'Non-violent protest was the most effective method used by civil rights activists between 1955 and 1968.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues the case for non-violent protest (Birmingham's media impact; March on Washington's political pressure; Selma leading to Voting Rights Act; moral authority of movement) AGAINST other methods (NAACP legal strategy; Malcolm X/Black Power political pressure; economic boycotts; urban rebellions as catalyst for legislation). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes methods without weighing effectiveness. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the economic boom in the United States in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: Mass production allowed goods to be manufactured far more cheaply [1] — the cost of Henry Ford's Model T car fell from $825 in 1908 to $260 by 1925, bringing car ownership within reach of ordinary workers. [1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the policy of laissez-faire followed by Republican administrations in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature: one for the feature, one for supporting detail.
Feature 1: Republican governments cut taxes for wealthy individuals and reduced business regulation [1], based on the belief that what was good for big business was good for America as a whole. [1]
Feature 2: The Republicans introduced protective tariffs to shelter American manufacturers from foreign competition [1] — the Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922 raised import duties to their highest level since the Civil War. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the First World War contributed to the economic boom of the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise cause with specific evidence and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Valid cause with supporting detail and a developed link.
Developing: Names a cause without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid causes: American factories profited from wartime orders from Allied powers; European industrial capacity was devastated while US factories expanded; US became world's leading creditor after lending billions to Britain and France; high wartime demand for American goods built industrial capacity that continued post-war.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why hire purchase helped fuel the economic boom of the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces the mechanism clearly with precise evidence.
Secure: Valid explanation with supporting detail.
Developing: Names hire purchase but mechanism poorly explained.
Emerging: Simple point.
Hire purchase allowed consumers to buy goods they could not afford outright — by the late 1920s around 60% of cars and 80% of radios were bought on credit. This extended demand beyond what wages alone could support, keeping factory output high and sustaining the boom — at the cost of rising household debt.

practice_questions.text:
How significant was Henry Ford's contribution to the economic boom of the 1920s?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Significance at the time and over time; precise evidence; sustained analysis.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation; may focus on only one aspect.
Emerging: Simple points.
At the time: assembly line reduced Model T price from $825 to $260; car ownership transformed daily life and geography; car industry drove demand across steel, rubber, glass, oil; created roughly 1 in 9 US jobs.
Over time: established mass production as the model for American industry; transformed consumer culture; Ford's methods copied worldwide; helped create the conditions for the over-production that contributed to the Crash.

practice_questions.text:
'The prosperity of the 1920s was shared by all Americans.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Points for and against; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.
Agreement: real wage growth for many industrial workers; consumer goods more affordable; car ownership spread down the social scale; new industries created employment.
Disagreement: farmers suffered from low prices throughout the decade; Black Americans largely excluded from prosperity; top 5% received approximately one-third of personal income in 1929; unskilled workers' wages grew more slowly than profits; many prosperity gains financed by credit.
Judgement: boom was real but deeply unequal — the phrase 'nation of contrasts' applies directly to the gap between the prosperous middle class and struggling farmers, rural poor and minority communities.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Wannsee Conference (January 1942).
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• The Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942) was a meeting of senior Nazi officials that coordinated the bureaucratic machinery for the systematic murder of all European Jews — the 'Final Solution'. By involving multiple government departments, the conference ensured that the genocide was carried out as an organised state programme. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of opposition to the Nazi regime during the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two features identified with basic description.
Secure: Each feature described with context, e.g.:
• The White Rose student group at Munich University distributed leaflets calling for passive resistance to Hitler in 1942–43. Its leaders, Hans and Sophie Scholl, were arrested in February 1943, tried before the People's Court and executed. [2 marks]
• The July Plot (20 July 1944) was an attempt by Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg and other military officers to assassinate Hitler. The bomb failed to kill Hitler; approximately 7,000 people were arrested in reprisals, and around 4,980 were executed. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the deteriorating conditions on the German Home Front after 1943.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses the mechanism and its impact on civilian life.
Example: Allied bombing campaigns caused enormous damage to German cities and industrial production from 1943 onwards. The firebombing of Hamburg in July–August 1943 killed an estimated 37,000 civilians and left around one million homeless. Factories were destroyed or forced to disperse, disrupting military production. The psychological impact was equally significant — civilians could no longer feel safe in major German cities. The bombing consumed enormous German resources in anti-aircraft defences, diverting them from the military front.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the declaration of 'total war' in February 1943 for life in Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores longer-term consequences and links to other developments.
Example: Goebbels' declaration of total war in February 1943 led to the full mobilisation of the German economy. Women who had previously been encouraged to stay at home were drafted into factory and agricultural work, directly contradicting the pre-war Nazi ideology of Kinder, Küche, Kirche. The regime's willingness to abandon its own social policies under military pressure demonstrated the priority it placed on survival over ideology, and also showed how war transformed German society in ways that were hard to reverse.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the July Plot (1944) for the Nazi regime.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description.
Developing: Some assessment.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time.
Mastering: Weighs significance against other events; considers what the plot revealed about the regime.
At the time: The failure strengthened Hitler's belief in his destiny; approximately 7,000 arrests and around 4,980 executions followed; the role of the SS and Gestapo was enhanced relative to the traditional military.
Over time: Symbolically important — demonstrated that resistance existed even within the military and Nazi elite; the conspirators have been commemorated as evidence that 'another Germany' existed beneath the dictatorship.

practice_questions.text:
'Goebbels' propaganda was the most important factor in maintaining German civilian support during the Second World War.' How far do you agree?
In your answer consider other factors alongside propaganda and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, no judgement.
Developing: Some argument on both sides, limited evidence.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Weighs propaganda against other factors (economic conditions, fear of the SS/Gestapo, genuine belief in Nazism, military success) and argues a nuanced position.

For propaganda: Controlled all media; celebrated early victories; 'total war' speech in 1943 rallied support even after Stalingrad.
Against as most important: Fear of the Gestapo may have suppressed dissent rather than generating genuine support; economic policy (consumer goods, employment) was more material; military success in early years generated real enthusiasm; total war conditions from 1943 reduced genuine support despite propaganda.

before.exam_tip_html: For questions about the Final Solution, handle with precision: name the Wannsee Conference (January 1942), the Einsatzgruppen killings in the Soviet Union from 1941, and the death camps in occupied Poland. Avoid vague references — examiners reward specific evidence. For significance questions on the July Plot or White Rose, remember to assess both contemporary significance (immediate impact on the regime) and long-term significance (how they are remembered and what they reveal about the limits of dissent).

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the impact of the Great Depression on German society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific social impact with precise detail (e.g. by 1932 over six million officially unemployed; families unable to afford food; collapse of savings in bank failures). Secure (1–2): feature identified with some detail. Developing (1): vague reference to poverty or unemployment. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Hitler's electoral appeal between 1929 and 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise detail — e.g. Hitler promised economic recovery and jobs to the unemployed; he offered anti-communism and protection of property to the middle classes and farmers; he exploited nationalist resentment of Versailles. Secure (3): two features with development. Developing (2): two features briefly stated. Emerging (1): one feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the rapid growth of the Nazi Party's electoral support between 1928 and 1932.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear cause (e.g. the Great Depression caused mass unemployment and social despair, making voters receptive to radical promises; middle-class fear of communism drove voters to the Nazis as a bulwark against the KPD) with specific evidence and link to electoral growth. Secure (3–4): cause identified and developed. Developing (2): cause stated briefly. Emerging (1): simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the role played by the SA in German politics between 1930 and 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear consequence (e.g. SA street violence created an atmosphere of instability that discredited the Weimar Republic's ability to maintain order; this paradoxically boosted Nazi support among voters who feared chaos; OR: the SA provided a movement for unemployed young men, turning personal desperation into political energy for the Nazis). Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the role played by Franz von Papen and President Hindenburg in Hitler's appointment as Chancellor.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): significance at the time (Papen persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler, believing he could control him; significance was it bypassed democratic process) AND over time (Papen's fatal miscalculation — Hitler destroyed the constitutional order within eighteen months). Secure (5–6): both time periods addressed. Developing (3–4): mainly descriptive. Emerging (1–2): brief mention without analysis.

practice_questions.text: 'The Great Depression was the main reason why the Weimar Republic collapsed.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): sustained agreement (Depression caused mass unemployment, drove voters to extremes, paralysed Reichstag decision-making, brought existing structural weaknesses to a crisis point) AND disagreement (structural weaknesses pre-dated Depression — proportional representation, Article 48, hostile judiciary; elite scheming of Papen/Hindenburg; Hitler's own political skills and propaganda). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both sides developed; judgement present. Developing (4–6): one side stronger. Emerging (1–3): mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the campaign for equal pay for women in the 1960s and 1970s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- The 1968 Ford Dagenham strike, in which 187 women sewing machinists struck for three weeks demanding equal pay with male workers; they secured a wage increase to 92% of the male rate.
- The Equal Pay Act 1970 (in force 1975) made it illegal to pay women less than men for the same or equivalent work, a direct result of the campaign's pressure.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growth of the women's liberation movement in Britain in the late 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple cause identified, limited explanation.
Secure: Clear cause with explanation and factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation, precise evidence, chain of causation clear.

Causes may include:
- Influence of American feminist activism, particularly Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963) and the National Organization for Women (NOW, 1966), which provided a framework and inspiration for British feminists.
- The growth of women in higher education and the workforce created a generation with both higher expectations and daily experience of discrimination.
- Existing legal inequalities (unequal pay, abortion illegal, limited divorce access) provided concrete grievances around which women could organise.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Abortion Act 1967.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple consequence, limited development.
Secure: Clear consequence with explanation and evidence.
Mastering: Detailed consequence, precise evidence, wider significance addressed.

Consequences may include:
- Legal abortions were now available, ending the dangerous practice of illegal 'back-street' abortions that had caused injury and death; women's health outcomes improved.
- The Act was politically controversial, fuelling ongoing debate about women's rights over their bodies and the role of the state in personal decisions.
- It was part of a wider social liberalisation in the 1960s that changed the relationship between law and personal morality in Britain.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was the contraceptive pill in changing women's lives in Britain between 1961 and 1979? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence.
Developing: Some significance explained, basic evidence.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time addressed, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis, precise evidence, sustained argument weighing the pill's impact against other factors.

At the time: reliable contraception enabled women to plan careers around choices not pregnancies; married women's workforce participation rose; the pill contributed to changing sexual norms in the 1960s.
Over time: the pill is seen as a key enabler of second-wave feminism and the sexual revolution; its long-term effect on women's participation in the workforce was profound.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'By 1979 women had achieved genuine equality with men in Britain.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation, limited range of evidence.
Secure: Clear evaluation, agreement and disagreement addressed, factual knowledge used.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation, precise evidence, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: Equal Pay Act (1970), Sex Discrimination Act (1975), Abortion Act (1967) removed major legal barriers; the pill gave women reproductive control; first female Prime Minister elected 1979.

Disagreement: pay gap persisted due to workplace segregation; only 19 women MPs in 1979; childcare provision remained private; domestic violence not adequately addressed; women still underrepresented in senior management and professions.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Sex Discrimination Act 1975.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- The Act made it illegal to treat women less favourably than men in employment, education, and the provision of goods and services; it applied to hiring, promotion, and training decisions.
- The Equal Opportunities Commission was created to enforce the Act, providing an institutional mechanism for women to bring complaints of discrimination.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Alexander Fleming's discovery of penicillin in 1928.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with supporting detail. Example: Fleming noticed that a mould (Penicillium notatum) growing on a petri dish had killed the surrounding bacteria, suggesting the mould produced a substance that could destroy bacteria. [2 marks: 1 for feature, 1 for detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the development of penicillin as a practical medicine.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford developed a method to extract and purify penicillin in 1940–41, and tested it successfully in mice and then in a human patient. Feature 2: US government funding during the Second World War enabled mass industrial production of penicillin; by 1944 it was available to treat Allied troops in large quantities. [2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the development of penicillin for the treatment of disease in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of one consequence (e.g. bacterial infections that had previously been fatal became treatable; surgery became safer because post-operative infections could be controlled; the antibiotic era opened, transforming medicine) with embedded evidence. Secure: Clear consequence with evidence. Developing: Consequence identified, explanation limited. Emerging: Simple statement. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the work of Florey and Chain in the development of penicillin.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (converted Fleming's unusable discovery into a medicine, saved lives in WWII, demonstrated industrial-scale drug production was possible) AND over time (established the template for pharmaceutical development, launched the antibiotic era). Secure: Both dimensions with evidence. Developing: One dimension. Emerging: Description only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Marie Curie's contribution to medicine was more significant than that of Alexander Fleming.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates both sides with evidence. Curie: radiotherapy still central to cancer treatment, two Nobel Prizes, wartime X-ray units. Fleming: penicillin launched the antibiotic era, directly saved millions of lives, but dependent on Florey/Chain for practical application. Considers criteria for 'more significant' — immediate impact vs long-term impact. Substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: One side argued. Emerging: Descriptive. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How far did the treatment of disease change during the twentieth century? Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change across the century (Curie/radiotherapy 1900s; penicillin 1928/1944; Barnard transplant 1967; chemotherapy; keyhole surgery; genetic medicine), weighs against continuity (alternative medicine; some conditions still incurable), reaches substantiated judgement. Secure: Multiple developments with evidence, clear line of argument. Developing: Two or three developments, limited weighing. Emerging: Single development. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of bubonic plague.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: Bubonic plague caused large painful swellings called buboes at the lymph nodes [1]; these typically appeared in the armpit, groin or neck and, without treatment, killed approximately half to two thirds of those infected within days [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the way the Black Death spread in England.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: The plague spread along trade and communication routes [1], reaching England through southern ports in summer 1348 and moving northward to Scotland within approximately eighteen months [1]. Feature 2: Urban overcrowding and poor sanitation aided spread [1] — waste in streets, ubiquitous rats and fleas in every settlement created ideal conditions for the flea-borne bubonic form to pass to humans [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the high death rate during the Black Death in England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (miasma theory preventing effective action; pneumonic form's airborne transmission; malnutrition weakening immunity; congregation for prayer spreading infection) and explains it in depth with precise factual knowledge. Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with relevant factual support. Developing: States a cause with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference without specific factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the contemporary belief that the Black Death was God's punishment for sin.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains a consequence in depth — e.g. mass religious gatherings (flagellant processions, communal prayer) may have accelerated the spread; the Church's failure to stop the plague through prayer damaged its authority; the desperate search for explanations led to persecution of Jewish communities in mainland Europe. Secure: Explains a consequence with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Black Death's arrival in 1348 to the history of England in this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (overwhelming mortality, collapse of Church pastoral care, abandonment of villages) and over time (population decline drove labour shortages, wage rises, and Statute of Labourers in 1351; ultimately contributed to conditions that produced the Peasants' Revolt in 1381). Precise factual knowledge throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes the Black Death without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The main reason the Black Death killed so many people was the lack of medical knowledge at the time.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with precise factual knowledge. Agrees: miasma theory and religious explanations prevented effective preventive action; physicians had no understanding of bacteria, fleas or rats as vectors; congregations for prayer may have spread the disease. Disagrees: structural factors were equally important — poor sanitation, urban overcrowding, malnutrition and trade routes would have facilitated spread even with better medical knowledge; pneumonic plague's airborne transmission was virtually impossible to prevent without modern medicine. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence. Developing: Describes features without evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple response; no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the County of Edessa.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students may describe: it was the northernmost and most exposed crusader state; it was founded in 1098 by Baldwin of Boulogne; it lacked natural defensive boundaries; it was surrounded by Muslim-ruled territory; it was the first crusader state to fall, in 1144. 1 mark for a simple point; 2 marks for a developed point.

practice_questions.text: Describe two difficulties faced by the crusader states after their establishment.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should identify two difficulties with supporting detail.
Difficulty 1: The Latin ruling class was a tiny minority governing a much larger Muslim, Christian and Jewish population; military manpower was always scarce and relied on reinforcements from Europe.
Difficulty 2: The four states had separate rulers and frequently failed to cooperate militarily; disputes between leaders prevented unified responses to Muslim threats.
2 marks per difficulty: 1 mark for a simple point, 2 marks for a developed point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the difficulties faced by the crusader states in maintaining themselves in the Levant.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (e.g. demographic imbalance between Latin settlers and indigenous population; lack of unified command; dependence on Italian maritime cities; fragile feudal military system) and explains it with precise detail and links it clearly to the difficulty faced. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a cause with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a cause but limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Pullani for understanding life in the crusader states.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At the time — the Pullani's cultural adaptation allowed crusader states to function economically and politically in a multi-faith society; their Arabic knowledge made them effective diplomats and administrators. Over time — their existence showed that Western and Eastern cultures could coexist in Outremer; but their accommodation also created tension with new crusaders, weakening crusading ideology. Sustained judgement.
Secure: Covers both dimensions with evidence.
Developing: Mainly covers one dimension.
Emerging: Describes the Pullani with little sense of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the small size of the Latin settler population in the crusader states.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific consequence (chronic military shortage; dependence on Italian fleets; need to recruit military orders; cultural accommodation with local populations; dependence on indigenous labour) and explains it with precise detail. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a consequence with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a consequence but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: 'The crusader states' greatest challenge was their small military population.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues in support (small settler class could not defend extended borders without reinforcements; feudal levy produced limited forces; comparison with Muslim neighbours who could mobilise much larger armies) and against (internal political divisions were equally damaging; Muslim fragmentation was as important as crusader strength; the castle system and military orders partially compensated for manpower shortages; diplomatic failures were as damaging as military ones). Substantiated judgement.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence; conclusion reached.
Developing: Mainly one-sided, limited evidence.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Aztec tribute system.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (e.g. subject towns paid goods twice yearly / goods included maize, textiles, gold, cacao / failure to pay resulted in military punishment). Two marks for a developed explanation of its significance for Aztec power.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Tenochtitlán that made it an impressive city by early sixteenth-century standards.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was built on an island in Lake Texcoco, connected by three great causeways, with canals and an aqueduct supply system.
• It had a population of 200,000–300,000 — larger than any contemporary European city.
• At its centre stood the Templo Mayor, a massive pyramid dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc.
• The market at Tlatelolco was described by Spanish observers as larger and better organised than any in Europe.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of human sacrifice in Aztec religion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the cosmological belief that Huitzilopochtli required human blood to sustain the movement of the sun, and develops this fully — the Aztecs believed the sun would stop if sacrifice ceased, meaning all life would end; the “Flower Wars” with neighbouring states were specifically organised to supply captives for this purpose; links to the Templo Mayor as the central site.
Secure: Identifies a cause with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Aztec tribute system for the peoples of central Mexico.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the tribute system created deep resentment among subject peoples who paid goods and supplied sacrificial victims; this resentment meant that groups like the Tlaxcalans were willing to ally with Cortés against the Aztecs in 1519 — a consequence that directly contributed to the empire’s fall. Links specific evidence.
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Aztec codices as a historical source.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (codices recorded history, religion, tribute and astronomical knowledge; scribes maintained cultural memory; destroyed by Spanish, so pre-conquest ones are rare) AND over time (post-conquest codices like the Florentine Codex are the main written record of Aztec civilisation; used by historians to understand Aztec society from an indigenous perspective). Developed with evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with evidence; may lack the over-time dimension fully.
Developing: Describes what codices are without fully analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Human sacrifice was the most important feature of Aztec civilisation.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• Human sacrifice was central to Aztec cosmology — without it, the Aztecs believed the sun would stop; it shaped political and military strategy (Flower Wars, tribute of captives).
• It was the feature that most shocked Spanish observers and shaped European representations of the Aztecs.
• The Templo Mayor — the physical and spiritual heart of the empire — was primarily a sacrificial site.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• The tribute system was arguably more important as the economic foundation of Aztec power; it sustained the capital, funded warfare and bound hundreds of towns into the empire.
• Tenochtitlán’s urban sophistication (grid plan, aqueducts, large population) reflects advanced civilisation beyond religion.
• The codices show a complex intellectual and administrative culture that goes far beyond sacrifice.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive, no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of mystery plays in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with detail: e.g. performed on wagons by town guilds on the feast of Corpus Christi / dramatised Bible stories from Creation to the Last Judgement / the York and Chester cycles are the most famous surviving examples. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Elizabethan playhouse.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. open-air, circular, three-tiered structures accommodating thousands of spectators (feature + detail of the Globe in Southwark); penny admission in the pit made theatre accessible to all social classes including apprentices and craftsmen (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why theatre became popular with ordinary Londoners in the Elizabethan period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking penny admission, central Southwark location, range of content (tragedy, comedy, history) and performance quality to broad popular appeal; evidence-based. Secure: Clear explanation with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the closure of theatres by Parliament in 1642.
