practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Consequence developed, e.g. eighteen years of suppression ended the tradition of public outdoor theatre; when theatres reopened in 1660, the Restoration format was different (indoor, women on stage, scenic). Specific evidence. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant were music halls in the development of popular entertainment in Victorian Britain?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (dominant entertainment venue, national celebrities, 200+ London halls by 1860s) AND over time (model for variety theatre, television light entertainment format). Uses evidence. Secure: Clear analysis with examples. Developing: Some points. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Popular entertainment in Britain became increasingly accessible to ordinary people between c.500 and 1900.' How far do you agree with this view?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substantiated judgement tracing accessibility across all three eras. Agrees: mystery plays (communal/free), penny admission at Globe, mass music halls. Challenges: Elizabethan theatre still excluded women from the stage; music halls catered to urban workers, not rural poor. Weighs change vs continuity. Overall conclusion. Secure: Evidence from at least two eras, some weighing. Developing: Limited range. Emerging: Basic agree/disagree. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Act of Supremacy (1559).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with supporting detail, e.g. the Act of Supremacy gave Elizabeth the title 'Supreme Governor' of the Church of England, a more cautious claim than Henry VIII's 'Supreme Head' (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Elizabeth's Religious Settlement of 1559.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: precise feature with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth Supreme Governor; Act of Uniformity made church attendance compulsory; twelve-pence fine for non-attendance; compromise Book of Common Prayer introduced; Royal Injunctions instructed clergy; retained clerical vestments. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Act of Uniformity (1559) for English Catholics.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a detailed chain linking the Act to outcomes, e.g. the Act made church attendance compulsory and fined absentees twelve pence per absence — this created the category of 'recusants' (Catholics who paid the fines rather than attend) whose loyalty was publicly uncertain, laying the groundwork for the Catholic threat of the 1570s. Secure: clear consequence with some evidence. Developing: relevant consequence with limited development. Emerging: simple point. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Religious Settlement of 1559 for the stability of Elizabeth's reign.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (established royal authority over the Church; created workable religious stability; avoided open religious war) AND over time (provided the foundation for the permanent Church of England). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation. Emerging: simple descriptive points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a sermon preached by a bishop in 1560 praising the Religious Settlement as a godly compromise for understanding how Elizabethans responded to the settlement?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (the bishop's praise), provenance (a bishop — appointed by Elizabeth, whose authority depended on the settlement; likely to present a favourable view) and contextual knowledge (most clergy did conform; but recusants and Puritans were also real responses) to give a substantiated judgement. Secure: addresses two elements. Developing: mainly describes source content. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'The Religious Settlement of 1559 was a complete success for Elizabeth I.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: argues for (survived the whole reign; provided workable stability; avoided civil war; established Church of England permanently) AND against (displeased Puritans who wanted further reform; created recusants who were a potential security threat; Pope excommunicated Elizabeth in 1570; enforcement was uneven) before a substantiated judgement. Secure: both sides with evidence and clear conclusion. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: simple. Maximum 12 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the National Health Service when it was launched in 1948.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• The NHS provided free medical treatment at the point of use, including GP visits, hospital care, dental and optical treatment.
• It was funded by national taxation rather than fees paid by patients.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the nationalisation programme carried out by the Attlee government.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• Between 1946 and 1951, key industries including coal, railways, electricity, gas and steel were transferred to public ownership.
• Nationalisation aimed to ensure strategic industries served the national interest rather than private profit.
• Management structures largely remained unchanged after nationalisation, limiting the transformation in practice.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the creation of the National Health Service in 1948 was significant.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. free healthcare reduced the link between poverty and illness; or demonstrated that the state could deliver universal services effectively) and develops a chain — millions who previously could not afford treatment now accessed care, the principle of healthcare as a right was established, and the NHS became a foundational institution defended by all major parties.
Secure: Names a consequence with a clear linked explanation and some development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Labour's landslide election victory in 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. the Beveridge Report 1942 creating public expectation of welfare reform, or popular rejection of the pre-war Conservative governments associated with unemployment and appeasement) and develops the mechanism in detail — wartime experience of collective solutions, soldiers who remembered the Depression voting for change, the Beveridge Report raising expectations of a better post-war Britain.
Secure: Names a clear cause and provides a linked explanation with development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without identifying a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Beveridge Report (1942) in shaping post-war Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (gave the public a clear vision of post-war reform, influenced the 1945 election, shaped Labour’s programme) AND over time (underpinned the welfare state created 1945–1951, established principles that remained central to British politics for decades). Weighs extent: Report was a plan not a policy; Attlee’s government had to fight to implement it.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions with clear explanation.
Developing: Addresses one dimension only.
Emerging: Describes the Report without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The creation of the NHS was the most important development in Britain between 1945 and 1960.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the NHS’s importance alongside other developments (nationalisation, education reform, rising affluence, housing). Weighs factors with evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement on relative importance.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on the NHS and at least one other development. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the feudal levy as a method of military recruitment.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• The feudal levy required lords and barons to provide knights to the king in exchange for their land grants [1], typically for a period of around forty days per year [1].
• Below the knights, the fyrd — ordinary freemen — could also be called up in emergencies [1+1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Pals Battalions in the First World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature:
• Feature 1: Men were recruited from the same town, workplace or community [1], with the promise that they would serve alongside friends and neighbours [1].
• Feature 2: While this created strong unit cohesion [1], it meant that heavy casualties fell disproportionately on single communities — the Accrington Pals suffered approximately 585 casualties on the first day of the Somme [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why conscription was introduced in Britain in 1916.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that voluntary recruitment had been successful initially (over a million men by early 1915) but that the scale of casualties on the Western Front, particularly during 1915, meant that voluntary enlistment could no longer replace losses fast enough. The Military Service Act (January 1916) introduced conscription for unmarried men aged 18–41 as a direct response. Analyses the wider context: the nature of industrial warfare, which consumed men at a rate no pre-industrial society would have recognised.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence.
Developing: Identifies the reason with limited analysis.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the New Model Army in the development of British military recruitment and training.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues significance at the time (1645 victories at Naseby and Langport ended the Civil War) and over time (established the principle of merit-based professional armies, regular pay, and systematic training that influenced all subsequent British army organisation). Concludes on why it was a landmark in the history of recruitment.
Secure: Explains significance with supporting evidence.
Developing: Identifies significance with limited development.
Emerging: Describes the New Model Army without evaluating significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did the methods used to recruit British soldiers change between c.500 and the present day?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues for and against significant change. For change: feudal obligation → professional army (1645) → propaganda/conscription (1914–18, 1939–45) → all-volunteer professional force (1960–present). Against: the need for training and discipline has been constant across all eras; voluntary service has existed alongside compulsion in most periods. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Arguments for and against with evidence; concludes.
Developing: Some argument, limited evidence.
Emerging: Describes rather than evaluates.

practice_questions.text: How far did Britain's approach to recruitment change between c.1500 and the present day? In your answer, refer to the New Model Army, conscription and modern professional service.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces change across early modern (Tudor militia → New Model Army 1645), modern industrial era (press gangs → Kitchener volunteers 1914 → conscription 1916 → National Service 1947–60) and contemporary (all-volunteer professional since 1960). Weighs change against continuity (discipline and training always central; voluntary ethos recurring). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Covers three periods with evidence and some change/continuity analysis.
Developing: Two periods covered, limited analysis.
Emerging: One period, no analytical framework.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Operation Barbarossa, launched in June 1941.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: the invasion covered a front of over 2,000 kilometres; it was the largest land invasion in history; three German army groups struck simultaneously; the Red Army was caught unprepared.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Battle of Stalingrad (1942–1943).
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: brutal street fighting in the city that reduced it to rubble; Soviet Operation Uranus in November 1942 encircled the German Sixth Army; General Paulus surrendered with approximately 91,000 survivors on 2 February 1943; it was Germany's first major defeat on the Eastern Front.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Soviet Union’s disorganised response to Operation Barbarossa in 1941.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates should identify a cause and explain why it led to the poor Soviet response. Key cause: the purge of the Red Army's officer corps in 1937-38 had removed thousands of experienced commanders; Stalin's refusal to believe intelligence warnings of a German attack also prevented adequate preparation.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise cause, causal chain explained, specific knowledge.
Secure: cause identified and explained with relevant knowledge.
Developing: cause identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point with no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Battle of Stalingrad for the outcome of the Second World War on the Eastern Front.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: Germany's first major defeat; encirclement and destruction of the Sixth Army; loss of approximately 300,000 German troops. Over time: strategic initiative shifted to the Soviet Union permanently; Soviet forces advanced westward for the rest of the war, eventually reaching Berlin in 1945.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of the Soviet war effort:

“The Soviet Union won the Great Patriotic War despite Stalin’s leadership, not because of it.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge of Soviet history in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: Stalin's pre-war purge of the officer corps weakened the Red Army; he ignored intelligence warnings before Barbarossa; early Soviet defeats were catastrophic; Stalin's initial paralysis after 22 June 1941 left the country leaderless at a critical moment.

Disagreement: Stalin rallied the nation with his broadcasts in July 1941; the relocation of Soviet industry eastward before the German advance was a remarkable logistical achievement; Stalin coordinated the war effort through the State Defence Committee (GKO); the personality cult helped maintain civilian morale.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Second World War in changing the Soviet Union between 1941 and 1950? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement.

Significant changes: USSR emerged as a superpower with a nuclear programme; territory expanded (Baltic states, parts of Poland, eastern Germany); liberation of Eastern Europe gave USSR a buffer zone of satellite states; war accelerated industrialisation in the Urals and Siberia.

Continuity/limits of change: Stalin's personal dictatorship continued unchanged; the Terror resumed after the war; living standards remained low; post-war famine 1946-47; political system did not liberalise.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing changes and continuities, clear judgement.
Secure: two or more factors explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: factors listed, limited weighing.
Emerging: one factor or descriptive throughout.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: The WSPU used militant tactics (1), including window-smashing, arson of post boxes and hunger strikes in prison, to pressure the government (1). Mastering: accurate feature with supporting detail. Developing: feature stated but undeveloped.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the campaign of the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies (NUWSS).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature examples: peaceful and constitutional methods only; petitions with hundreds of thousands of signatures; lobbying sympathetic MPs; public meetings; by 1913 had ~54,000 members in 400+ local societies; led by Millicent Fawcett. Mastering: two precise features with accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the WSPU adopted increasingly militant tactics after 1908.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Frustration at the failure of peaceful methods — several private members' bills had come close to passing but been blocked; Asquith personally opposed women's suffrage; the Liberal government, despite progressive credentials, repeatedly refused to act; the Suffragettes concluded that peaceful petitioning was insufficient to force change on an obstinate government. Secure (3–4): clear cause with some development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Emily Davison's death at the 1913 Epsom Derby.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Her death drew massive international attention to women's suffrage; her funeral procession through London attracted tens of thousands of supporters and was widely reported; it created a powerful martyr figure for the WSPU; it hardened both pro- and anti-suffrage opinion — some were moved by her sacrifice, while opponents used the incident to argue that militancy was irrational and dangerous. Secure (3–4): clear consequence with development. Developing (1–2): simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of women's wartime service (1914–1918) for the women's suffrage movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): At the time: women in munitions, nursing, land army and transport made the argument that they were unfit to vote almost impossible to sustain; politicians on all sides acknowledged women's contribution. Over time: directly contributed to the Representation of the People Act 1918 granting votes to women over 30; established the precedent that led to equal suffrage in 1928; transformed the social role of women and expectations about gender equality throughout the twentieth century. Secure (5–6): both dimensions with development. Developing (3–4): mainly one dimension. Emerging (1–2): simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'Militant tactics were the main reason women won the vote in 1918.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Agrees and disagrees, substantiated, overall judgement. Agree: WSPU militancy kept suffrage in public debate; embarrassed the government; martyrdom of Davison and prison hunger strikes attracted sympathy; forced the issue before the war. Disagree: the 1918 Act was triggered by the wartime electoral register problem (men lost residence qualification); women's wartime service changed political opinion; the age restriction (30+, not 21) suggests government was rewarding service not responding to militancy; NUWSS's patient lobbying created the legal and political groundwork. Balanced judgement: militancy maintained the campaign's profile but wartime service and the NUWSS's constitutional work were arguably more decisive in 1918. Secure (7–9): both arguments with development. Developing (4–6): limited. Emerging (1–3): one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Warsaw Pact, established in 1955.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: it was a Soviet-led military alliance of Eastern European communist states; it was formed as a direct response to NATO; members were required to support each other militarily; it gave the USSR formal military leadership over Eastern European states.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: the USA discovered Soviet nuclear missiles being installed in Cuba in October 1962; President Kennedy and Khrushchev faced a 13-day stand-off; the crisis was resolved with Soviet withdrawal of missiles in exchange for US pledges not to invade Cuba; a direct communication hotline was established between Washington and Moscow afterwards.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the collapse of the wartime alliance between the Soviet Union and the Western powers after 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates should identify a cause and explain why it led to the breakdown. Key causes: ideological differences between communism and capitalism that had always existed; Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe and refusal to allow free elections; the Truman Doctrine (1947) which committed the USA to containing communism.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise cause, causal chain explained, specific knowledge.
Secure: cause identified and explained with relevant knowledge.
Developing: cause identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point with no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 for Cold War relations.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: ended the era of détente; triggered US boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics; led to American support for mujahideen fighters. Over time: the nine-year war killed approximately 15,000 Soviet soldiers, damaged Soviet prestige, strained the economy and contributed to the conditions that produced Gorbachev's reforms and ultimately Soviet collapse.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of Cold War tensions:

“The Soviet Union was more responsible than the United States for causing and prolonging the Cold War.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: Soviet refusal to allow free elections in Eastern Europe broke wartime agreements; formation of Soviet satellite states created the Iron Curtain; the Berlin Wall was built to prevent emigration; the Brezhnev Doctrine justified Soviet intervention in sovereign states; invasion of Afghanistan was unprovoked aggression.

Disagreement: the Truman Doctrine of 1947 committed the USA to global anti-communism; the Marshall Plan excluded Eastern Europe, deepening division; Reagan's 'Second Cold War' military build-up was provocative; American nuclear monopoly (1945-49) forced Soviet nuclear development.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: How far did Cold War tensions change between 1945 and 1991? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement weighing change against continuity.

Change: from open confrontation (Berlin Blockade 1948) to arms control treaties (SALT I 1972); détente in the 1970s; Gorbachev's ending of the Cold War in the late 1980s.

Continuity: nuclear threat remained throughout; proxy conflicts continued (Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan); ideological competition never fully ended until 1991.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing change and continuity, clear judgement.
Secure: two or more factors or periods explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: factors listed, limited weighing.
Emerging: one factor or descriptive throughout.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of youth culture in Britain in the 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• Young people had greater spending power than previous generations, fuelling a boom in fashion, records and consumer goods.
• London became an international centre of fashion, with designers like Mary Quant introducing the mini-skirt.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Race Relations Act of 1965.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• The 1965 Act was the first legislation in Britain to make racial discrimination in public places unlawful.
• It applied to places such as restaurants and hotels but lacked strong enforcement mechanisms.
• It was the first step in a legislative programme extended by the 1968 Act to cover employment and housing.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the social reforms known as the 'permissive society' in the 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. changing social attitudes driven by youth culture, rising living standards, access to the contraceptive pill, or political will under Roy Jenkins as Home Secretary) and develops the mechanism in detail — how the cause led to specific legislative reforms and the wider cultural shift.
Secure: Names a clear cause with a linked explanation and some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without identifying a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Commonwealth migration to Britain in the 1950s and 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. racial tensions leading to riots, or the government introducing immigration controls, or the development of Race Relations legislation) and develops a chain — showing how the consequence unfolded and what further effects it had.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation of a consequence with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Enoch Powell's 'Rivers of Blood' speech of 1968 for British politics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (immediate political impact — dismissal from Shadow Cabinet, polarisation of opinion, dock workers’ march in support) AND over time (shaped Conservative politics on immigration for decades, contributed to hardening of immigration law, made race a permanent feature of British political debate). Weighs limits: speech did not directly change government policy in the short term.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions with clear explanation.
Developing: Addresses one dimension only.
Emerging: Describes the speech without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The 1960s transformed the lives of all British people.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges real changes (legal reforms, cultural revolution, immigration) but also challenges the extent (change concentrated in urban, young, middle-class groups; most working-class lives changed less dramatically; traditional attitudes persisted). Weighs evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence for and against transformation. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of early British cinema in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with detail: e.g. purpose-built picture palaces were constructed in the 1920s offering a glamorous escape / silent films were accompanied by live piano or organ music / cinema became the most popular form of mass entertainment for urban working-class audiences. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the development of television in Britain between 1936 and 1970.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. the BBC launched the world's first regular public television service in November 1936 (feature + detail); colour television was introduced on BBC2 in 1967, with BBC1 and ITV following in 1969, transforming the viewing experience (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why cinema attendance fell sharply in Britain during the 1950s and 1960s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed causal explanation linking rising television ownership (driven by the 1953 coronation and ITV launch in 1955), the convenience of home viewing, and the licence-fee model making television effectively free at the point of use. Specific evidence. Secure: Clear cause with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the introduction of ITV in 1955 for British television audiences.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Consequence developed, e.g. competition broke the BBC’s monopoly, improved programming quality, drove faster television adoption, introduced advertising-funded content distinct from the licence-fee model. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was the introduction of talking pictures in 1927 for the development of British cinema?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (rapid conversion of cinemas to sound equipment, audience growth, transformation of the film industry) AND over time (sound became the new baseline; silent film never returned; Hollywood dominance grew). Uses evidence. Secure: Clear analysis with examples. Developing: Some points. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Television was the single most important development in British entertainment in the twentieth century.' How far do you agree? Use evidence from the period 1896 to the present in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substantiated judgement weighing television against cinema, streaming, radio and music. Agrees with evidence (mass adoption, 1953 coronation, replacing cinema dominance, fragmented viewing). Challenges by noting cinema's peak was pre-television; streaming represents a further transformation; radio was also transformative (see 1920s). Traces the full modern period. Overall conclusion. Secure: Addresses both sides with evidence. Developing: Limited range. Emerging: Basic agree/disagree. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Profumo Affair of 1963.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- John Profumo, Secretary of State for War, lied to Parliament about his affair with Christine Keeler; on admission, he resigned in June 1963.
- The affair raised national security concerns because Keeler was also linked to Yevgeny Ivanov, a Soviet naval attaché; the scandal contributed to Macmillan's resignation and the Conservatives' 1964 election defeat.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growth of CND (Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament) in the late 1950s and early 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple cause identified, limited explanation.
Secure: Clear cause with explanation and factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation, precise evidence, chain of causation clear.

Causes may include:
- Growing public fear of nuclear war after British nuclear tests and the escalation of the Cold War arms race; the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) brought the world to the brink of nuclear war, swelling CND membership.
- Moral argument from scientists and clergy that nuclear weapons threatened mass civilian casualties and were ethically unacceptable.
- Opposition to Britain's dependence on American nuclear strategy and support for a specifically British 'third way' through unilateral disarmament.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Sexual Offences Act 1967.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple consequence, limited development.
Secure: Clear consequence with explanation and evidence.
Mastering: Detailed consequence, precise evidence, wider significance addressed.

Consequences may include:
- Private consensual acts between men aged 21 or over were no longer criminal; gay men could live without the immediate threat of prosecution, though discrimination in employment and public life continued.
- The Act was a partial reform with significant limitations (age 21 not 16; excluded armed forces); campaigners argued for full equality, which took decades to achieve.
- The 1967 Act began a legislative process that eventually produced equal age of consent (2001) and same-sex marriage (2014).

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant were the student protests of 1968 in challenging authority in Britain? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence.
Developing: Some significance explained, basic evidence.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time addressed, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis, precise evidence, sustained argument.

At the time: 10,000 marched to Grosvenor Square; 246 arrested; university sit-ins spread; pressure for student representation in governance.
Over time: limited long-term impact on UK political structures compared to France; but part of a broader generational shift away from deference that shaped 1970s political culture.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The social reforms of the 1960s made Britain a more tolerant and fair society.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation, limited range of evidence.
Secure: Clear evaluation, agreement and disagreement addressed, factual knowledge used.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation, precise evidence, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: Sexual Offences Act (1967) freed gay men from criminal prosecution; abolition of death penalty ended risk of executing the innocent; abortion Act saved women's lives; divorce reform freed people from unhappy marriages.

Disagreement: reforms were limited in scope (e.g. homosexuality for men aged 21+ only, not in armed forces); public attitudes remained hostile in many areas; women still faced discrimination; racial discrimination remained widespread (see immigration lesson); 'tolerance' was not equally available to all groups.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of CND's campaign methods in the late 1950s and early 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Annual marches between Aldermaston (Atomic Weapons Establishment) and London drew tens of thousands; the first march in Easter 1958 attracted an estimated 4,000 participants.
- CND used the peace symbol (designed by Gerald Holtom in 1958) as a highly visible and internationally recognised symbol of the nuclear disarmament cause.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Edwardian music hall.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: The music hall was a form of variety entertainment (1) performed in purpose-built theatres with comedy, song, dance and novelty acts, attracting audiences across social classes (1). Mastering: accurate feature with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Edwardian cinema.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature examples: moving pictures arrived in Britain in 1896; early films were short novelties shown at music halls; by 1914 there were over 3,000 cinemas; cheap admission (penny or twopence) made it accessible to the poor; first truly democratic mass entertainment. Mastering: two precise features with accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which Edwardian literature reflected the social concerns of the period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Developed explanation with specific author and work. E.g. H.G. Wells's The War of the Worlds (1898) reflected anxieties about empire — the Martian invasion can be read as an inversion of British imperial conquest, asking what it would feel like to be on the receiving end of a technologically superior invader; Wells also wrote Ann Veronica (1909), sympathetically portraying the suffragette movement. Shaw's Pygmalion (1913) attacked the class system's obsession with accent. Secure (3–4): clear point with some development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the rise of mass spectator sport in Edwardian Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Football became a central ritual of working-class life; the 1901 FA Cup Final attracted over 110,000 spectators, showing the scale of popular engagement; the growth of professional football created a new leisure industry (clubs, stadiums, pools betting) that generated income and employment; it provided a shared cultural identity for working-class communities separated from political power. Secure (3–4): clear consequence with development. Developing (1–2): simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the development of cinema in Edwardian Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): At the time: first truly democratic mass entertainment (cheap, accessible to the poor); by 1914, 3,000+ cinemas and millions of weekly viewers; provided shared cultural experience cutting across class. Over time: cinema became central to twentieth-century culture and shaped how events (including the First World War) were perceived and commemorated; the newsreel tradition born in this period shaped public information. Secure (5–6): both dimensions developed. Developing (3–4): mainly one dimension. Emerging (1–2): simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'Edwardian literature was primarily concerned with social criticism.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Agree and disagree, substantiated, overall judgement. Agree: Shaw's plays explicitly attacked class and gender inequality; Hardy's novels exposed social injustice and class; Wells used science fiction to interrogate empire and gender; many writers were linked to socialist or suffrage movements. Disagree: Beatrix Potter's books were primarily aimed at entertaining children, not social commentary; much popular culture (music hall, cinema) was escapist entertainment; even Shaw's comedy was entertainment as much as polemic. Balanced: social criticism was a dominant strain but coexisted with entertainment; the era was diverse enough to contain both. Secure (7–9): argument both ways. Developing (4–6): limited. Emerging (1–3): one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Statute of Labourers of 1351.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: The Statute of Labourers fixed wages at the levels that had prevailed before the Black Death [1]; it also forbade labourers from leaving their place of work to seek higher pay elsewhere, with fines for employers who offered more than the legal rate [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the labour shortage that followed the Black Death.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: The massive population decline meant there were not enough workers to farm the land [1]; lords competed for surviving labourers by offering higher wages, reversing the pre-plague surplus of agricultural workers [1]. Feature 2: Many serfs, who were legally bound to their lords' manors, simply left to seek work elsewhere [1]; lords were often too desperate for labour to pursue them effectively, undermining the legal basis of serfdom [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the resentment created by the Statute of Labourers.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (the Statute reversed economic gains survivors had made; it was an explicit use of state power to benefit lords at workers' expense; enforcement by Justices of the Peace was resented as class bias) and explains it in depth with precise factual knowledge. Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with relevant factual support. Developing: States a cause with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference without specific factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Black Death for the culture of fourteenth-century England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains a cultural consequence in depth — e.g. the memento mori tradition produced art, poetry and church paintings reflecting on human mortality and death as the great leveller; or the failure of the Church to prevent the epidemic damaged its authority. Secure: Explains a consequence with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Statute of Labourers (1351) to the history of England between 1348 and 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (attempted to reverse the economic gains of survivors; created deep resentment; shows the ruling class's determination to maintain the pre-plague social order) and over time (its enforcement contributed directly to the conditions that produced the Peasants' Revolt of 1381; its ultimate failure showed the limits of law against structural economic change). Precise factual knowledge throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes the Statute without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The Statute of Labourers of 1351 made the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 inevitable.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with precise factual knowledge. Agrees: the Statute created deep resentment; its enforcement was seen as class exploitation; it represented the ruling class's refusal to accept the economic changes the Black Death had brought. Disagrees: other causes were also important — the Poll Tax of 1380/1381, the cost of the French wars, the religious ideas of John Ball, and the issue of serfdom all contributed; calling the Revolt 'inevitable' overstates the Statute's single importance. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence. Developing: Describes features without evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple response; no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the trebuchet as a medieval siege weapon.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• The trebuchet used a heavy counterweight [1] to hurl stones or other projectiles at castle walls, capable of throwing objects weighing up to approximately 150 kg [1].
• It was a siege weapon requiring significant engineering [1+1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the introduction of gunpowder weapons in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature:
• Feature 1: Early cannon (artillery) could demolish medieval stone walls [1], making the castle obsolete as a military stronghold from the mid fifteenth century [1].
• Feature 2: The flintlock musket, standard from the mid seventeenth century, combined a more reliable firing mechanism [1] with the bayonet, giving infantry both ranged and close-combat capability [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the development of the Maxim gun (1884) was significant for British military power.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains how the Maxim gun’s automatic firing mechanism (~600 rounds per minute) gave British colonial forces an overwhelming firepower advantage over opponents without comparable weapons. Analyses the longer-term consequence: that the same technology, when deployed by both sides in 1914, would make offensive infantry tactics extremely costly and contribute to trench warfare.
Secure: Clear explanation with supporting evidence.
Developing: Identifies the Maxim gun’s significance with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the change in British weapons technology between c.1300 and c.1900.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces change from longbow (effective but requiring lifetime training) → matchlock and flintlock muskets (gunpowder; slower but less training required) → rifled musket (1840s; longer range) → breech-loading rifle and Maxim gun (1860s–1884; industrially produced, much higher rate of fire). Explains why each shift occurred (technology, industrial capacity, tactical demand) and reaches a conclusion about the most significant change.
Secure: Covers at least two stages with evidence and explanation.
Developing: One stage with limited analysis.
Emerging: Describes a weapon without analysing change.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Industrial Revolution in changing British weapons technology in the nineteenth century?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues significance at the time (mass production of standardised rifles; Maxim gun in colonial campaigns) and over time (the same technology applied to European warfare in 1914 created the conditions for the Western Front stalemate). Concludes on degree of significance compared to earlier technological changes.
Secure: Explains significance with two examples and some analysis.
Developing: One example, limited analysis.
Emerging: Describes industrialisation without evaluating significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did the technology used in British warfare change between c.500 and c.1900? In your answer, refer to at least two major technological developments.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces change across medieval (trebuchet, longbow), early modern (gunpowder → matchlock → flintlock), and industrial modern (rifling, breech-loading, Maxim gun). Identifies continuity (competition between offensive and defensive technology is constant across all eras). Weighs change against continuity and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Covers at least two eras with evidence and some analysis of change/continuity.
Developing: Two developments described, limited analysis.
Emerging: One development, no analytical framework.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Kennedy's 'New Frontier' domestic programme.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names feature (plans for Medicare; federal aid to education; civil rights legislation; tackling poverty) AND develops it. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Watergate scandal (1972-1974).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) In June 1972 operatives from Nixon's re-election campaign broke into Democratic Party headquarters at the Watergate Hotel to plant listening devices; (2) Nixon participated in covering up White House involvement and resigned on 9 August 1974 when impeachment became inevitable. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Nixon's resignation in 1974.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (the cover-up; White House tape recordings; Supreme Court ruling in United States v Nixon; Congressional investigations) AND develops the chain of reasoning explaining how it led to resignation. Secure: Cause with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Reaganomics for American society in the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (reduced inflation and economic growth; increased income inequality; growth of national debt; cuts to social programmes affecting poor Americans; deregulation of industries) AND develops the chain of effects. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Watergate scandal for US political development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (first presidential resignation; collapse of public trust in government; congressional investigations limiting executive power; War Powers Act 1973) AND over time (lasting decline in public trust in political institutions; 'gate' suffix for scandals; precedent for presidential accountability; contrast with Clinton's survival of impeachment). Secure: One time frame well-covered. Developing: Describes Watergate without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'The most significant political change in the USA between 1960 and 2000 was the shift from liberal to conservative politics.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues the case for (Kennedy/LBJ Great Society liberalism gave way to Reagan's conservatism from 1980; tax cuts replaced social spending; deregulation reversed New Deal era regulation; Clinton's Third Way accepted conservative economic framework) AGAINST (civil rights legislation under LBJ a major liberal change; Watergate showed limits of executive power; Clinton's social liberalism on healthcare and welfare). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes presidents without developing an argument. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the work of Andreas Vesalius.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with supporting detail. Example: Vesalius conducted systematic human dissections and published De Humani Corporis Fabrica in 1543, correcting over 200 errors in Galen's anatomy — such as showing the human jaw is a single bone, not two. [2 marks: 1 for feature, 1 for detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Robert Koch's contribution to medical knowledge.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: Koch developed techniques to isolate and culture specific bacteria and proved that particular bacteria caused particular diseases, identifying the bacterium for tuberculosis in 1882 and cholera in 1883. Feature 2: Koch developed Koch's postulates — a set of criteria for proving a specific bacterium causes a specific disease — providing a scientific framework for bacteriology. [2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Galen's medical theories remained dominant in Europe for over 1,000 years.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of one reason (e.g. Church backing of ancient authority; lack of printing to spread alternatives; training of physicians to reconcile observation with theory rather than to question it; absence of dissection due to religious restrictions) with embedded evidence. Secure: Clear cause with evidence. Developing: Cause identified, explanation limited. Emerging: Simple statement. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of William Harvey's discovery of the circulation of blood in 1628.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (directly contradicted Galen, demonstrated circulation vs liver-production, established experiment as the method) AND over time (foundation of understanding cardiovascular disease, surgical techniques, blood transfusion). Secure: Both dimensions with evidence. Developing: One dimension. Emerging: Description only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The discovery of germ theory was the most significant advance in medical knowledge in British history.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates germ theory's significance (enabled vaccines, antiseptics, antibiotics, public health reform) AND challenges with other candidates (Harvey's circulation, DNA double helix, scanning technology). Considers criteria for 'most significant'. Substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: One side argued. Emerging: Descriptive. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How did advances in medical knowledge change understanding of the body between c.1500 and the present day? Use evidence across the period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change across early modern (Vesalius 1543, Harvey 1628), modern (Pasteur/Koch germ theory 1861–1890s, X-rays 1895), contemporary (Watson/Crick DNA 1953, Human Genome 2003). Weighs change against continuity (herbal and humoral elements persisted in popular medicine; alternative medicine today). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Three periods with evidence. Developing: Two periods. Emerging: Single period. [16 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: For questions about advances in medical knowledge, you need to be clear about what was new and what it replaced. When writing about Vesalius or Harvey, explain what was wrong before (Galenic theory) and why the new knowledge was significant. For DNA and germ theory, link to broader consequences: germ theory enabled vaccines and antiseptics; DNA knowledge is enabling targeted therapies. Examiners reward responses that track the knock-on consequences of new knowledge, not just descriptions of the discovery itself.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Zengi's capture of Edessa in 1144.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students may describe: Zengi besieged Edessa in late November 1144; the city fell on 24 December 1144; Count Joscelin II was absent with his military forces; the Latin population was slaughtered or enslaved; it was the first crusader state to fall to Muslim forces. 1 mark for a simple point; 2 marks for a developed point.

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons for the failure of the Second Crusade.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should identify two reasons with supporting detail.
Reason 1: Conrad III's German army was heavily defeated by the Seljuks at the Battle of Dorylaeum in October 1147, and Louis VII's French army suffered serious losses in Anatolia, so both armies arrived in the Holy Land greatly weakened.
Reason 2: The crusaders made the strategic blunder of attacking Damascus, a traditional ally of Jerusalem, rather than targeting Edessa; the siege lasted only five days (24–28 July 1148) before the army retreated.
2 marks per reason: 1 mark for a simple point, 2 marks for a developed point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the failure of the Second Crusade.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (e.g. the decision to attack Damascus; losses in Anatolia; lack of coordination between French and German armies; Byzantine hostility; poor strategic judgment at Acre) and explains it with precise detail and links it clearly to the failure of the crusade. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a cause with some explanation and link to outcome.
Developing: Identifies a cause but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the fall of Edessa in 1144 for the crusader states.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At the time — first major Muslim recapture of crusader territory; showed Outremer was not permanently secure; shock in the West triggered a new crusade. Over time — the Second Crusade's failure to recover Edessa left the northern crusader frontier permanently weakened; established the pattern of Muslim reconquest that would culminate in Saladin's campaigns. Sustained judgement throughout.
Secure: Covers both dimensions with evidence.
Developing: Mainly covers contemporary significance with limited long-term analysis.
Emerging: Describes the fall of Edessa with little sense of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the crusaders' decision to attack Damascus in 1148.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific consequence (destruction of the Jerusalem-Damascus alliance; drove Damascus into cooperation with Zengi's successor Nur ad-Din; left Outremer surrounded by unified Muslim enemies; humiliating failure undermined the reputation of crusading) and explains it with precise detail. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a consequence with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a consequence but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: 'Bernard of Clairvaux's preaching was the main reason why the Second Crusade attracted so many participants.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues in support (Bernard's preaching at Vézelay attracted huge crowds; his personal authority was unrivalled in Western Europe; he toured France and Germany generating mass enthusiasm) and against (the fall of Edessa was the fundamental trigger; the involvement of two great monarchs — Louis VII and Conrad III — was essential for scale; religious culture created by Cluniac reform made audiences receptive). Substantiated judgement.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence; conclusion reached.
Developing: Mainly one-sided, limited evidence.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Enabling Act of March 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific feature with precise detail (e.g. gave Hitler the power to pass laws without Reichstag approval for four years; required a two-thirds majority to pass). Secure (1–2): feature identified with some detail. Developing (1): vague reference to Hitler gaining power. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the process by which Hitler consolidated power between January and July 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise detail — e.g. the Reichstag Fire Decree (February 1933) suspended civil liberties and enabled mass arrests of communists; the Enabling Act (March 1933) gave Hitler power to govern by decree for four years. Secure (3): two features with development. Developing (2): two features briefly stated. Emerging (1): one feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Night of the Long Knives in June 1934.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear cause (e.g. Röhm's demands that the SA replace the regular army threatened Hitler's relationship with conservative generals and industrialists he needed; OR: Hitler needed to destroy the SA as an independent political power base that challenged his own authority) with specific evidence and link to the purge. Secure (3–4): cause identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Night of the Long Knives for the Nazi regime.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear consequence (e.g. the SA was destroyed as an independent force and subordinated to the SS; the army's loyalty was secured because Hitler had protected its institutional position; conservatives who had feared a SA 'second revolution' were reassured) with specific evidence and further effects. Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the political system in Germany changed in the period from January 1933 to August 1934.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): tracks change at multiple points — January 1933 (Hitler Chancellor, constitutional position, coalition cabinet), Reichstag Fire Decree, Enabling Act, Gleichschaltung (trade unions, parties dissolved), Night of the Long Knives, August 1934 Führer, army oath — with analysis of HOW change occurred at each stage. Secure (5–6): covers most stages with development. Developing (3–4): some stages covered but limited analysis of process of change. Emerging (1–2): broadly describes the outcome without tracking change.

practice_questions.text: 'The Enabling Act of March 1933 was the most important step in Hitler's consolidation of power.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): agreement (Enabling Act gave legal foundation for dictatorship, bypassed democratic checks, enabled all subsequent legislation) AND disagreement (Reichstag Fire Decree came first and was equally enabling; Night of the Long Knives eliminated internal Nazi rivals and secured army; Hindenburg's death and the Führer oath completed the process). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both sides developed; judgement present. Developing (4–6): one side stronger; limited judgement. Emerging (1–3): mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the practice of buying shares on the margin.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: Investors typically paid only 10 per cent of a share's price upfront [1], borrowing the remaining 90 per cent from their stockbroker with the shares as security — if prices fell, the broker could demand immediate repayment, forcing panic selling. [1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Wall Street Crash of October 1929.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature.
Feature 1: Black Thursday (24 October 1929) saw approximately 12.9 million shares sold in panic [1], the biggest single-day trading volume the exchange had seen and the beginning of the market collapse. [1]
Feature 2: By mid-November 1929, share prices had fallen approximately 40 per cent from their September peak [1]; the Dow Jones Index eventually fell nearly 90 per cent from its 1929 high of 381 to a low of 41 in July 1932. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why overproduction was a major cause of the Wall Street Crash.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear causal chain from overproduction through declining profits to loss of investor confidence, with precise evidence.
Secure: Valid explanation with supporting detail.
Developing: Names overproduction but mechanism poorly explained.
Emerging: Simple point.
Overproduction: factories produced more than consumers could buy — unsold stock piled up; companies cut output and laid off workers; reduced wages reduced consumer demand further; declining corporate profits spooked investors and contributed to the selling that triggered the Crash.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Wall Street Crash for ordinary Americans.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces a consequence with precise evidence and a clear link from Crash to outcome.
Secure: Valid consequence with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a consequence without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid consequences: bank failures as banks that had lent for speculation collapsed; mass unemployment (approximately 25% by 1933); falling wages and consumer spending; evictions from homes as mortgages were called in; the Great Depression's human cost.

practice_questions.text:
How significant was buying on the margin in causing the Wall Street Crash of 1929?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance with both evidence and analysis of how buying on margin connected to the Crash's mechanism.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation; may not fully develop the mechanism.
Emerging: Simple points.
Significance: enabled mass participation in stock market with borrowed money; made investors vulnerable to any price fall (margin calls forced selling); self-reinforcing downward spiral once selling began; banks exposed through their lending; billions in paper wealth wiped out within days. Limits: overproduction and structural weaknesses in the economy were the deeper cause; the Crash would not have been as severe without those foundations.

practice_questions.text:
'The Wall Street Crash was mainly caused by speculation rather than economic weaknesses.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Points for and against; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple agreement.
Agreement: buying on margin made crash catastrophic — 10% down meant small falls triggered mass selling; millions of ordinary Americans speculating with borrowed money; Florida land bubble showed same speculative pattern earlier.
Disagreement: overproduction made corporate profits unsustainable; agricultural decline removed rural consumers; unequal wealth distribution limited real consumer demand; weak banking regulation; these structural factors meant a crash was likely even without reckless speculation.
Judgement: speculation was the trigger but structural economic weaknesses were the underlying cause — without those, the damage of speculation would have been far smaller.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Bow Street Runners established in 1749.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Feature may include: established by Henry Fielding at Bow Street Magistrates' Court; paid officers rather than unpaid volunteers; investigated crimes and served warrants; small in number but a prototype for professional detective work. Simple identification (1 mark); developed with context or significance (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Metropolitan Police established in 1829.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Officers wore a civilian blue uniform specifically designed to distinguish them from the military (blue tailcoat, top hat) and were initially unarmed, carrying only a truncheon and handcuffs. Feature 2: The force was based on the principle of policing by consent — officers were paid professionals forbidden from taking gifts, and their authority rested on public approval rather than coercion.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Metropolitan Police Act of 1829 was so significant for law enforcement in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States it set up a police force. Developing: Notes it replaced the old amateur system. Secure: Explains how it replaced over a thousand years of unpaid, part-time community policing with a paid, professional, uniformed force accountable to commissioners and government — a fundamental transformation in how law enforcement worked. Mastering: Sustains analysis of significance, linking urbanisation (the problem) to the solution; evaluates the innovative philosophy of policing by consent; may address limitations (only London initially; national coverage required 1856).

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the County and Borough Police Act (1856) for law enforcement in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States it made police forces compulsory. Developing: Notes inspection system created. Secure: Analyses significance at the time: it closed the gap between London (reformed 1829) and the rest of the country; the inspection system created national minimum standards; it completed the transition from community to professional policing. Mastering: Evaluates significance over time — the Act created the template for accountable public services; the Inspectors of Constabulary model set a precedent for state oversight of local services that persists today; compares the 1856 achievement to the pre-1829 system.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that Robert Peel deserves to be called the founder of modern policing in Britain?
Give reasons for your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments for: the Metropolitan Police Act 1829 was the decisive break from the old system; Peel introduced paid professionalism, civilian uniform, policing by consent and accountability to commissioners; his force became the model for all subsequent forces. Arguments against: Henry Fielding's Bow Street Runners (1749) pioneered the concept of paid investigators 80 years earlier; the 1856 Act completed what Peel started; others (Rowan, Mayne) developed the daily practice. Emerging: one-sided description. Developing: notes Fielding as a precursor. Secure: argues a position weighing Peel's contribution against Fielding and the 1856 Act. Mastering: evaluates the relative significance of each development, argues a justified overall conclusion about who or what deserves most credit.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the Metropolitan Police differed from the parish constable system it replaced.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per difference. Difference 1: Metropolitan Police officers were paid, full-time professionals with a structured command (two commissioners, ranks of officers) — parish constables served unpaid, part-time on a one-year rotation. Difference 2: Metropolitan officers were uniformed (blue tailcoat, top hat) and operated a regular beat system covering specific areas — parish constables had no uniform and no systematic patrol.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Berlin Blockade (1948–1949).
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• The Soviet Union cut all road, rail and canal links between West Berlin and the Western zones in June 1948, intending to force the Western powers to abandon the city or accept Soviet terms for Germany's future. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the division of Germany after 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two features identified with basic description.
Secure: Each described with context, e.g.:
• Germany was divided into four occupation zones (American, British, French and Soviet) agreed at the Yalta and Potsdam conferences in 1945. Berlin was also divided, despite lying entirely within the Soviet zone. [2 marks]
• In 1949 the three Western zones merged to form the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG), a democratic state with its capital at Bonn, while the Soviet zone became the German Democratic Republic (GDR), a communist one-party state with East Berlin as its capital. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Berlin Blockade (1948–1949) was important for Germany's future.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses significance both immediately and in longer-term context.
Example: The blockade crisis accelerated the formal division of Germany. Before June 1948, the four zones, though separately administered, remained theoretically part of one Germany. The confrontation over Berlin — and its resolution with the creation of two separate states in 1949 — made the political division permanent and institutional. It also deepened the ideological gulf: West Berlin became a symbol of democratic resistance, while the GDR's foundation on Soviet terms entrenched communist rule in the East.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Marshall Plan for West Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores longer-term consequences.
Example: Marshall Aid, which provided West Germany with approximately $1.4 billion, helped fund industrial reconstruction and stabilise the Deutschmark, enabling rapid economic recovery. By the mid-1950s West Germany was experiencing annual growth rates around 8% — the Wirtschaftswunder. This economic success strengthened democracy: the FRG's prosperity made its citizens far less likely to turn to extremist politics, unlike in Weimar Germany, and encouraged political stability under Konrad Adenauer's Christian Democratic government.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Berlin Blockade (1948–49) for the Cold War in Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description.
Developing: Some assessment.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time.
Mastering: Weighs the blockade's significance against other factors in Cold War Germany.
At the time: Demonstrated Western resolve to defend West Berlin; the airlift became a propaganda victory for the West; Stalin's failure forced him to lift the blockade without gaining concessions.
Over time: Cemented Germany's permanent division into two states (1949); established the pattern for Berlin as the central flashpoint of the Cold War, eventually leading to the Wall in 1961.

practice_questions.text:
'The Berlin Blockade of 1948–1949 was the most important cause of Germany's permanent division.' How far do you agree?
Consider other factors alongside the Blockade and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, no judgement.
Developing: Some argument on both sides.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Weighs blockade against earlier causes (1945 zone division, growing Cold War tensions, currency reform) and later developments, arguing where the decisive moment of division was.

For the Blockade: Accelerated the creation of two states in 1949; established a political settlement that lasted until 1990.
Against as most important: Division began in 1945 when zones were created; ideological incompatibility meant reunification was unlikely regardless; currency reform in June 1948 had already deepened tensions before the blockade began.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Northern Rebellion of 1569.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with detail, e.g. the earls of Northumberland and Westmorland led approximately 5,000 men south, carrying banners of the Five Wounds of Christ, intending to free Mary Queen of Scots (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Babington Plot (1586).
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: precise feature with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: Anthony Babington planned to assassinate Elizabeth; the plot involved freeing Mary Queen of Scots; Spanish military support was expected; Walsingham's agents intercepted the letters; Mary approved the assassination in writing; the conspirators were arrested and executed. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the papal bull Regnans in Excelsis (1570) for English Catholics.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a detailed chain with evidence, e.g. the bull excommunicated Elizabeth and released Catholics from obedience — this made every Catholic's loyalty suspect and prompted the government to take a much harder line on recusancy, increasing fines and eventually introducing the death penalty for harbouring Catholic priests. Secure: clear consequence with supporting evidence. Developing: relevant consequence with limited development. Emerging: a simple point. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the execution of Mary Queen of Scots (1587) for the security of Elizabeth's reign.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (removed the main Catholic claimant; eliminated the focus of conspiracies; set a precedent for executing a monarch) AND over time (contributed to Philip II's decision to launch the Armada in 1588; confirmed Protestant succession). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation. Emerging: simple descriptive points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a government report on the Babington Plot (1586) written by Francis Walsingham for understanding the Catholic threat to Elizabeth?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (what the report reveals about the plot), provenance (Walsingham — the spymaster who uncovered the plot; likely to exaggerate threat to justify harsh response) and contextual knowledge (the plot was real; Mary's letters were genuine; but Walsingham's network may have entrapped plotters) to give a substantiated judgement. Secure: addresses two elements. Developing: mainly describes source. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.
