Feature 2: Condemned prisoners were sometimes treated as celebrities, their final speeches printed and sold as 'last dying confessions'; the intended lesson of deterrence was undermined by this popular culture around executions.

before.exam_tip_html: For questions on punishment, examiners want you to explain the purpose behind each method, not just describe it. Deterrence, retribution and public shaming are the key concepts for the medieval and early modern periods. For the 16-mark thematic essay, the shift from public/physical punishment (mutilation, stocks, public execution) to imprisonment and rehabilitation (nineteenth century onwards) is the central change — make sure you can explain why attitudes changed, not just that they did.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Soviet economy during the Brezhnev era (1964–1982).
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: the economy became over-reliant on oil and gas exports; consumer goods were scarce and of poor quality; official statistics exaggerated growth; corruption was widespread among party officials.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Helsinki Accords of 1975.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: signed by 35 countries including the USSR and USA; confirmed existing European borders (a diplomatic achievement for Brezhnev); included human rights provisions which Soviet dissidents used to demand government compliance; enabled dissident monitoring groups to operate.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of economic stagnation in the Soviet Union during the Brezhnev era.
practice_questions.marks:
Key causes: over-reliance on oil and gas revenue meant the economy was vulnerable to falling energy prices; central planning removed incentives for efficiency and innovation; the nomenklatura system rewarded loyalty over competence; huge military spending crowded out investment in consumer industries.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise cause, causal chain explained, specific knowledge.
Secure: cause identified and explained with relevant knowledge.
Developing: cause identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point with no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 for the future of the Soviet Union.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: ended détente, caused international isolation, triggered US support for mujahideen. Over time: nine-year war killed approximately 15,000 Soviet soldiers; enormous financial cost; exposed military limitations; contributed to the economic and institutional crisis that brought Gorbachev to power and led him to pursue radical reform.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of the Brezhnev era:

“The Soviet Union’s problems in the Brezhnev years were caused more by political corruption than by economic weakness.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: the nomenklatura enjoyed privilege while ordinary workers faced scarcity; corruption undermined economic efficiency; leaders prioritised personal and elite security over reform; official statistics were falsified to maintain the illusion of success; Brezhnev and his circle were personally corrupt.

Disagreement: structural economic problems existed independently of corruption: the central planning system was inherently inefficient; military spending was a structural drain; the oil-dependent economy was structurally vulnerable; agricultural inefficiency predated Brezhnev.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: Was economic stagnation the main problem facing the Soviet Union by 1985? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement.

For the argument: GDP growth had slowed dramatically; consumer goods shortage; agricultural underperformance; over-reliance on oil revenue; gap between living standards and the West.

Alternative/related problems: military overstretch (Afghanistan); political gerontocracy unable to reform; dissident movements challenging legitimacy; nationalities problem in the USSR; loss of ideological credibility.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing multiple problems, clear judgement.
Secure: two or more problems explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: problems listed, limited weighing.
Emerging: one problem or descriptive throughout.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the three-day week introduced in January 1974.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Commercial and industrial electricity use was limited to three days per week to conserve coal stocks during the miners' strike; offices worked by candlelight and television broadcasts ended at 10:30 pm.
- The measure was introduced by Edward Heath on 1 January 1974 and was seen as a dramatic demonstration of the government's inability to manage the energy crisis caused by industrial action.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Winter of Discontent in 1978–1979.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple cause identified, limited explanation.
Secure: Clear cause with explanation and factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation, precise evidence, chain of causation clear.

Causes may include:
- Callaghan's government attempted to hold pay rises to 5%, well below inflation; unions whose members' real wages were falling refused to accept this cap.
- Long-term frustration with wage restraint after years of economic crisis; unions had cooperated with the Social Contract but felt Labour had failed to deliver.
- The OPEC oil shock and inflation had eroded living standards through the mid-1970s, making workers determined to claw back purchasing power.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Edward Heath's decision to call a general election in February 1974 on the question 'Who governs Britain?'
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple consequence, limited development.
Secure: Clear consequence with explanation and evidence.
Mastering: Detailed consequence, precise evidence, wider significance addressed.

Consequences may include:
- Labour won more seats than the Conservatives despite fewer votes; Heath was unable to form a government and Wilson returned to power — demonstrating that Heath's gamble had failed.
- Heath was later replaced as Conservative leader by Thatcher in 1975, who drew the lesson that the unions must be confronted and defeated, not negotiated with.
- The election result was seen as demonstrating trade union power: the miners had, in effect, determined the outcome of a general election.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was the 1973 OPEC oil embargo in causing Britain's economic problems in the 1970s? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence.
Developing: Some significance explained, basic evidence.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time addressed, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis, precise evidence, sustained argument weighing OPEC against other factors.

At the time: quadrupled oil prices overnight; combined with miners' strike to create energy crisis requiring three-day week; contributed to stagflation and 25% inflation in 1975.
Limits: long-term industrial decline pre-dated OPEC; trade union power was a domestic factor; the oil shock affected all Western economies but Britain's response was uniquely disruptive.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The trade unions were the main cause of Britain's political and economic problems in the 1970s.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation, limited range of evidence.
Secure: Clear evaluation, agreement and disagreement addressed, factual knowledge used.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation, precise evidence, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: miners' strikes (1972, 1974) brought down the Heath government; the Winter of Discontent ended the Callaghan government; industrial disputes in manufacturing damaged productivity and competitiveness.

Disagreement: external factors (OPEC oil shock 1973) caused immediate crisis; long-term industrial decline (failing car, steel, shipbuilding industries) was structural; government mismanagement (IMF crisis 1976) also played a role; union militancy was partly a response to falling real wages caused by inflation.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Margaret Thatcher's 1979 general election campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- The Conservative campaign used the slogan 'Labour isn't working' alongside an image of a long unemployment queue, directly attacking Labour's economic management.
- Thatcher promised to control inflation, reduce trade union power, cut taxes, and reduce government spending — a platform presenting a clear break from the post-war consensus.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Puritan opposition to the Religious Settlement in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with supporting detail, e.g. Puritans argued that the Church should be governed by elected elders (presbyters) rather than bishops, because bishops had no basis in scripture (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Archbishop Whitgift's response to Puritanism.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: precise feature with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: required all clergy to subscribe to the Three Articles (royal supremacy, prayer book, Thirty-Nine Articles); used the Court of High Commission to discipline non-conforming clergy; suspended clergy who refused to subscribe; appointed as Archbishop of Canterbury in 1583. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Elizabeth I's opposition to presbyterianism.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: detailed causal chain with evidence, e.g. Elizabeth opposed presbyterianism because bishops were appointed by the Crown and enforced royal religious policy — replacing them with elected elders would have removed the Queen's control over the Church, creating an independent religious authority with the potential power to defy royal commands. Secure: clear cause with some evidence. Developing: relevant cause with limited development. Emerging: simple point. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Marprelate Tracts (1588–1589) for relations between Elizabeth I and Puritanism.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (hardened government's stance; led to arrests and executions; pushed Puritanism towards the edges of respectability) AND over time (demonstrated the limits of radical Puritanism; contributed to the later conflict between Crown and Puritans in the seventeenth century). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation. Emerging: simple points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a pamphlet written by a Puritan MP arguing for greater religious reform for understanding the nature of the Puritan challenge to Elizabeth?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content, provenance (a Puritan MP — committed reformer, wants change; may overstate urgency) and contextual knowledge (Puritan MPs were real; Cope's Bill and Book shows the parliamentary dimension; but most Puritans worked within the Church) to give a substantiated judgement. Secure: addresses two elements. Developing: mainly describes source. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'Elizabeth I successfully dealt with the Puritan challenge to the Religious Settlement.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: argues for (Whitgift contained presbyterianism; Cope's Bill suppressed; no Puritan rebellion; settlement survived the reign) AND against (Puritanism was not destroyed; it re-emerged in the seventeenth century; the Marprelate affair showed how difficult control was; some councillors were sympathetic to reform) before a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: simple. Maximum 12 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Rhineland Massacres of 1096.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students may describe: they were carried out by participants in the People's Crusade; they targeted Jewish communities in towns including Worms, Mainz and Cologne; they were not officially sanctioned by the papacy (some bishops tried to protect Jewish communities); they killed thousands of Jewish people. 1 mark for a simple point; 2 marks for a developed point.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the Crusades affected European trade and commerce.
practice_questions.marks:
Feature 1: Italian maritime cities (Venice, Genoa, Pisa) supplied the crusader states in return for trading concessions and grew enormously wealthy, stimulating European commerce on a new scale.
Feature 2: New goods — spices, silk, cotton, sugar, dyes — entered European markets in greater quantities through trade networks opened up by the Crusades, and credit instruments and banking developed to handle the expanded commerce.
2 marks per feature: 1 mark for simple point, 2 for developed point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the increased religious intolerance towards Jewish communities in Europe during the crusading period.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (the ideology of holy war demonising non-Christians; the rhetoric of defending Christ's land extending to persecuting those seen as his enemies at home; the role of the People's Crusade in spreading popular violence) and explains it with precise detail, linking cause to the pattern of persecution. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a cause with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a cause but limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the translation movement for European intellectual development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At the time — Arabic and Greek scientific texts entered European universities; Arabic numerals transformed mathematics and calculation; Aristotle's philosophy became foundational for university education. Over time — the translation movement is widely seen as a precondition for the Renaissance; advances in astronomy, medicine and mathematics that depended on this knowledge shaped the later Scientific Revolution. Sustained judgement.
Secure: Covers both dimensions with evidence.
Developing: Mainly covers one dimension.
Emerging: Describes the translation movement with little sense of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Crusades for the growth of Italian trading cities.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific consequence (Venice, Genoa or Pisa gained trading concessions that gave them privileged access to Levantine and Byzantine markets; their wealth funded urban growth, art and banking; the commercial revolution of the twelfth century was substantially powered by this trade) and explains it with precise detail. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a consequence with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a consequence but limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: 'The most significant effect of the Crusades on Europe was the growth of trade.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues in support (Italian city wealth transformed European commerce; new goods reached wider populations; banking and credit developed; indirect funding of the Renaissance) and against (the translation movement had equally or more transformative intellectual effects; Arabic numerals and algebra permanently changed mathematics; the Rhineland Massacres and growth of antisemitism had devastating social consequences for Jewish communities; religious intolerance outlasted the Crusades). Substantiated judgement.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence; conclusion reached.
Developing: Mainly one-sided, limited evidence.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of public health in medieval British towns.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with supporting detail. Example: Medieval towns had open sewers running through streets and animals slaughtered in public spaces, creating conditions in which disease could spread rapidly. [2 marks: 1 for feature, 1 for detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Edwin Chadwick's 1842 Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: The report documented the shocking disparity in life expectancy between industrial districts and rural areas, with some urban areas showing average life expectancy far below 30 years. Feature 2: Chadwick recommended a centralised system of clean water supply and sewage removal, with standardised pipes to flush waste away efficiently. [2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the cholera epidemics of the nineteenth century for public health reform in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of one consequence (e.g. cholera forced government to act on sanitation: 1848 Public Health Act; Snow's work linking cholera to water; Great Stink 1858 leading to Bazalgette's sewers; 1875 Act making sanitation compulsory). Embedded evidence. Secure: Clear consequence with evidence. Developing: Consequence identified, explanation limited. Emerging: Simple statement. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of John Snow's investigation into cholera in 1854.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (demonstrated cholera spread through water not miasma; removal of pump handle ended local outbreak; evidence-based approach to public health) AND over time (contributed to germ theory; showed value of epidemiological mapping; influenced 1875 Public Health Act). Secure: Both dimensions with evidence. Developing: One dimension. Emerging: Description only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Government action was the most important factor in improving public health in Britain between 1800 and 1900.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates government action (1848 Act, 1875 Act, Bazalgette commission) against other factors (individual reformers — Chadwick, Snow; scientific advance — germ theory; public pressure — Great Stink). Considers what drove government action itself. Substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: One side argued. Emerging: Descriptive. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How far did public health in Britain improve between the medieval period and 1900? Use evidence across all three eras to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change across medieval (mixed — some town regulations, plague orders), early modern (Tudor plague orders; reactive not systematic), modern (cholera crises; Chadwick 1842; Snow 1854; Great Stink 1858; Bazalgette; 1875 Act). Weighs change against continuity (disease continued to spread in cities; action always reactive to crisis). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Three periods with evidence. Developing: Two periods. Emerging: Single period. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of children's play in the medieval period.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with detail: e.g. children played with simple toys made from wood, clay, leather or cloth, such as hobby horses or clay figures / children participated in adult games and festivals from an early age. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of children's comics in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. the Beano (1938) and Dandy (1937) became the most enduring British children's comics, published weekly by D.C. Thomson (feature + detail); the Eagle (1950) targeted older boys with science fiction and adventure, selling nearly a million copies a week at its peak in the 1950s (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Victorian toys became more varied and commercially produced compared with medieval toys.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking industrialisation (factory production making toys cheaper and more varied), growing middle-class prosperity and the 1870 Education Act driving literacy and demand for educational toys. Evidence-based. Secure: Clear cause with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the decline of outdoor play for children in Britain by the early twenty-first century.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Consequence developed, e.g. children's home range shrank by approximately 90% between the 1970s and 2000s; reduced physical activity has been linked to health concerns; loss of unsupervised communal play changed child development and social bonding patterns. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was the development of television in changing how children spent their leisure time in the second half of the twentieth century?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses television's significance at the time (Blue Peter from 1958, Watch with Mother, children's BBC as public service remit) AND over time (laid the basis for screen-based leisure that video games and streaming extended). Uses evidence. Secure: Clear analysis with examples. Developing: Some points. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Children's leisure became less physical and less communal between c.500 and the present day.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substantiated judgement tracing change across all three eras. Agrees: screen-based, solitary video games contrast with medieval communal play; decline of outdoor play. Challenges: children's sports still flourish; gaming can be social and online; continuity in storytelling and role-play. Overall weighing conclusion. Secure: Evidence from at least two eras, some weighing. Developing: Limited range. Emerging: Basic agree/disagree. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the encomienda system in New Spain.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (e.g. Spanish settlers were allocated the right to demand labour and tribute from a group of indigenous people / in theory they were to Christianise and protect workers; in practice it was forced labour / encomiendas were used in agriculture and mining). Two marks for a developed explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Columbian Exchange.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Food crops transferred from the Americas to Europe: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chilli peppers, cacao, tobacco — transforming European diets.
• European crops, animals and diseases transferred to the Americas: wheat, cattle, horses, sugar cane, smallpox, measles — devastating indigenous populations.
• The transfer created a new Atlantic trading economy linking Europe, Africa and the Americas.
• The Columbian Exchange is named by historian Alfred Crosby and is seen as one of the most significant ecological events in human history.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the European Price Revolution in the sixteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the influx of American silver (particularly from Potosí, opened 1545) into European circulation as a cause; explains the mechanism — increased money supply exceeded growth in goods, so prices rose; links specifically to the Spanish silver trade and its impact on wages and prices across Europe.
Secure: Identifies a cause with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the imposition of Christianity on indigenous peoples of New Spain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains the destruction of indigenous cultural heritage (codices burned, temples demolished, churches built on sacred sites); or the creation of syncretic religious practices as indigenous beliefs blended with Catholic Christianity; develops with specific evidence (Bishop Zumárraga burning codices; Templo Mayor replaced by cathedral).
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Bartolomé de las Casas for the history of the Spanish conquest.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (documented Spanish atrocities; petitioned the crown; contributed to New Laws of 1542 restricting encomienda abuses; former encomendero giving testimony unusual credibility) AND over time (his Brief Account became one of the most influential texts challenging colonialism; contributed to the Black Legend; cited by later human rights campaigners). Developed with evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with evidence; may lack full over-time analysis.
Developing: Describes what Las Casas did without fully analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Disease was a more significant consequence of the Spanish conquest than the imposition of Christianity for the peoples of central Mexico.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• Disease caused a population collapse of 50–90% — the largest demographic catastrophe in the history of the Americas.
• Unlike cultural suppression, death was irreversible; the loss of people also weakened indigenous capacity to resist or maintain cultural practices.
• Disease spread independently of individual Spanish actions, killing millions before missionaries arrived.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• The imposition of Christianity destroyed codices, temples and religious knowledge that could never be recovered.
• Forced labour (encomienda and mita) directly killed people through overwork, particularly in silver mining.
• The Christianisation created a permanent cultural rupture; religious syncretism shows indigenous people resisting, but the original practices were suppressed and distorted.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, reaches substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive, no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Defence of the Realm Act (DORA) of 1914.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: DORA gave the government power to censor newspapers (1), restricting reporting of military operations and information that could aid the enemy (1). Mastering: accurate feature with precise supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of women on the Home Front during the First World War.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature examples: munitionettes in factories making shells and explosives (handling toxic TNT — 'canary girls'); Women's Land Army working on farms; nursing close to the front line; taking on jobs as bus conductresses, delivery drivers, police officers, civil servants; around 800,000 women in munitions by 1918. Mastering: two precise features with accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the British government introduced conscription in January 1916.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Volunteer recruitment had fallen short of the army's needs by late 1915; the enormous casualties of 1914–1915 could not be replaced by volunteers alone; the campaign for Kitchener's army had successfully recruited over a million men but numbers were declining; the Military Service Act was necessary to maintain army strength for the campaigns planned for 1916, including the Somme. Secure (3–4): clear cause with development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the government's use of propaganda during the First World War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Government propaganda (posters, censored press, the Somme film watched by ~20 million) sustained public support for the war in the critical early years; it shaped public understanding of the enemy (German atrocity stories) and encouraged enlistment; however, when casualty lists contradicted optimistic propaganda by 1917, the gap between official narrative and reality fuelled disillusionment and anti-war sentiment. Secure (3–4): clear consequence with development. Developing (1–2): simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of growing disillusionment with the war in Britain by 1917.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): At the time: Sassoon's public protest in 1917 and the circulation of anti-war poetry by Owen challenged the official narrative; food shortages and casualty lists eroded morale; the government had to use DORA to suppress dissent. Over time: the anti-war tradition shaped interwar pacifism and the 'never again' mood of the 1920s–30s; war poetry by Owen and Sassoon became central to twentieth-century cultural understanding of the war; the 'lost generation' narrative influenced the decision not to resist Hitler more forcefully in the 1930s. Secure (5–6): both dimensions with development. Developing (3–4): mainly one dimension. Emerging (1–2): simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'Propaganda was the main reason why public support for the war was maintained in Britain until 1918.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Agree and disagree, substantiated, overall judgement. Agree: propaganda shaped public understanding at a critical time; censorship prevented accurate reporting of defeats; the Somme film maintained public engagement; white feather campaigns and social pressure enforced conformity. Disagree: genuine patriotism and belief in the justice of Britain's cause (Belgian neutrality, German militarism) were real motivations; the practical difficulty of opposing a war once it had started (legal penalties under DORA) was a constraint; many families were invested through the loss of relatives and had personal reasons to want victory. Balanced: propaganda was essential but worked because it reinforced existing beliefs — when reality diverged too far (by 1917) it began to fail. Secure (7–9): argument both ways. Developing (4–6): limited. Emerging (1–3): one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Truman Doctrine (1947).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names feature (commitment to support free peoples resisting communist takeover; the promise of military and economic aid; the policy of containment) AND develops it. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) American U-2 spy planes discovered Soviet nuclear missile installations under construction in Cuba in October 1962, just 90 miles from the US coast; (2) Kennedy imposed a naval blockade of Cuba and the 13-day standoff came close to nuclear war before Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the escalation of US involvement in the Vietnam War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (the Gulf of Tonkin incident and resulting congressional resolution; domino theory fears; containment policy; France's defeat at Dien Bien Phu leaving a power vacuum) AND develops the chain of reasoning. Secure: Cause with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Berlin Airlift (1948-1949) for the Cold War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (the Soviet Union ended the blockade in May 1949; the West demonstrated resolve; it was a propaganda victory showing the USA would defend West Berlin; it hardened the division of Germany and Europe; it accelerated the formation of NATO in 1949) AND develops the chain of effects. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) for US-Soviet relations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (most dangerous episode of the Cold War; nuclear war narrowly averted; demonstrated limits of brinkmanship) AND over time (led to Moscow-Washington hotline; influenced SALT negotiations; led to period of detente in the 1970s; shaped Cold War strategy). Secure: One time frame well-covered. Developing: Describes the crisis without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'The Vietnam War was the most significant challenge to US foreign policy between 1945 and 1973.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs Vietnam (military failure; domestic division; 58,000 dead; undermined containment) against other challenges (Berlin blockade 1948 – resolved successfully; Korean War 1950-53 – costly stalemate; Cuban Missile Crisis 1962 – diplomatically managed). Substantiated overall judgement about relative significance. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes challenges without weighing them. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Thatcher's privatisation programme.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• State-owned industries including British Telecom (1984) and British Gas (1986) were sold to private shareholders.
• The government used advertising campaigns like 'Tell Sid' to encourage ordinary people to buy shares for the first time.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the right-to-buy policy introduced by the Housing Act 1980.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• Council tenants were given the legal right to buy their homes at discounts of up to 50 per cent (based on tenancy length).
• Over one million properties had been sold by 1987, significantly expanding homeownership.
• Councils could not use sale receipts to build replacement housing, reducing the affordable housing stock.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the economic recession of 1980-81 in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the cause (Thatcher’s monetarist policies — raising interest rates sharply and cutting public spending to control inflation) and develops the mechanism — high interest rates increased borrowing costs for businesses, reduced investment, cut consumer spending, and hit manufacturing hard at a time when it was already uncompetitive globally, causing unemployment to spiral.
Secure: Names a clear cause with a linked explanation and some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the privatisation of British industries in the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. growth of share ownership among ordinary people, or transformation of natural monopolies into private companies requiring regulation, or the shift from manufacturing to services in the British economy) and develops a chain of effects.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the right-to-buy policy for British society in the long term.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (over one million new homeowners by 1987, created working-class property-owning stake in the economy, politically popular) AND over time (depletion of social housing stock contributed to housing crisis in 1990s-2000s, rising private rents, homelessness). Weighs the real immediate gains against longer-term costs.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions with clear explanation.
Developing: Addresses one dimension only.
Emerging: Describes the policy without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Thatcher's economic policies caused more harm than good to Britain in the 1980s.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing both harm (3 million unemployed, destruction of manufacturing communities, riots, social division) and benefit (inflation controlled, efficiency improved, homeownership extended, financial sector boom). Weighs factors with evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement on balance of harm vs benefit.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence for both sides. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Viking longship as a naval vessel.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• The longship had a shallow draft [1], which meant it could navigate rivers and be beached directly, allowing warriors to disembark immediately for raids [1].
• It combined oars and a sail [1], making it effective in both calm conditions and open-sea voyages [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Battle of Trafalgar (1805).
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature:
• Feature 1: Nelson attacked in two columns rather than the conventional line of battle [1], cutting the Franco-Spanish fleet in three and creating close-quarters fighting where British gunnery was decisive [1].
• Feature 2: The British captured or destroyed 22 enemy ships without losing a single vessel of their own [1], though Nelson was mortally wounded during the battle [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Battle of Trafalgar was significant for Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains both immediate significance (destruction of the Franco-Spanish fleet removed the threat of invasion; Napoleon could no longer challenge British naval power directly) and longer-term significance (secured British naval supremacy for a generation, enabling trade, army supply in the Peninsula, and blockade of Napoleonic Europe to continue).
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence.
Developing: Identifies significance with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the causes of the Battle of the Atlantic (1939–1945) and why it was significant for Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains Germany’s strategic aim (cut British transatlantic supply lines to force surrender), the means (U-boat campaign), and Britain’s vulnerability as an island dependent on imports. Analyses significance: without winning the Atlantic, Britain could not have remained in the war — food, fuel and equipment all depended on the supply lines.
Secure: Identifies cause and significance with supporting evidence.
Developing: One aspect with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Spanish Armada (1588) in the development of English/British naval power?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues significance at the time (defeat secured England from invasion; demonstrated the value of nimble, gun-armed galleons over larger vessels; boosted national morale and Protestant propaganda) and over time (reinforced investment in the Royal Navy; contributed to the naval culture that would culminate at Trafalgar). Reaches a substantiated conclusion.
Secure: Explains significance with two horizons and relevant evidence.
Developing: One time horizon, limited analysis.
Emerging: Describes the Armada without evaluating significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did the nature of British naval warfare change between c.500 and the present day? In your answer, refer to at least three periods.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces change from Viking longship raids (c.800–1000) → Tudor sail and gunpowder navy (1509 onwards; Armada 1588) → steam-powered, armoured Dreadnought-era (1906 onwards; Jutland 1916) → submarine and air-power Atlantic warfare (1939–45) → modern carrier and nuclear submarine force. Identifies continuity (control of sea lanes as strategic constant; discipline and training as recurring factors). Weighs change against continuity; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Covers at least three periods with evidence and some analysis.
Developing: Two periods, limited analysis.
Emerging: One period, no analytical framework.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Stasi in East Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• The Stasi employed approximately 175,000 civilian informants (Inoffizielle Mitarbeiter) who reported on colleagues, neighbours and family members, creating a pervasive atmosphere of mutual suspicion throughout East German society. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of SED control over East Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two features identified with basic description.
Secure: Each described with context, e.g.:
• The SED held a political monopoly — elections were held but candidates were pre-selected by the party, and opposing the list carried serious professional and social consequences, ensuring the SED never faced meaningful electoral challenge. [2 marks]
• The planned economy, in which the state owned all industry and set production quotas, eliminated market competition and ensured the regime controlled the economic lives of all East Germans. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the 1953 East German workers' uprising.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses mechanism and relates to wider context of communist rule.
Example: The immediate cause was the SED's decision to increase industrial work norms — requiring workers to produce more for the same pay. This came on top of food shortages, collectivisation of agriculture and generally low living standards. Workers in East Berlin's construction industry struck on 16 June 1953 in protest; the grievances rapidly spread to demands for free elections and political change, revealing that the work norms increase had triggered a much deeper well of resentment against the regime.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the 1953 uprising for the SED government.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores longer-term consequences.
Example: The crushing of the uprising by Soviet tanks demonstrated that the SED could not maintain power without direct Soviet military intervention — a consequence with long-term significance. The regime became even more dependent on Soviet backing and more cautious about any reforms that might generate popular pressure. The uprising was never forgotten: in West Germany, 17 June was made a national holiday of German unity. In East Germany it was a subject of intense official denial — the regime claimed it had been an imperialist provocation rather than a genuine popular revolt.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Stasi for control in East Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description of the Stasi.
Developing: Some assessment.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time.
Mastering: Weighs the Stasi against other methods of control (SED political monopoly, planned economy, Soviet backing) and argues its relative importance.
At the time: The network of Inoffizielle Mitarbeiter created pervasive self-censorship; Zersetzung undermined dissidents without imprisoning them; Stasi files informed all aspects of SED governance.
Over time: The opening of Stasi files after 1990 caused enormous social trauma — many East Germans discovered they had been reported on by spouses, friends and colleagues.

practice_questions.text:
'Fear of the Stasi was the main reason East Germans accepted communist rule until 1989.' How far do you agree?
Consider other factors alongside fear and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, no judgement.
Developing: Some argument on both sides.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Weighs fear against genuine belief in communism, material benefits, and the absence of alternatives.

For fear as main reason: The Stasi's vast network made opposition extremely dangerous; Zersetzung undermined those who tried to organise; Soviet tanks in 1953 showed the ultimate sanction.
Against as most important: Some East Germans genuinely believed in socialist ideals; the GDR provided full employment, free healthcare and housing at low cost; international recognition (Helsinki 1975) gave the regime some legitimacy; the lack of information about the West (before TV signals could be received) meant many had no reference point for comparison.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the rebel attack on London in June 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: The rebels breached the Tower of London on 13–14 June 1381 [1]; they dragged out Archbishop Sudbury (the Lord Chancellor) and Robert Hales (the Lord Treasurer) and executed them on Tower Hill [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the meeting at Mile End on 14 June 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: Richard II rode out to meet the Essex rebels and agreed to their principal demands [1]; these included the abolition of serfdom, a fixed low rent for land, freedom to trade and a general pardon, backed by written charters drawn up on the spot [1]. Feature 2: The meeting persuaded many Essex rebels to leave London, satisfied that their demands had been granted [1]; however, the Kentish rebels under Wat Tyler remained with additional demands, meaning the revolt was not yet over [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the rebels' entry into London in June 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (sympathy from Londoners who opened the gates; the king and government retreating to the Tower; the rebels' organisation and rapid march from Essex and Kent) and explains it in depth with precise factual knowledge. Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with relevant factual support. Developing: States a cause with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the death of Wat Tyler at Smithfield on 15 June 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains a consequence in depth — the loss of the rebels' leader caused confusion; Richard II's direct address exploited the moment to disperse the crowd; the revolt in London collapsed; or the longer-term: the promises made at Mile End were all revoked, and reprisals followed across England. Secure: Explains a consequence with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Richard II's role in suppressing the Peasants' Revolt.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (his personal courage at Mile End and Smithfield; his promises that dispersed the rebels; the way his authority was used by the ruling class to crush the revolt after Tyler's death) and longer-term (his subsequent revocation of all promises; the reprisals he authorised; the perception that he had both negotiated and betrayed the rebels). Precise factual knowledge throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes Richard's actions without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The death of Wat Tyler at Smithfield was the most important reason the Peasants' Revolt failed.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with precise factual knowledge. Agrees: Tyler's death removed the revolt's organising focus; the rebels were leaderless at the decisive moment; Richard II exploited the confusion immediately. Disagrees: Other factors were equally important — the ruling class had vastly greater military resources once they organised; the promises at Mile End had already split the rebel coalition by sending Essex contingents home; John Ball's subsequent capture and execution removed the revolt's ideological leadership. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Makes points for and against with evidence. Developing: Describes events without evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple response; no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Nuremberg Laws of 1935.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific feature with precise detail (e.g. the Reich Citizenship Law stripped Jews of German citizenship, making them subjects rather than citizens; the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honour banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews). Secure (1–2): feature identified with some detail. Developing (1): vague reference to discrimination. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Kristallnacht pogrom of November 1938.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise detail — e.g. approximately 7,500 Jewish businesses smashed and windows broken (giving the event its name); approximately 30,000 Jewish men arrested and sent to concentration camps; around 267 synagogues burned to the ground (and many more damaged); Jews fined one billion Reichsmarks for the damage to their own property. Secure (3): two features with development. Developing (2): two features briefly stated. Emerging (1): one feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the escalation of anti-Jewish persecution in Germany between 1935 and 1938.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear cause (e.g. the regime used Aryanisation to seize Jewish economic assets from 1937, driven by desire for wealth transfer and ideological goals of removing Jews from economic life; OR: Herschel Grynszpan's shooting gave Goebbels a pretext for orchestrated violence) with specific evidence and link to escalation. Secure (3–4): cause identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Nuremberg Laws for the Jewish community in Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear consequence (e.g. Jews were made legally stateless — this gave state and local authorities the legal basis to exclude Jews from any area of life; the definition of 'Jewishness' by grandparentage trapped people who had not considered themselves Jewish; emigration became more attractive but assets could not be taken) with specific evidence and further effects. Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Kristallnacht for the treatment of Jews in Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): significance at the time (open state-directed violence; mass arrests; billion-mark fine; immediate acceleration of emigration) AND over time (marked transition from legal discrimination to physical violence; international response inadequate, emboldening regime; precedent for further violence). Secure (5–6): both time periods. Developing (3–4): mainly descriptive. Emerging (1–2): brief mention without analysis.

practice_questions.text: 'The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 were the most significant turning point in the Nazi persecution of the Jews.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): agreement (Nuremberg Laws provided legal framework for all subsequent persecution; stripped citizenship; banned intermarriage; created bureaucratic definition of Jewishness) AND disagreement (Kristallnacht arguably more significant as turning point — shifted from legal discrimination to open violence; 1933 boycott and professional exclusions were the starting point; emigration pressure and Aryanisation also important). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both sides developed; judgement. Developing (4–6): one side stronger. Emerging (1–3): mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the British response to Argentina's invasion of the Falkland Islands in 1982.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• Thatcher dispatched a task force of over 100 ships including aircraft carriers to the South Atlantic within days of the invasion.
• After diplomatic efforts failed, British forces entered the Total Exclusion Zone and began combat operations to retake the islands.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Miners' Strike of 1984-85.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• NUM president Arthur Scargill called the strike from 6 March 1984 without holding a national ballot of all members, which undermined its legal standing.
• The most violent clashes occurred at Orgreave coking plant in Yorkshire in June 1984, between police and striking miners.
• Miners in Nottinghamshire continued working and formed the breakaway Union of Democratic Mineworkers.
• After a year on strike, miners returned to work in March 1985 without having achieved their aims.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the failure of the Miners' Strike of 1984-85.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. absence of a national ballot, government coal stockpiles, or division among miners) and develops the mechanism in detail — showing how the cause operated and what specific effects it had on the strike’s ability to succeed.
Secure: Names a clear cause with a linked explanation and some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Falklands War victory for Margaret Thatcher's government.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (the “Falklands factor” reviving Conservative support, or the 1983 landslide election victory with a 144-seat majority) and develops a chain — how the consequence unfolded and what further effects it had on Thatcher’s ability to pursue her economic programme.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Miners' Strike of 1984-85 for British industrial relations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (defeat of the NUM broke the most powerful union in Britain, accelerated pit closures, devastated mining communities) AND over time (weakened the trade union movement broadly, confirmed the shift from manufacturing to service economy, left enduring divisions in coalfield communities). Weighs limits: some mining communities retained strong union culture.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions with clear explanation.
Developing: Addresses one dimension only.
Emerging: Describes the strike without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The Falklands War was more important than the Miners' Strike in shaping Thatcher's Britain.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument comparing both events — Falklands (boosted popularity, enabled 1983 mandate, shaped foreign policy image) and Miners’ Strike (broke union power, transformed industrial relations, devastated communities, accelerated economic shift). Weighs which had longer-lasting significance with evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence for both events. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but comparison is thin or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account of one or both events without sustained comparison.
[16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Berlin Wall built in August 1961.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• The Berlin Wall included a 'death strip' — a stretch of raked sand between the inner wall and the outer fence — monitored by guards with shoot-to-kill orders, designed to make escape across the Wall almost impossible. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Describe two consequences of the building of the Berlin Wall for East and West Berlin.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two consequences identified with basic description.
Secure: Each described with context, e.g.:
• The Wall physically divided the city and separated thousands of families, some of whom were unable to see each other for decades. East Berliners who had previously worked in West Berlin lost their jobs overnight. [2 marks]
• West Berlin became even more symbolically important to the West — Kennedy's 1963 speech ('Ich bin ein Berliner') demonstrated American commitment to defending the city, which stood as a symbol of democratic freedom surrounded by communist territory. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the GDR decided to build the Berlin Wall in 1961.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses the mechanism and relates to GDR's structural problems.
Example: By summer 1961 the GDR was losing skilled workers at an unsustainable rate. Between 1949 and 1961 approximately 3.5 million East Germans had emigrated — disproportionately professionals such as doctors, teachers and engineers. In the weeks before the Wall, the rate was up to 2,000 per day. This 'brain drain' threatened economic collapse: the GDR's healthcare and educational systems could not function with so many trained professionals leaving. Building the Wall was therefore primarily an economic emergency measure, though it also served political purposes — stopping the visible evidence of East Germans 'voting with their feet' against communist rule.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Helsinki Accords (1975) for East Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores longer-term consequences.
Example: The Helsinki Accords committed the GDR to respect basic human rights and freedom of movement in exchange for Western recognition of post-war European borders. Although the GDR did not honour these commitments, the Accords provided a legal framework that East German civic groups — centred on Protestant churches — used to challenge the regime's legitimacy. These groups became the seeds of the civic movement that organised the Monday Demonstrations of 1989, contributing directly to the fall of the Wall.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Berlin Wall for Cold War relations between 1961 and 1989.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description of the Wall.
Developing: Some assessment.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time.
Mastering: Weighs the Wall's significance at different stages of the Cold War and argues how its symbolic importance changed.
At the time: Solved GDR's emigration crisis; confirmed the failure of communism to provide freedom; created a dangerous flashpoint (Checkpoint Charlie October 1961).
Over time: Became the defining symbol of the Cold War's human cost; its fall in November 1989 became the defining symbol of communism's collapse.

practice_questions.text:
'The building of the Berlin Wall in 1961 was the most important moment in Cold War relations involving Germany.' How far do you agree?
Consider other moments alongside the Wall and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, no judgement.
Developing: Some argument on both sides.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Weighs the Wall against Berlin Blockade (1948–49), Checkpoint Charlie (1961), Ostpolitik (1969–74), Helsinki (1975), and eventual reunification (1990).

For the Wall: Physically divided city and nation; killed at least 140 people; became the defining symbol of Cold War division.
Against as most important: Berlin Blockade (1948) was arguably the decisive moment of Germany's division — the Wall was a consequence; Ostpolitik (1969–74) arguably transformed relations more constructively; the fall of the Wall itself (1989) could be argued as most important as it ended the Cold War.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the role played by the Gestapo in Nazi Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific feature with precise detail (e.g. could arrest and imprison people without trial; operated largely on the basis of denunciations from ordinary citizens). Secure (1–2): feature with some detail. Developing (1): vague reference to secret police. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Nazi use of propaganda to control Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise detail — e.g. Goebbels' Ministry controlled all newspapers via daily approved story lists; the Volksempfänger radio reached approximately 70% of households by 1939; Nuremberg rallies staged spectacular displays of unity. Secure (3): two features with development. Developing (2): two features briefly. Emerging (1): one feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the effectiveness of Nazi censorship in controlling information in Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear cause (e.g. the Reich Chamber of Culture excluded Jews and political opponents from all media professions, meaning no dissenting voice could legally work; OR: the combination of book burning, gallery purges and approved newspaper lists created an information environment with no alternative perspective) with evidence and link to effectiveness. Secure (3–4): cause identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Gestapo's use of informers and denunciations for ordinary Germans.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear consequence (e.g. the fear of being reported induced powerful self-censorship — people avoided expressing dissent even privately; OR: the denunciation system allowed personal grievances to be settled through the state, giving ordinary people power over their neighbours; OR: the reality that the Gestapo was small meant that compliance owed as much to fear and uncertainty as to actual surveillance) with evidence and further effects. Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Nuremberg rallies for maintaining Nazi control over Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): significance at the time (spectacle communicated total national unity, divine leadership, invincibility; filmed and broadcast nationally; created emotional bond between audience and Hitler) AND over time (the imagery of the rallies shaped international perceptions of Nazi power; Triumph of the Will as a document of propaganda techniques still studied). Secure (5–6): both time periods addressed. Developing (3–4): mainly describes the rallies without analysis. Emerging (1–2): brief mention.

practice_questions.text: 'Terror was more important than propaganda in maintaining Nazi control over Germany.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): agreement (SS/Gestapo/concentration camps created climate of fear; self-censorship spread widely; People's Court showed no legal protection) AND disagreement (propaganda reached every home via radio by 1939; genuine popular enthusiasm for Hitler especially 1933–1939; Gestapo was small and relied on voluntary denunciations, suggesting consent was important; many Germans actively supported the regime). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both sides developed; judgement. Developing (4–6): one side stronger. Emerging (1–3): mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the policy of internment introduced in August 1971.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Internment allowed detention without trial; Operation Demetrius on 9 August 1971 arrested 342 people, almost all Catholic or nationalist.
- The policy backfired: it fuelled nationalist anger and IRA recruitment rather than suppressing the IRA; the 1972 death toll (approximately 470) was the worst of the Troubles.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the events of Bloody Sunday on 30 January 1972.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple cause identified, limited explanation.
Secure: Clear cause with explanation and factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation, precise evidence, chain of causation clear.

Causes may include:
- Continuing civil rights marches against internment brought thousands onto the streets of Derry despite a ban on marches; the army's presence at such events was already tense after months of violence.
- Escalating IRA violence and internment had created a confrontational atmosphere; paratroopers deployed believing intelligence that IRA snipers would be present.
- The previous deployment of the 1st Parachute Regiment in violent crowd control situations had conditioned soldiers to act aggressively; command and control failures on the day allowed an uncontrolled shooting incident.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Birmingham pub bombings of November 1974.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple consequence, limited development.
Secure: Clear consequence with explanation and evidence.
Mastering: Detailed consequence, precise evidence, wider significance addressed.

Consequences may include:
- The Prevention of Terrorism Act was passed within two days, introducing extended detention powers and travel bans — rushed legislation that critics later argued led to miscarriages of justice.
- Six men (the 'Birmingham Six') were wrongly convicted; their imprisonment until 1991 became a major civil liberties scandal and undermined confidence in the criminal justice system.
- Public hostility towards the Irish community in Britain intensified, with harassment and physical attacks on ordinary Irish people who had no connection to the IRA.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant were the events of Bloody Sunday in shaping the Troubles in Northern Ireland? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence.
Developing: Some significance explained, basic evidence.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time addressed, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis, precise evidence, sustained argument.

At the time: fuelled massive IRA recruitment; the Irish government withdrew its ambassador; the British Embassy in Dublin was burned; Stormont was suspended and direct rule imposed in March 1972.
Over time: became the defining symbol of British injustice in nationalist memory; sustained Republican support for decades; the Saville Inquiry (1998-2010) and Cameron's apology (2010) showed it remained a live political wound for nearly four decades.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Internment was the most significant cause of the escalation of violence in Northern Ireland in 1971-1972.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation, limited range of evidence.
Secure: Clear evaluation, agreement and disagreement addressed, factual knowledge used.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation, precise evidence, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: internment swelled IRA recruitment; the 1972 death toll (approx. 470) was the worst of the Troubles; targeting almost exclusively Catholics alienated moderate nationalist opinion.

Disagreement: Provisional IRA violence had already escalated before internment; systemic discrimination and the events of 1969-70 had already created the conditions for violence; Bloody Sunday (January 1972) may have been as or more significant in sustaining the conflict; the removal of Stormont and imposition of direct rule contributed further.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the IRA mainland bombing campaign in the 1970s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- The Birmingham pub bombings (21 November 1974) killed 21 people and injured 182 in the Mulberry Bush and Tavern in the Town pubs — the deadliest mainland IRA attack of the Troubles.
- The Guildford pub bombings (October 1974) killed five people; the Guildford Four were wrongly convicted — one of the major miscarriages of justice arising from the mainland campaign.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Florentine Codex as a historical source.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (e.g. compiled by Sahagún using Nahua informants in the 1570s / contains the Nahua account of the conquest in Book 12 / compiled in Nahuatl and Spanish). Two marks for a developed explanation of its value or limitations.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Bernal Díaz del Castillo's account of the conquest.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• He was an eyewitness who served under Cortés, giving his account first-hand credibility.
• He wrote his Historia Verdadera around 1568, approximately fifty years after the events, relying on memory.
• He is often considered more reliable than Cortés because he had less personal incentive to distort the record.
• His account describes both the wonders of Tenochtitlán and the brutality of the conquest with unusual frankness.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Cortés’s Cartas de Relación present a favourable view of the Spanish conquest.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that Cortés was writing to King Charles I to justify his unauthorised expedition and secure royal backing; he therefore emphasised Spanish bravery, the justice of bringing Christianity and the barbarism of indigenous practices, while minimising Spanish brutality; develops with specific evidence (unauthorised departure from Cuba; need to claim royal authority retroactively).
Secure: Identifies reason with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a reason with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Las Casas’s 'Brief Account' (1542) for how Europeans understood the Spanish conquest.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the Brief Account, translated into multiple European languages, was used by Protestant rivals (England, the Netherlands, France) to construct the Black Legend of Spanish colonial brutality; contributed to a negative international image of Spain that shaped diplomacy and propaganda for generations; the irony that Las Casas intended to reform Spain from within but his words were used externally to condemn it.
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Compare how a sixteenth-century Spanish chronicler and a modern historian might interpret the conquest of Mexico differently. Explain why these interpretations differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Focuses on WHY interpretations differ (not just what they say). Spanish chronicler (e.g. Bernal Díaz or Cortés): eyewitness; writing in or shortly after colonial context; shaped by purpose (justification, memoir for posterity); limited access to indigenous perspectives; operating within Spanish Catholic worldview. Modern historian (e.g. Hugh Thomas): access to multiple sources including Nahuatl codices and indigenous accounts not available to contemporaries; writing with benefit of hindsight and subsequent scholarship; influenced by late 20th-century debates about colonialism and indigenous rights; no personal stake in justifying the conquest. Clear explanation of WHY these factors produce different interpretations.
Secure: Identifies differences in interpretation with some explanation of why they differ.
Developing: Mainly explains what each says, limited focus on why they differ.
Emerging: Describes one view only.

practice_questions.text: 'The conquest of Mexico is best understood as an invasion rather than a discovery.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• The Americas were home to millions of people with complex civilisations; calling Europeans’ arrival a “discovery” erases their existence.
• The term “discovery” reflects a Eurocentric perspective; from an indigenous viewpoint, it was an invasion followed by genocide and cultural destruction.
• Decolonial historians argue the language of “discovery” legitimised colonial violence by suggesting the Americas had no value before European contact.

Arguments challenging or complicating the interpretation:
• “Conquest” rather than “invasion” may be more accurate — the term “invasion” implies a foreign attack on a unified state, when in fact many indigenous peoples actively allied with Cortés against the Aztecs.
• Contemporary Spanish sources genuinely believed they were bringing civilisation and Christianity, making “discovery” meaningful within their own worldview even if problematic from a modern perspective.
• Historians like Hugh Thomas argue for a more complex multi-actor analysis that avoids reducing events to a single framing.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive, no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the government's response to the Great Smog of 1952.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with supporting detail. Example: The government passed the Clean Air Act 1956, which introduced smokeless zones banning the burning of coal in domestic fires in urban areas and setting emission standards for industry, to reduce the air pollution that had caused the Smog. [2 marks: 1 for feature, 1 for detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of government public health campaigns in the twenty-first century.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: The Change4Life campaign, launched in 2009, used advertising and community programmes to encourage healthier eating, more physical activity and reduced alcohol consumption, particularly targeting children and families. Feature 2: The sugar tax, introduced in 2018 on soft drinks, used taxation rather than persuasion to discourage consumption of high-sugar products linked to obesity and type 2 diabetes. [2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the introduction of the smoking ban in 2007 for public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of one consequence (e.g. reduction in passive smoking in public places; decline in smoking rates over decades; reduced hospital admissions for smoking-related diseases; cultural normalisation of non-smoking) with embedded evidence. Secure: Clear consequence with evidence. Developing: Consequence identified, explanation limited. Emerging: Simple statement. [6 marks]
