practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the council housing programme launched by the 1919 Addison Act for public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (moved families from slums to homes with indoor sanitation and ventilation; reduced disease linked to overcrowding and damp) AND over time (established the principle that the state should provide housing for health reasons; continued by post-WWII slum clearance and tower block building). Secure: Both dimensions with evidence. Developing: One dimension. Emerging: Description only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Government campaigns have been more effective than legislation in improving public health in modern Britain.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates campaigns (Change4Life, five-a-day, NHS stop-smoking services — persuasion approach) against legislation (Clean Air Act 1956, smoking ban 2007, sugar tax 2018 — compulsion approach). Considers which has achieved more measurable impact. Substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: One side argued. Emerging: Descriptive. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How far has the focus of public health in Britain changed between 1900 and the present day? Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change (1900s housing/TB; 1950s air pollution/smoking; 1980s–2000s lifestyle diseases/obesity; 2020 COVID-19), weighs change against continuity (government always responding reactively to crises; quarantine and sanitation principles persist; health inequalities between rich and poor throughout). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Multiple periods with evidence. Developing: Two periods. Emerging: Single period. [16 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about modern public health, show awareness of the shift in the nature of health problems across the twentieth century: from infectious diseases (tuberculosis, cholera) to non-communicable lifestyle diseases (heart disease, cancer, obesity). Examiners reward responses that show this transition rather than treating all health threats as the same type. For thematic essays, link modern campaigns (smoking ban, Change4Life) back to the same underlying driver as Victorian sanitation — government responding to evidence that preventable conditions are killing people — to show change and continuity together.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of how historians have interpreted the First World War.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: Some historians (such as those influenced by war poetry) have argued that the war was needlessly costly slaughter managed by incompetent generals (1), an interpretation sometimes summarised as 'lions led by donkeys' (1). Mastering: accurate feature with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Wilfred Owen's war poetry as a historical source.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature examples: written at Craiglockhart hospital 1917-18 by a shell-shocked officer — making it valuable evidence of psychological impact; graphic anti-war imagery (Dulce et Decorum Est) challenges official propaganda — useful for understanding disillusionment; limited as evidence of typical soldiers' views since Owen was an educated officer not representative of all ranks. Mastering: two precise features with accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why John Keegan's interpretation of the First World War differed from earlier interpretations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Keegan pioneered 'history from below' in The Face of Battle (1976), focusing on the experience of ordinary soldiers rather than commanders' strategies; earlier interpretations were shaped by the anti-war literature of the 1920s–30s (Sassoon, Owen, Graves) which reflected officer perspectives; Keegan used different source types and asked a different question — what was combat actually like for the men who fought? — giving a more grounded, less political picture. Secure (3–4): clear reason with development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why two historians might reach different interpretations of women's suffrage in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Historians ask different questions — one might focus on the short-term impact of WSPU militancy (arguing it forced the government's hand), while another might focus on long-term constitutional pressure (arguing the NUWSS's 20-year campaign created the political conditions); they might also be influenced by the values of the era in which they write — feminist historians from the 1970s recovered Fawcett's role that had been overlooked by earlier histories focused on dramatic Suffragette action. Secure (3–4): clear reason with development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Compare what the recruitment posters of 1914-1916 and Wilfred Owen's war poetry suggest about the First World War.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per source, comparing what each suggests. Recruitment posters: suggest the war was a patriotic duty, heroic and necessary; emphasise nation, family and obligation; produced by the government to encourage enlistment. Owen's poetry: suggests the war was brutal, psychologically damaging and based on a lie; produced by a disillusioned officer recovering from shell shock. The sources differ because they were produced by people with fundamentally different purposes and experiences — government propagandists versus a traumatised soldier-poet. Mastering: precise comparison with reference to both provenance and content.

practice_questions.text: 'Niall Ferguson's interpretation of Britain's entry into the First World War is more convincing than the traditional view.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Agree and disagree, substantiated, overall judgement. Agree: Ferguson's access to post-Cold War archives and his counterfactual approach reveals choices that earlier historians treated as inevitable; his critique of British decision-making is supported by evidence of how the cabinet debated entry in late July 1914. Disagree: the traditional view — that German aggression (invasion of Belgium, militarism, the Schlieffen Plan) made British entry necessary — is supported by the evidence of Germany's own planning; Ferguson underestimates the strategic threat a German-dominated Europe would have posed; most professional historians continue to see Britain's entry as justified by circumstances. Balanced judgement: Ferguson raised important questions but the traditional view remains more convincing on the primary evidence. Secure (7-9): argument both ways. Developing (4-6): limited. Emerging (1-3): one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the reservation system in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: Reservations confined Native Americans to areas of often poor-quality land far from their traditional territories [1], following the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and subsequent treaties which stripped tribes of their original lands. [1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Native American boarding school system.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature.
Feature 1: Children were removed from their families, sometimes by force, and forbidden to speak their native languages or practise their religions [1] — punishments for breaking these rules could be severe, and the philosophy was explicit in the motto 'Kill the Indian, save the man.' [1]
Feature 2: Death rates in boarding schools were high due to disease in crowded conditions and inadequate care [1] — thousands of Native American children passed through the system annually by the early twentieth century. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Dawes Act of 1887 harmed Native American communities.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear causal chain from the Act's provisions to the harm caused, with specific evidence.
Secure: Valid explanation with supporting detail.
Developing: Names the Dawes Act but mechanism poorly explained.
Emerging: Simple point.
The Act broke up communally held tribal land into individual allotments and sold the 'surplus' to white settlers — between 1887 and 1934 Native Americans lost approximately 90 million acres. The destruction of communal land ownership eliminated the economic and social structures tribal life depended on, while the individual allotments of 160 acres were too small and often unsuitable for successful farming.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 for Native Americans.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces a consequence with precise evidence; clear causal link from the Act to the outcome.
Secure: Valid consequence with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a consequence without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid consequences: formal recognition of Native Americans as citizens for the first time; symbolic acknowledgement of military service in WWI; some Native Americans welcomed it as a step to equality; others saw it as undermining tribal sovereignty; practical limitation — several states still blocked Native Americans from voting into the 1940s.

practice_questions.text:
How significant was the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 in improving the lives of Native Americans?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time and over time; weighs the symbolic value against practical limitations; precise evidence.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation; may not distinguish between symbolic and practical significance.
Emerging: Simple points.
At the time: granted citizenship to all Native Americans born in the US; partly recognised 12,000 Native American First World War veterans; did not automatically grant voting rights — several states maintained restrictions.
Over time: laid symbolic groundwork for later civil rights recognition; however, reservation poverty, inadequate healthcare and education continued unchanged through the 1920s boom; the 1928 Meriam Report documented catastrophic conditions; real change came only with the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934.

practice_questions.text:
'The 1920s economic boom showed that America truly was a nation of contrasts.'
Using the treatment of Native Americans as evidence, how far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees using Native American experience alongside broader 1920s evidence; substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Points for and against; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple agreement.
Agreement: while Wall Street boomed, Native Americans lived in chronic poverty on reservations; 90 million acres lost since Dawes Act; boarding schools deliberately destroyed culture; BIA corruption and neglect documented; voting rights withheld in several states even after 1924; 1928 Meriam Report confirmed catastrophic conditions.
Disagreement (limits of the contrast argument): the 1920s boom was also unequal for farmers, Black Americans and recent immigrants — Native Americans were not uniquely excluded; the 1924 Act was at least a step.
Judgement: Native American experience is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that the boom was built on deep inequality — the 'nation of contrasts' thesis holds strongly here.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Gorbachev’s policy of glasnost.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: censorship was relaxed and previously banned books and articles were published; media could discuss Soviet failures and corruption; public debate about Stalinist crimes was permitted; the Chernobyl disaster could not be concealed.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of perestroika as introduced by Gorbachev from 1986.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: state enterprises were given more autonomy and some market mechanisms were introduced; small private businesses and cooperatives were permitted; a new parliament (Congress of People's Deputies) was established with competitive elections in March 1989; price controls were partially relaxed, causing inflation.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Chernobyl disaster of 1986 for the Soviet Union.
practice_questions.marks:
Key consequences: the disaster exposed the gap between official Soviet claims of technological achievement and the reality of a failing infrastructure; glasnost made it impossible to conceal the scale of the disaster; it undermined public confidence in the Soviet system; it reinforced Gorbachev's case that radical reform was necessary.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise consequence, causal chain explained, specific knowledge.
Secure: consequence identified and explained.
Developing: consequence identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point, no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the INF Treaty of 1987 for relations between the Soviet Union and the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: first agreement to eliminate rather than cap nuclear weapons; ended the Second Cold War tensions; demonstrated Gorbachev was a different kind of Soviet leader. Over time: opened the door to further arms reductions; contributed to Eastern European revolutions of 1989 by signalling the USSR would not use force to defend regimes; marked the practical end of the Cold War.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of Gorbachev’s reforms:

“Glasnost was more important than perestroika in destabilising the Soviet Union.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: glasnost allowed public exposure of Soviet failures, corruption and the Afghan War; it enabled nationalist and democratic movements to organise and speak openly; exposure of Stalinist crimes undermined the party's legitimacy; Chernobyl and Afghanistan coverage eroded trust.

Disagreement: perestroika directly disrupted the economy by dismantling central planning without replacing it with an effective market; rising inflation, supply chain disruption and falling output created genuine material grievances; democratisation through the Congress of People's Deputies gave a platform to political opposition.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: Was glasnost the main reason for the problems facing the Soviet Union by 1990? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement.

For glasnost: enabled nationalist movements, democratic opposition, public criticism of party; gave platform to Yeltsin and others; exposed institutional failures including Chernobyl and Afghan War.

Alternative factors: long-term economic stagnation predating Gorbachev; perestroika's failure to deliver prosperity while disrupting supply chains; nationalities problem in republics seeking independence; conservative coup plotters undermining reform; external factors (US military pressure, oil price falls reducing Soviet revenue).

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing multiple factors, clear judgement.
Secure: two or more factors explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: factors listed, limited weighing.
Emerging: one factor or descriptive throughout.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Florence Nightingale's contribution to nursing in the Crimean War.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Florence Nightingale reorganised the military hospital at Scutari [1], introducing rigorous sanitation that dramatically reduced the death rate among wounded soldiers [1].
• She used statistical evidence to campaign for healthcare reform [1+1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of women's roles in the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature:
• Feature 1: Women in the ATS, WRENs and WAAF performed support roles including radar operation, driving, communications and intelligence [1], releasing men for frontline combat duties [1].
• Feature 2: The Women’s Land Army employed approximately 80,000 women on farms by 1944 [1], maintaining food production while German U-boats threatened supply lines [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the role of women in British warfare changed significantly during the First World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the scale of casualties and the demands of industrial warfare created a need for large numbers of support workers; the QAIMNS and other organisations were created or expanded to fill gaps left by men serving at the front. The contribution of women on the home front and in support roles changed public and official attitudes, setting the stage for expanded roles in the Second World War.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence.
Developing: Identifies a cause with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Flora Sandes in the context of women's roles in warfare.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains her significance at the time (the only British woman to serve formally as a soldier in an Allied army in the First World War; wounded in action and decorated) and her broader significance as evidence that women were capable of frontline service when given the opportunity, even when contemporary Britain maintained a clear prohibition. Analyses what her example shows about the gap between capability and social/institutional permission.
Secure: Explains significance with evidence.
Developing: Describes Flora Sandes with limited analysis.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Second World War in changing the role of women in British warfare?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues significance at the time (hundreds of thousands of women formally mobilised; ATS, WRENs, WAAF; Women’s Land Army) and over time (established the principle of systematic female military contribution; set precedents for later equality measures; the 2016 lifting of the frontline ban was the logical endpoint). Reaches a substantiated conclusion on significance compared to the Crimean War changes.
Secure: Explains significance with two horizons and relevant evidence.
Developing: One horizon, limited analysis.
Emerging: Describes the Second World War role without evaluating significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did the role of women in British warfare change between c.500 and the present day?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces change across medieval (Nicolaa de la Haye exceptional; general exclusion), nineteenth century (Nightingale, Seacole — nursing beginning formal recognition), First World War (QAIMNS; Flora Sandes exceptional; Dorothy Lawrence excluded), Second World War (ATS/WRENs/WAAF systematic mobilisation), modern (2016 all roles open). Identifies continuity (nursing/support roles persistent; change in combat roles came slowly and against resistance). Weighs change against continuity; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Covers three periods with evidence and analysis.
Developing: Two periods, limited analysis.
Emerging: One period, no analytical framework.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of bull-baiting as a popular entertainment in medieval or early modern England.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with detail: e.g. a bull was tethered to a stake and dogs set against it, with crowds betting on the outcome / the contest could last for hours and was a standard feature of market towns and village fairs. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of public executions as entertainment in early modern England.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. public hangings at Tyburn attracted enormous crowds who treated the event as a spectacle — cheering, jeering and sometimes throwing food (feature + detail); they were designed by the authorities to deter crime and display royal justice, but became occasions for popular participation (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Cruelty to Animals Act of 1835 was passed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking Evangelical Christian reform movements, the founding of the RSPCA in 1824, growing middle-class belief that animal cruelty brutalised human beings, and scientific understanding of animal pain. Secure: Clear cause with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the introduction of the Marquess of Queensberry rules in 1867 for the sport of boxing.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Consequence developed, e.g. gloves, three-minute rounds and a knock-down count transformed boxing from an unregulated brawl to an organised sport; bare-knuckle fighting declined by the 1890s; boxing became acceptable as amateur and professional sport. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of organised pressure groups in reducing cruelty in sport and entertainment between 1824 and 2004?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses RSPCA (1824) and League Against Cruel Sports (1924) significance at the time AND over time; notes legislative outcomes (1835 Act, 2004 Hunting Act) driven partly by their campaigns. Weighs against parliamentary politics and changing public attitudes. Secure: Clear analysis with evidence. Developing: Some points. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The treatment of animals in sport and entertainment improved steadily throughout the period from 1800 to the present day.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees with evidence of progressive improvement (1835 Act, Queensberry rules, RSPCA, 2004 Hunting Act). Challenges by noting that: cockfighting continued illegally after 1835; fox hunting persisted legally until 2004 despite animal welfare concerns; the Burns Inquiry showed contested evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Both sides with evidence, overall judgement. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Simple agree/disagree. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of transportation as a punishment in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Feature may include: convicts were shipped to Botany Bay, Australia; the First Fleet arrived in 1788; approximately 162,000 convicts transported over 80 years; transportation ended in 1868; it replaced the death penalty for many offences. Simple identification (1 mark); developed with dates or scale (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of John Howard's campaign for prison reform.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Howard systematically inspected prisons across England and Europe and published his findings in The State of the Prisons (1777), documenting appalling conditions including overcrowding, fee-charging warders and rampant disease. Feature 2: Howard's proposals included separating different categories of prisoner, providing adequate food and healthcare without extortion, ending warder fees and establishing regular inspection — creating the framework for all subsequent prison reform.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which Elizabeth Fry's approach to prison reform differed from John Howard's.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States Fry worked with female prisoners. Developing: Notes she introduced education and religious instruction. Secure: Explains how Fry moved beyond Howard's focus on physical conditions to introduce the concept of rehabilitation — she believed prisoners could be genuinely reformed through education, Bible reading and moral guidance, not just better fed and separated; the Association for the Reformation of Female Prisoners (1817) embodied this rehabilitative aim. Mastering: Sustains analysis of how this distinction matters — Howard set the humanitarian baseline (adequate food, no fee extortion), Fry introduced the idea of reforming character; this distinction shaped the entire subsequent debate about what prisons were for.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Pentonville Prison, opened in 1842, for the history of punishment in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Describes what Pentonville was. Developing: Notes it used the separate system. Secure: Analyses significance at the time: it was the government's flagship model of the separate system; its design (individual cells, masks, separate chapel cubicles) was deliberately intended to prevent criminal contamination and encourage moral reflection; it influenced prison building across the country. Mastering: Evaluates significance over time: Pentonville's failures (high rates of mental breakdown and suicide) were significant because they demonstrated that deterrence-through-isolation did not work; the resulting abandonment of the separate system, and the eventual return to rehabilitative approaches in the twentieth century, can be traced partly to the evidence generated by Pentonville's harmful effects.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that prison reform in the nineteenth century represented a significant improvement in attitudes to punishment?
Give reasons for your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments for improvement: Howard's 1777 report revealed and began to address genuinely appalling conditions; Fry introduced rehabilitation as a concept; the prison-building programme replaced hanging for many offences; inspection created accountability. Arguments against/limits: the separate system caused serious mental harm; Du Cane's 1860s regime reversed reformatory progress (hard labour, hard board, hard fare); transportation itself was brutal; the rehabilitative ideal was not consistently applied. Emerging: one-sided. Developing: notes both progress and limits. Secure: argues a clear position with specific evidence. Mastering: evaluates the degree of improvement against its limits, reaches a justified conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the separate system used in Victorian prisons.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Each prisoner was kept in a separate cell with no contact with other prisoners — they wore masks when moved and worshipped in separate chapel cubicles — to prevent criminal contamination and encourage individual reflection. Feature 2: The separate system caused serious psychological harm in practice; Pentonville Prison reported high rates of mental breakdown and suicide, leading to its gradual abandonment as evidence of its harmful effects accumulated.

before.exam_tip_html: For questions on prison reform, name specific reformers (John Howard, Elizabeth Fry), specific dates (Howard’s 1777 publication; Pentonville 1842) and specific innovations (separate system, silent system). Examiners want you to evaluate as well as describe: was the separate system successful? (No — it caused mental breakdowns.) Was Elizabeth Fry’s approach different from Howard’s? (Yes — she added rehabilitation to Howard’s humanitarian improvements.) For the 16-mark thematic essay on punishment, the shift from public/physical punishment to imprisonment is the key nineteenth-century change.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the SALT I treaty (1972).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names feature (froze numbers of ICBMs and submarine-launched missiles; first major nuclear arms limitation agreement; signed by Nixon and Brezhnev) AND develops it. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Gorbachev's reform programme in the USSR from 1985.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) Perestroika aimed at economic restructuring by decentralising decision-making and introducing market-like incentives into the Soviet economy; (2) Glasnost introduced greater freedom of expression and openness, allowing public debate about Soviet problems. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (Gorbachev's glasnost unleashed demands for freedom in Eastern Europe; East German government's loss of nerve; mass protests in Leipzig and other East German cities; the Soviet Union's refusal to send troops to suppress protests as it had in previous decades) AND develops the chain of reasoning. Secure: Cause with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Reagan's 'Evil Empire' speech and his defence buildup for US-Soviet relations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (reversed détente; increased Cold War tensions in early 1980s; forced Soviet Union into expensive arms competition it could not sustain; paradoxically contributed to Gorbachev seeking negotiations; led to INF Treaty 1987) AND develops chain of effects. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Nixon's visit to China in 1972 for Cold War diplomacy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (first US president to visit Communist China; opened diplomatic channel; exploited Sino-Soviet split; gave USA more leverage) AND over time (led to full normalisation of relations in 1979; shaped US-China relations for decades; demonstrated that Cold War alignments were not fixed). Secure: One time frame well-covered. Developing: Describes the visit without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'The main reason the Cold War ended was Gorbachev's reforms.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues the case for Gorbachev (perestroika and glasnost; INF Treaty; refusal to use force in Eastern Europe in 1989) AGAINST other factors (Reagan's defence spending; long-term economic weaknesses of the Soviet system; pro-democracy movements in Eastern Europe; Afghan quagmire). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Attributes end of Cold War to single factor. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Armada Portrait as a piece of royal propaganda.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with detail, e.g. the portrait shows Elizabeth with her hand resting on a globe, symbolising imperial authority, while the wrecked Armada is visible in the background to reinforce her triumph (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 'Gloriana' cult as a propaganda technique.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: precise feature with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: presented Elizabeth as a semi-divine virgin queen; used by poets such as Edmund Spenser in The Faerie Queene; Accession Day celebrations were quasi-religious; channelled religious feeling towards the monarch; helped deflect criticism of Elizabeth's unmarried state. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Whig interpretation of Elizabeth I's reign became popular in the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: detailed causal chain with evidence, e.g. nineteenth-century Britain was at the height of its imperial power — historians looking for an inspiring origin story found one in Elizabethan England, where Protestant England first challenged Catholic Spain and produced Shakespeare; this narrative of national greatness served both nationalism and imperial pride. Secure: clear reason with some evidence. Developing: relevant reason with limited development. Emerging: simple point. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Rainbow Portrait (c.1600–1602) as historical evidence for Elizabeth's reign.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance — what the portrait reveals about Elizabeth's propaganda strategy (eternal youth, wisdom, all-seeing authority) AND what it reveals about the anxieties of the final years (succession crisis, Essex's rebellion, an aging queen needing to project strength). Secure: clear analysis with specific detail. Developing: some analysis. Emerging: description of the portrait without analysis. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is the Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I for understanding the way Elizabeth I projected royal authority?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (powerful symbols — globe, pearls, wrecked Armada), provenance (a commissioned royal portrait designed for propaganda) and contextual knowledge (portraits were official tools; no realistic likeness was permitted; the Gloriana cult operated through this kind of imagery) to give a substantiated judgement on utility and limitations. Secure: addresses two of three elements. Developing: mainly describes. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'The Whig interpretation presents a misleadingly positive view of Elizabeth I's reign.' How far do you agree with this interpretation from a revisionist perspective?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains WHY the two interpretations differ — the Whig view was shaped by nineteenth-century nationalism, imperial pride and access to different archives; the revisionist view emerged in a post-imperial era, influenced by social history and wider source evidence (poverty records, church court records, regional studies). Addresses what each interpretation can and cannot explain. Reaches a substantiated overall assessment. Secure: explains both interpretations with some reference to their origins. Developing: mainly describes what each says. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement. Maximum 10 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe one immediate consequence of the failure of the Peasants' Revolt in 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: Richard II revoked all the charters granted at Mile End [1]; peasants who had believed their freedom was secured returned to find serfdom still legally intact and the promises of abolition cancelled [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the decline of serfdom in England after 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: Although serfdom was not legally abolished, it declined steadily over the century following the revolt [1]; most lords found it more practical to convert labour obligations to money rents than to enforce them against an assertive, post-plague peasantry [1]. Feature 2: The revolt had demonstrated that the peasantry would resist when pushed too far [1]; this changed how lords calculated the risks of reasserting their rights, contributing to a more cautious approach to serfdom enforcement [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Peasants' Revolt for the Hundred Years' War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains a consequence in depth — the government's caution about heavy direct taxation after 1381 constrained resources available for French campaigns; or the revolt had been partly caused by the costs of a failing war, demonstrating the connection between foreign policy and domestic stability. Secure: Explains a consequence with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Poll Tax was a more significant concession than it appeared at the time.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies the significance — the Poll Tax was never levied in this form again; it showed that popular resistance could force a retreat by the government on fiscal policy; it set a precedent that direct flat-rate taxation was politically dangerous. Explains this in depth with precise factual knowledge. Secure: Identifies the significance with relevant factual support. Developing: States a point with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference without specific factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 in the history of England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (immediate defeat, executions, revocation of promises, but Poll Tax abandoned) and over time (gradual decline of serfdom; rising real wages; rulers more cautious about extreme taxation; revolt as a founding moment in popular political tradition). Precise factual knowledge throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes the revolt without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was a failure because it did not achieve its immediate aims.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with precise factual knowledge. Agrees: the Mile End charters were all revoked; serfdom was not abolished; hundreds were executed; John Ball was killed. Disagrees: the Poll Tax was permanently abandoned; serfdom declined over the following century; wages rose; the revolt demonstrated that rulers faced limits on what they could demand; it shaped the political consciousness of ordinary people. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement about whether short-term failure equals long-term failure. Secure: Makes points for and against with evidence. Developing: Describes outcomes without evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple response; no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Steven Runciman's interpretation of the Crusades.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students may describe: Runciman presented the Crusades as a disaster and 'a long act of intolerance in the name of God'; he sympathised with Byzantine and Islamic culture; he portrayed Western crusaders as brutal; he wrote in three volumes (1951–1954) drawing on Western and some Eastern sources. 1 mark for a simple point; 2 marks for a developed point.

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why historians' interpretations of the Crusades differ from each other.
practice_questions.marks:
Feature 1: Historians write at different times and are shaped by their own era — Runciman wrote after the Second World War when Western imperialism and religious violence were being questioned; Riley-Smith wrote in a later period with different concerns.
Feature 2: Historians use different sources — Western historians until the late twentieth century largely relied on Latin chronicles; Hillenbrand used Arabic literary and artistic sources that revealed Islamic perspectives invisible in Western accounts.
2 marks per reason: 1 for simple point, 2 for developed point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Jonathan Riley-Smith's interpretation of crusading motivation differed from Steven Runciman's.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific reason (different evidence used — Riley-Smith used charter records showing financial sacrifice, where Runciman focused on narrative accounts; different historical questions — Riley-Smith asked about motivation, Runciman about moral consequences; different perspectives — Riley-Smith wrote within the Catholic scholarly tradition; the passage of time and new scholarship had made more archival sources available to Riley-Smith) and explains it with precise detail, linking it to the difference in interpretation. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a reason with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a reason but limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Carole Hillenbrand's work on Islamic perspectives for understanding the Crusades.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At the time — her work brought Arabic literary, artistic and theological sources into mainstream crusade historiography; it shifted the debate from Western moral judgements to the experience of Muslim populations. Over time — it influenced subsequent scholarship to adopt a more multi-perspectival approach; it demonstrated that the crusades looked fundamentally different depending on whose sources you used. Sustained judgement.
Secure: Covers both dimensions with evidence.
Developing: Mainly describes Hillenbrand's approach with limited sense of significance.
Emerging: Describes her work with little sense of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the medieval chroniclers' accounts of the First Crusade are limited as historical sources.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific limitation (written by Western Christian participants with a theological agenda; deliberately framed events as divine Providence; excluded Muslim, Jewish and Byzantine perspectives; written years after events with retrospective shaping; intended for audiences already committed to the crusade) and explains it with precise detail, linking the limitation to what the source cannot tell us. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a limitation with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a limitation but limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: 'Steven Runciman's interpretation of the Crusades is no longer useful for historians.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues in support (revisionist historians like Riley-Smith challenged his negative portrayal of crusading motivation; Hillenbrand showed his neglect of Islamic sources was a serious omission; his romantic sympathy for Byzantium and post-war perspective distorted his judgements) and against (Runciman remains valuable for his literary quality and the questions he raised about moral responsibility; his emphasis on violence and intolerance anticipated later scholarly concerns; his synthesis of a vast body of medieval evidence was a major scholarly achievement). Substantiated judgement.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence; conclusion reached.
Developing: Mainly one-sided, limited evidence.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.

practice_questions.text:
Study the extract below from a medieval chronicle written by a participant in the First Crusade. How useful is this type of source for a historian studying the motivations of crusaders?

[Source: A chronicle account describing Urban II's speech at Clermont and the crowd's response, written by a crusader participant shortly after the event]
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Integrates content (what the source says about motivation — religious devotion, call to liberate Jerusalem), provenance (written by a participant shortly after the event; Christian perspective shapes what is recorded and emphasised; purpose to celebrate the crusade as God's work limits coverage of material motives) and contextual knowledge (historians like Riley-Smith have shown financial sacrifice through charters; the chronicle's emphasis on faith alone gives an incomplete picture). Reaches a clear judgement about utility for this specific enquiry.
Secure: Covers content and provenance with some contextual knowledge; judgement present.
Developing: Covers two elements but not all three; judgement may be absent.
Emerging: Describes the source with little analysis of utility.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the way source utility questions should be answered.
practice_questions.marks:
Feature 1: A source utility answer must address the specific enquiry stated in the question — not usefulness in general, but usefulness for that particular historical question.
Feature 2: The highest marks require integrating all three elements: content (what the source says), provenance (who created it, when and why) and contextual knowledge (what you know that helps evaluate it).
2 marks per feature: 1 mark for simple point, 2 for developed point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the interpretations of Steven Runciman and Jonathan Riley-Smith about crusading motivation differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific reason for the difference (different time of writing — Runciman wrote post-WWII, Riley-Smith later; different sources used — Runciman relied on chronicles, Riley-Smith on charter records; different historical questions — Runciman asked about moral consequences, Riley-Smith about motivation; different perspectives — Runciman sympathised with Byzantium, Riley-Smith wrote from within Catholic scholarship) and explains it with precise detail. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a reason with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a reason but limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: 'The failure of the Second Crusade was mainly caused by poor leadership.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues in support (Conrad III advanced into Anatolia without adequate preparation and was defeated at Dorylaeum; Louis VII lost control of his rear guard at Cadmus; the Council of Acre made the strategically incoherent decision to attack Damascus) and against (structural problems were as significant — both armies had already suffered serious losses before reaching the Holy Land; the Byzantine failure to provide adequate support; Muslim unity under Zengi's successors made the strategic environment more hostile regardless of leadership; the fundamental miscalculation about Damascus reflected institutional not just individual failure). Substantiated judgement.
Secure: Both sides with evidence; conclusion.
Developing: Mainly one-sided.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.

practice_questions.text: 'The religious ideology developed by the papacy before 1095 was the most important reason for the success of the First Crusade.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Structured argument across multiple analytical paragraphs. Supports the interpretation: the Cluniac reform movement created a militarised Christian culture; the offer of plenary indulgence made participation spiritually irresistible; the concept of Jerusalem as a sacred space charged the whole enterprise with emotional power; Urban II's rhetoric at Clermont fused pilgrimage with warfare. Challenges: the specific political context (Seljuk pressure on Byzantium, Alexios's appeal) created the opportunity; individual military leadership at Antioch and Jerusalem was crucial; the failure of Muslim coordination was equally important. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement weighing ideological, military and political factors.
Secure: Multiple factors addressed with evidence; judgement present.
Developing: Mainly narrative or one-sided.
Emerging: Simple or purely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of using second-order historical concepts (such as cause, consequence, significance) when answering extended response questions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At the time of the exam — second-order concepts allow the student to organise evidence into an argument rather than a narrative; they are explicitly rewarded in the mark scheme for explanation and analysis (analysis and explanation); they differentiate between identifying a point and explaining its significance. Over time — the habit of thinking in terms of cause/consequence/significance/change/continuity is the skill that historians actually use to make sense of the past; building this habit at GCSE prepares for A-level and beyond. Sustained judgement.
Secure: Covers both dimensions with explanation.
Developing: Mainly describes what second-order concepts are without explaining significance.
Emerging: Very limited response.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the borstal system introduced in 1908.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Feature may include: borstals were reformatory institutions for young offenders aged 16-21; established by the Prevention of Crime Act 1908; used education, training and discipline rather than punitive adult prison regimes; based on the theory that youth crime stemmed from poverty and lack of opportunity. Simple identification (1 mark); developed with context or theory (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the debate about the abolition of capital punishment in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: High-profile miscarriage-of-justice cases shaped public opinion — Timothy Evans was hanged in 1950 for murders later shown to have been committed by John Christie, providing a powerful argument that the irreversible nature of execution made it unacceptable. Feature 2: Ruth Ellis, the last woman hanged in Britain (1955), generated public sympathy for the abolitionist cause; alongside the political campaign of MPs such as Sidney Silverman, this contributed to the passing of the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why community service was introduced as an alternative to short custodial sentences in 1972.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States community service was introduced. Developing: Notes it was an alternative to prison. Secure: Explains how short prison sentences were considered expensive and counterproductive — they disrupted employment and housing, and did not reduce reoffending; community service provided a constructive alternative that kept offenders in the community while requiring a reparative contribution. Mastering: Sustains analysis linking community service to the broader rehabilitative philosophy of twentieth-century punishment; evaluates how it reflected a fundamental shift from punishment as deterrence to punishment as repair and reintegration.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 for the history of punishment in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States the death penalty was abolished. Developing: Notes specific cases contributed. Secure: Analyses significance at the time: the abolition removed a punishment that had been central to English law for over a thousand years; the Timothy Evans case demonstrated that execution was irreversible and therefore unacceptable if mistakes could be made; the abolition reflected a broader shift in attitudes towards rehabilitation and the role of the state. Mastering: Evaluates significance over time: the 1965 abolition is the culmination of a trend from hundreds of capital offences (Bloody Code) to one (murder, 1861) to none (1965); it represents the most dramatic single change in punishment history; it also shifted the debate to life imprisonment as the maximum sentence.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that attitudes to punishment changed fundamentally in the twentieth century compared with earlier periods?
Give reasons for your answer. Refer to different periods in your response.
practice_questions.marks: Change: borstals (1908), open prisons (1936), probation (1907), parole (1967), community service (1972), abolition of death penalty (1965), restorative justice (1980s onwards) all represent a shift from deterrence/retribution to rehabilitation/reparation. Continuity: imprisonment remained the dominant sentence; property crime remained the most common offence; poverty as a driver of crime was not addressed by penal policy. Medieval era comparison: from wergild and mutilation to community service is a radical transformation in the theory of what punishment is for. Emerging: one-sided. Developing: notes change and continuity. Secure: argues a position, covers multiple eras, uses specific evidence. Mastering: evaluates the degree of change, argues a sustained case across all three eras, reaches a justified conclusion about whether the change was fundamental or more limited.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of restorative justice as an approach to punishment.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Restorative justice brings together offender, victim and community to acknowledge the harm caused and agree on how it can be repaired — rather than simply imposing a punishment without the victim's involvement. Feature 2: Research suggests restorative justice can reduce reoffending and improve victim satisfaction, providing an evidence base for its continued use alongside traditional custodial sentences.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Nazi-Soviet Pact of August 1939.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific feature with precise detail (e.g. a non-aggression agreement between Germany and the USSR; the secret protocol divided eastern Europe into German and Soviet spheres of influence). Secure (1–2): feature with some detail. Developing (1): vague reference to Germany and USSR agreeing something. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Hitler's foreign policy aims as outlined in Mein Kampf.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise detail — e.g. Hitler aimed to destroy the Treaty of Versailles and restore German greatness, including rearmament and recovery of lost territory; he sought Lebensraum — conquest of living space in eastern Europe at the expense of Slavic peoples. Secure (3): two features with development. Developing (2): two features briefly. Emerging (1): one feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Anschluss between Germany and Austria in March 1938.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear cause (e.g. Hitler exploited the Nazi movement within Austria to create internal pressure; he pressured Chancellor Schuschnigg to resign and forced cancellation of the independence plebiscite; the absence of any Allied willingness to use force made the takeover possible) with evidence and link to the outcome. Secure (3–4): cause developed but linkage limited. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the reoccupation of the Rhineland in 1936 for Hitler's foreign policy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear consequence (e.g. lack of Allied response boosted Hitler's confidence and confirmed his belief the Western powers could be faced down; secured Germany's western frontier, freeing Hitler to plan eastward expansion; huge domestic popularity boost strengthened his position at home) with evidence and further effects. Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Munich Conference of September 1938 for the course of German foreign policy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): significance at the time (Britain and France conceded the Sudetenland, Chamberlain's 'peace for our time', Czechoslovakia abandoned by its allies) AND over time (within six months Hitler broke his promise and invaded the rest of Czechoslovakia; this ended appeasement and led to Anglo-French guarantees to Poland; the logic that aggressive demands could be satisfied with territorial concessions was completely discredited). Secure (5–6): both time periods. Developing (3–4): mainly describes Munich without analysis. Emerging (1–2): brief mention.

practice_questions.text: 'Hitler's own determination and decision-making was the main reason why Germany was able to pursue an aggressive foreign policy between 1935 and 1939.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (13–16): agreement (Hitler's clarity of purpose from Mein Kampf, willingness to gamble e.g. Rhineland, step-by-step escalation timed to exploit Western weakness) AND disagreement (appeasement policy of Britain and France made each step easier; German rearmament gave military credibility; widespread German popular support for Versailles revision; divisions within the League of Nations; Stalin's willingness to sign the Nazi-Soviet Pact). Substantiated overall judgement that weighs factors against each other. Secure (9–12): both sides developed; judgement present. Developing (5–8): one side stronger; limited weighing. Emerging (1–4): mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Chatham Dockyard that made it important to the Tudor navy.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• The Medway at Chatham provided deep, sheltered water [1] suitable for large warships and protected from open-sea storms [1].
• Proximity to timber from the Weald of Kent and Sussex [1] provided essential building materials for wooden warships [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Chatham Dockyard during the Victorian period.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature:
• Feature 1: New dry docks and metalworking facilities were built [1] to accommodate the transition from wooden sailing ships to iron and steel steam-powered vessels [1].
• Feature 2: The dockyard became a major industrial employer [1], with tens of thousands of workers including skilled shipwrights, caulkers and rope-makers, as well as Brompton Barracks housing the Royal Marines garrison [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain how the history of Chatham Dockyard reflects the wider changes in British naval warfare between c.1567 and 1984.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses how the dockyard’s evolution from Tudor wood-and-sail infrastructure to Victorian iron-and-steam facilities to twentieth-century submarine refitting mirrors the broader technological and tactical changes in British naval warfare. Uses specific examples: HMS Victory (Trafalgar connection), Victorian mechanisation, submarine era, 1984 closure reflecting smaller modern fleet.
Secure: Two examples with clear links to wider themes.
Developing: One example with limited thematic connection.
Emerging: Describes Chatham without linking to wider themes.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Chatham Dockyard to the development of British naval power.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues significance at the time across multiple periods (Tudor naval establishment; building HMS Victory 1765; Victorian mechanisation) and over time (the site’s 417-year operational lifespan reflects the centrality of industrial dockyard infrastructure to naval supremacy; its closure in 1984 marks the end of an era). Reaches a substantiated conclusion.
Secure: Significance across two or more periods with relevant evidence.
Developing: One period, limited analysis.
Emerging: Describes the dockyard without evaluating significance.

practice_questions.text: How useful is the surviving historic environment at Chatham Dockyard for understanding the development of British naval warfare c.1567 to 1984?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates usefulness in terms of content (what the site shows: surviving buildings from Tudor, Georgian, Victorian and twentieth-century periods), provenance (authentic physical evidence not filtered by a human author's perspective or purpose), and contextual knowledge (the limitations: not all periods are equally well represented; some buildings have been modified). Reaches a substantiated judgement about overall usefulness for this specific enquiry.
Secure: Uses content and provenance with supporting contextual knowledge.
Developing: Content only, or superficial provenance comment.
Emerging: Simple statement about the site.

practice_questions.text: How far does the history of Chatham Dockyard illustrate the theme of change in British naval warfare between c.1567 and 1984?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues for change illustrated by the dockyard (Tudor wooden ships → Georgian ship-of-the-line → Victorian iron → twentieth-century submarines) and acknowledges continuity (the fundamental function of building, supplying and maintaining the fleet was constant across 417 years). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement on how well Chatham illustrates change vs continuity.
Secure: Arguments for change and continuity with evidence from the dockyard; concludes.
Developing: Some argument, mainly describing the dockyard.
Emerging: Describes without evaluating.

practice_questions.text: Describe one way in which Britain had changed politically between 1890 and 1918.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: The Parliament Act 1911 removed the House of Lords' power to block money bills (1), fundamentally shifting constitutional power from the unelected Lords to the elected Commons (1). Mastering: accurate point with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which women's lives had changed in Britain by 1918.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature examples: women over 30 with property qualification gained the vote (Representation of the People Act 1918); women had entered paid employment in large numbers during the war (munitions, land army, nursing); women had proved capacity in professional and industrial roles previously closed to them. Mastering: two precise features with accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Labour Party's position had strengthened by 1918.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6): The Liberal Party split in 1916 (Lloyd George vs Asquith coalition split) destroyed the main centre-left political force; Labour participated in the wartime coalition, gaining government experience; its 1918 socialist constitution (Clause IV) gave it a clear ideological identity; trade union membership had grown substantially during the war, expanding Labour's organisational base. Secure (3-4): clear cause with development. Developing (1-2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the First World War for Britain's relationship with its empire.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6): Soldiers from India, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and South Africa fought and died for the empire, creating expectations of greater political autonomy; the Dominion contribution at battles such as Gallipoli created powerful national identities in Australia and New Zealand; post-war nationalist movements in India drew directly on the contrast between wartime sacrifice and continued colonial rule; this began the process of imperial dissolution that accelerated after 1945. Secure (3-4): clear consequence with development. Developing (1-2): simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Liberal reforms (1906-1911) for the development of the welfare state in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): At the time: the reforms established the principle that the state had a duty to protect citizens from poverty — Old Age Pensions Act, National Insurance Act; helped ~650,000 elderly and ~10 million sick workers; challenged Victorian laissez-faire orthodoxy. Over time: the 1906-1911 reforms directly prefigured the Beveridge Report (1942) and the post-1945 welfare state; the administrative machinery of national insurance was the template for later expansion; the political argument that Booth/Rowntree had made the case for government action remained influential throughout the twentieth century. Secure (5-6): both dimensions with development. Developing (3-4): mainly one dimension. Emerging (1-2): simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'By 1918, Britain had been fundamentally transformed since 1890.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (13-16): Sustained argument covering multiple themes, substantiated overall judgement. Change: Parliament Act 1911 ended Lords' absolute veto; welfare safety net (pensions, national insurance) created; women over 30 gained the vote; Labour Party established as a major force; Boer War and First World War challenged unquestioning imperialism. Continuity: most women still excluded from voting; class inequality entrenched; empire still large; poverty reduced not eliminated; Lords still had delaying power. Judgement: 'Fundamental' is too strong — Britain had been significantly reformed in politics and welfare, partially in gender rights, while imperial and class structures largely persisted. The period laid foundations for later transformation rather than completing it. Secure (9-12): clear argument both ways, some judgement. Developing (5-8): partial coverage, limited judgement. Emerging (1-4): simple listing.

practice_questions.text:
A student is reading an extract from Cortés’s Cartas de Relación describing the wonders of Tenochtitlán.
Describe one feature of the extract that is useful to a historian studying the Spanish perception of the Aztec Empire.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a relevant feature (e.g. Cortés describes the scale and organisation of the city / the markets and canals). Two marks for explaining why it is useful for a specific enquiry.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 5-mark Source Utility question technique.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A top-band answer integrates content, provenance and contextual knowledge — not just one or two of the three.
• Provenance alone does not make a source useless — a biased source is still useful for revealing the author’s perspective and purpose.
• You must judge usefulness for the specific enquiry stated in the question, not usefulness in general.
• Contextual knowledge should confirm, challenge or contextualise the source’s claims.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Bernal Díaz del Castillo's account of the conquest may be more reliable than Cortés’s Cartas de Relación.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that Cortés wrote directly to the king to justify an unauthorised expedition and secure royal favour — a clear incentive to distort; Díaz wrote a memoir for posterity with less personal stake in the outcome; develops the argument with specific evidence about Cortés’s circumstances and the purpose of the letters.
Secure: Identifies reason with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a reason with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: How useful is an extract from the Florentine Codex for an enquiry into the Nahua experience of the Spanish conquest? Explain your answer using the source, provenance and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Integrates content (the Nahua descriptions of terror, gunpowder, horses and the siege), provenance (compiled by Sahagún in the 1570s using elderly Nahua informants; compiled fifty years after events; in colonial conditions; mediated by a Spanish friar) and contextual knowledge (confirms historical events of the conquest; but informants’ testimony may have been shaped by the post-conquest environment and Sahagún’s own agenda). Makes a clear judgement about usefulness for the specific enquiry.
Secure: Addresses two of the three elements with relevant evidence.
Developing: Addresses one element only.
Emerging: Describes the source without making a usefulness judgement.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Bartolomé de las Casas and a modern decolonial historian might interpret the Spanish conquest differently. Explain why these interpretations differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Focuses on WHY they differ. Las Casas: a former encomendero turned reformer; writing in 1542 within the colonial era; purpose was to change Spanish policy from within; used his personal experience and observation; constrained by the worldview of a Spanish Catholic. Modern decolonial historian: writing in a postcolonial context; influenced by late twentieth-century indigenous rights movements; access to Nahua codices, modern scholarship and comparative colonial histories unavailable to Las Casas; purpose is academic analysis and challenging Eurocentric narratives. These differences in background, purpose, available evidence and time produce fundamentally different interpretations.
Secure: Identifies differences in interpretation with some explanation of causes.
Developing: Mainly what each says, limited focus on why.
Emerging: Describes one view only.

practice_questions.text: 'The fall of the Aztec Empire was primarily caused by the military superiority of the Spanish rather than by divisions within the Aztec Empire.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• Spanish steel armour, firearms and horses gave a tactical advantage in open combat.
• Cortés’s strategic decisiveness (scuttling ships, alliances, use of terror at Cholula) was a product of individual military genius.
• The thirteen brigantines on Lake Texcoco were a decisive technical innovation during the siege.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• Without Tlaxcalan and Totonac alliances — rooted in anti-Aztec resentment — a force of ~500 Spaniards could not have fought an empire of millions.
• Smallpox killed Emperor Cuitláhuac and devastated the population — arguably the single most important cause, beyond Spanish military capability.
• The tribute system’s resentments produced the internal divisions Cortés exploited; without them, the alliances would not have been possible.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive, no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Frederick Lewis Allen's interpretation of the 1920s in 'Only Yesterday' (1931).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: Allen's 1931 account emphasised the social energy and optimism of the decade [1], focusing on flappers, jazz, cinema and the stock market boom as he had personally experienced them as a contemporary observer. [1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the rural-urban divide in the United States in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature.
Feature 1: The 'Roaring Twenties' was primarily an urban experience [1] — cities like New York, Chicago and Los Angeles had cinemas, speakeasies, jazz clubs and consumer goods, while rural America suffered from chronically low farm prices throughout the decade. [1]
Feature 2: The Scopes Trial of 1925 illustrated a cultural rural-urban divide [1] — rural Protestant conservatives used the Tennessee Butler Act to fight the teaching of evolution, while urban modernists and national media treated fundamentalism with ridicule. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain why Frederick Lewis Allen and Lynn Dumenil offer different interpretations of the 1920s United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Focuses primarily on WHY interpretations differ — author background, purpose, time of writing, sources and evidence used, questions asked. Uses precise evidence from both interpretations and contextual knowledge to support the explanation.
Secure: Explains why they differ with relevant detail; may occasionally slide towards describing how they differ.
Developing: Describes what each interpretation says but makes limited attempt to explain the differences.
Emerging: Simple points about the two historians with little explanation.
Key reasons for difference: Allen wrote in 1931 using personal memory as a contemporary urban white journalist — his perspective naturally emphasised the decade's vitality. Dumenil wrote in 1995 with access to sixty years of social, racial and women's history scholarship that had expanded understanding of who was excluded. She also wrote after the civil rights movement had made racial inequality central to historical consciousness. Students should use contextual knowledge (KKK growth, farm poverty, Sacco-Vanzetti, Native American conditions) to explain why Dumenil's later, broader sources led to a more complex picture.

practice_questions.text:
How significant was the Sacco and Vanzetti case in showing that the 1920s was a 'nation of contrasts'?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time and over time; weighs the case against other evidence of contrast; precise evidence.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation; may not distinguish between significance at the time and over time.
Emerging: Simple points.
At the time: provoked international protests; executed 1927 despite worldwide criticism; showed US justice system vulnerable to ethnic and political prejudice; confirmed fears about immigrant treatment.
Over time: Massachusetts acknowledged 1977 they had not received fair trial; became defining symbol of nativism and miscarriage of justice; shaped historical interpretation of the decade as a 'nation of contrasts'.

practice_questions.text:
'The United States in the 1920s was more defined by its contrasts than by its prosperity.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Points for and against; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple agreement.
Agreement: KKK 4-5 million members; Sacco and Vanzetti execution; farm poverty throughout the decade; Native American reservation conditions; top 5% receiving one-third of income; Black Americans excluded from most prosperity; immigration restriction driven by racism.
Disagreement: real economic growth (40% of world manufacturing output); mass car ownership spread down social scale; electrification reached 70% of homes; wages for industrial workers genuinely rose; cinema and radio created real shared culture; Nineteenth Amendment was a genuine advance.
Judgement: the prosperity was real but deeply unequal — the 'contrasts' interpretation captures something true about the decade that a simple 'roaring twenties' narrative does not.

practice_questions.text:
'The main reason historians disagree about the 1920s is because they are writing at different times.'
How far do you agree with this statement about why historical interpretations differ?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence; addresses multiple reasons why interpretations differ (time of writing, sources, purpose, standpoint); reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Considers multiple reasons with relevant evidence; judgement present.
Developing: Some range of reasons but analysis limited.
Emerging: Simple points.
Agreement (time of writing matters): Allen (1931) used personal memory and could not see the full picture; Dumenil (1995) had access to sixty years of additional scholarship including Black history, women's history and labour history that was not available in 1931; later historians had the civil rights movement as context.
Other reasons: sources used (Allen drew on journalism and personal experience; Dumenil on academic social history); purpose (Allen aimed at a popular audience celebrating the decade; Dumenil at academic analysis of social tensions); standpoint (Allen as an urban white journalist; Dumenil as an academic with later 20th-century perspective on race and gender).
Judgement: time of writing is an important reason but not the only one — sources, purpose and standpoint all contribute independently. Top answers show how all these factors interact.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Gorbachev's reforms and their impact on East Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• Gorbachev's refusal to use Soviet military force to maintain communist governments in Eastern Europe (reversing the Brezhnev Doctrine) meant that the GDR could no longer rely on Soviet tanks to crush popular opposition, making its regime fundamentally vulnerable when protests grew in 1989. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the events that led to the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two features identified with basic description.
Secure: Each described with context, e.g.:
• The Monday Demonstrations in Leipzig grew from small prayer meetings in September 1989 to approximately 120,000 demonstrators by mid-October, showing the scale of popular opposition to the SED regime. [2 marks]
• A confused SED press conference announcement on 9 November 1989 by Günter Schabowski led thousands of East Berliners to converge on border crossings; overwhelmed guards opened the gates without clear orders, and the Wall fell. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the GDR collapsed in 1989.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses the mechanism and relates to wider context.
Example: Gorbachev's decision not to use Soviet military force to save communist regimes in Eastern Europe was decisive. When Hungary opened its border with Austria in May 1989, approximately 30,000 East Germans escaped westward by September — demonstrating that the Wall could now be bypassed. The SED faced a choice between large-scale domestic violence (without Soviet backing) and reform. Neither Honecker nor his replacement Krenz could navigate this dilemma, and the regime collapsed under the weight of its own contradictions.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the fall of the Berlin Wall for Germany.
