practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores longer-term consequences.
Example: The fall of the Wall made reunification almost inevitable — once East Germans could move freely to the West, the GDR's continued existence as a separate state was difficult to justify. Kohl's Ten-Point Plan of November 1989 turned the political desire for reunification into a practical programme. The March 1990 free elections in East Germany produced a landslide for rapid reunification, and Germany was formally unified on 3 October 1990 — less than a year after the Wall had fallen. The speed of reunification surprised most observers and created significant economic and social challenges for the new unified state.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Helmut Kohl in the reunification of Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description of Kohl's role.
Developing: Some assessment.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time.
Mastering: Weighs Kohl's role against structural factors (Soviet withdrawal, popular pressure, GDR collapse) and argues a nuanced position.
At the time: Ten-Point Plan set the agenda; active campaigning in East Germany's March 1990 elections; negotiation of Two Plus Four Treaty securing international consent.
Over time: Reunification under Kohl set the terms — East German states joined the FRG, not a new shared state, meaning West German institutions were extended eastward; this shaped the successes and difficulties of post-1990 integration.

practice_questions.text:
'Gorbachev's reforms were the main reason why Germany was reunified in 1990.' How far do you agree?
Consider other factors alongside Gorbachev's role and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, no judgement.
Developing: Some argument on both sides.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Weighs Gorbachev against the GDR's own internal collapse, Kohl's political leadership, popular pressure from the Monday Demonstrations, and international diplomacy (Two Plus Four).

For Gorbachev: Removing the Soviet military backstop made the GDR's collapse possible; without glasnost/perestroika, the political space for 1989 revolutions would not have opened.
Against as most important: Internal GDR collapse (economic failure, emigration crisis, Monday Demonstrations) created the immediate pressure; Kohl's political skill accelerated the process; popular demand in both Germanies drove reunification's speed.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the revolutions that swept Eastern Europe in 1989.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: communist governments fell across Eastern Europe without Soviet military intervention; the Berlin Wall was demolished in November 1989; Solidarity won free elections in Poland in June 1989; the revolutions were mostly peaceful except in Romania where Ceauşescu was executed.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the failed August 1991 coup against Gorbachev.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: a group of senior officials including the KGB chief and Defence Minister staged the coup; Soviet tanks were deployed in Moscow; Yeltsin stood on a tank outside parliament to urge resistance; the coup collapsed within three days when military units refused to storm the parliament.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 for the Soviet Union.
practice_questions.marks:
Key consequence: the fall of the Berlin Wall demonstrated that Gorbachev would not use military force to save Soviet-backed regimes; this emboldened nationalist movements within the USSR itself; Baltic states, Ukraine and other republics accelerated their independence campaigns, eventually leading to the dissolution of the USSR.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise consequence, causal chain explained, specific knowledge.
Secure: consequence identified and explained.
Developing: consequence identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point, no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Boris Yeltsin’s election as President of Russia in June 1991 for the collapse of the Soviet Union.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: gave Yeltsin a democratic mandate Gorbachev lacked; created a second power centre challenging Soviet authority; boosted Russian independence from the USSR. Over time: Yeltsin's resistance during the August coup made him the hero of Russian democracy; after the coup, Yeltsin signed the Belavezha Accords dissolving the USSR.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of the Soviet collapse:

“The Soviet Union collapsed because of Gorbachev’s personal failures as a leader, not because of deep structural problems.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: Gorbachev underestimated the destabilising effects of glasnost; perestroika created economic chaos without delivering prosperity; he failed to suppress Baltic independence in 1990-91; he failed to build a coalition with Yeltsin; his personal indecisiveness during the coup allowed it to temporarily succeed.

Disagreement: deep structural problems existed: decades of economic stagnation, military overstretch in Afghanistan, nationalities tensions within a multi-ethnic empire, an uncompetitive economy unable to match the West. These problems predated Gorbachev and no Soviet leader had a credible solution.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: Was nationalism within the Soviet republics the main reason for the collapse of the USSR in 1991? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement.

For nationalism: Baltic independence movements; Ukrainian nationalism; the 'Baltic Way' human chain of 1989; Lithuania's March 1990 declaration; after the coup, republics rushed to declare independence; Belavezha Accords signed by republic leaders not Gorbachev.

Alternative factors: economic crisis (stagnation, failed perestroika); impact of the 1989 Eastern European revolutions; the failed August coup discrediting the Communist Party; Gorbachev's reforms creating uncontrolled political forces; Yeltsin's democratic challenge from within Russia.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing multiple factors, clear judgement.
Secure: two or more factors explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: factors listed, limited weighing.
Emerging: one factor or descriptive throughout.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Tehran hostage crisis (1979-1981).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names feature (52 US diplomats held hostage for 444 days; Iranian students stormed the embassy; failed rescue attempt in April 1980; released on the day Reagan took office) AND develops it. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Operation Desert Storm (1991).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) It was a US-led coalition operation of 35 nations, including Arab states such as Saudi Arabia and Egypt, assembled under a UN mandate after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait; (2) It began with a six-week air campaign on 17 January 1991 followed by a ground offensive starting 24 February 1991 that lasted just 100 hours and liberated Kuwait. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the 1979 Iranian Revolution and the hostility towards the USA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (American support for the Shah's authoritarian regime; US intervention in 1953 to reinstate the Shah; resentment of American cultural and economic influence; Khomeini's Islamist ideology opposing Western influence) AND develops the chain of reasoning. Secure: Cause with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Bush's decision not to advance to Baghdad after the liberation of Kuwait.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (Saddam Hussein remained in power; ongoing US military presence in Saudi Arabia required; sanctions regime imposed but Saddam survived; unresolved Iraqi threat shaped 1990s US policy; contributed to later 2003 invasion) AND develops the chain of effects. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Gulf War (1991) for the USA's role in the Middle East.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (demonstrated US military power; successfully assembled international coalition; liberated Kuwait; restored Saudi security; US seen as a credible Middle East power) AND over time (US military presence in Saudi Arabia became a grievance; Saddam remained a problem; shaped debates about interventionism; precedent for 2003 Iraq War). Secure: One time frame well-covered. Developing: Describes the Gulf War without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'The USA's foreign policy in the Middle East between 1979 and 1991 was largely unsuccessful.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs evidence for failure (Tehran hostage crisis; failed rescue operation; supporting Saddam who later became an enemy; failure to prevent Kuwait's invasion) AGAINST evidence of success (Gulf War coalition; quick liberation of Kuwait; 100-hour ground war; UN mandate respected; Arab states involved). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes events without weighing success or failure. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Community Charge (Poll Tax) introduced in 1989-90.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• The Poll Tax was a flat-rate local tax charged per adult, regardless of income or wealth.
• It replaced the domestic rates system that had been based on property values.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Trafalgar Square Poll Tax riots of 31 March 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• An estimated 200,000 people demonstrated against the Poll Tax in London; the march turned violent with cars overturned and shops looted.
• Approximately 339 people were arrested — the worst civil disorder in central London since 1886.
• Television images of burning vehicles in Trafalgar Square were broadcast worldwide, severely damaging the government’s authority.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the end of Margaret Thatcher's premiership in November 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. Poll Tax unpopularity, Geoffrey Howe’s resignation speech, or European divisions) and develops the mechanism in detail — showing how the cause led directly to the leadership challenge and Thatcher’s decision to resign.
Secure: Names a clear cause with a linked explanation and some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without identifying a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Thatcher's resignation for the Conservative Party.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. John Major becoming PM and adopting a more conciliatory style, or the Conservative Party remaining divided over Europe) and develops the chain — how the consequence unfolded and what further effects it had.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Bruges Speech of September 1988 for British European policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (explicitly challenged the direction of European integration, created Eurosceptic faction in Conservative Party, contributed to Cabinet resignations of Lawson and Howe) AND over time (shaped Conservative European policy for decades, fed into later Euroscepticism and debates about EU membership). Weighs extent: Thatcher remained in the EEC but set an ideological direction her successors had to navigate.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions with clear explanation.
Developing: Addresses one dimension only.
Emerging: Describes the speech without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The Poll Tax was the main reason for Margaret Thatcher's fall from power in 1990.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the Poll Tax (immediate trigger, riots, unpopularity) alongside deeper causes (European divisions, Cabinet tensions, leadership style, Lawson and Howe resignations). Weighs the relative importance of causes with evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement on whether Poll Tax was the main cause.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence for and against the interpretation. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Ebenezer Howard's garden city plan.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with supporting detail. Example: Howard planned for industry to be located separately from housing, divided by a railway line, so that workers would live in clean, smoke-free residential areas with gardens rather than adjacent to polluting factories. [2 marks: 1 for feature, 1 for detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Letchworth Garden City's design that reflect the public health ideas of the early twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: Workers' cottages were built with gardens in areas like Birds Hill, providing affordable low-density housing with fresh air and growing space — a direct contrast to the overcrowded slum housing that public health reformers had condemned. Feature 2: The town plan separated industrial areas from housing using a railway line, and included extensive green spaces to provide the clean, open environment that Howard believed was essential to healthy living. [2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one connection between Letchworth Garden City and the wider history of public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of one connection (e.g. Letchworth was a direct response to the public health failures of industrial cities documented by Chadwick in 1842; or Howard's planned environment embodied the same principles as the 1875 Public Health Act but applied proactively rather than reactively; or Letchworth influenced the New Towns Act 1946 and post-war planned housing). Embedded evidence. Secure: Clear connection with evidence. Developing: Connection identified, limited explanation. Emerging: Simple statement about Letchworth. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Letchworth Garden City for the history of public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (demonstrated planned environment as public health tool; attracted reformers and showed alternative to slums; provided model of healthy working-class housing) AND over time (influenced New Towns Act 1946; heritage foundation preserves model for study; planning principles still used). Secure: Both dimensions with evidence. Developing: One dimension. Emerging: Description only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Letchworth Garden City represents the most significant attempt to use the built environment to improve public health in twentieth-century Britain.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates Letchworth's significance (planned healthy housing; influenced new towns; embodied Edwardian public health ideals; long-lasting) against other candidates (council housing programmes; NHS; Clean Air Act). Considers what 'most significant' means (scale, reach, longevity). Substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: One side argued. Emerging: Descriptive. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How far does Letchworth Garden City reflect the public health concerns of the period c.1900 to the present day? Use your knowledge of the wider history of health and medicine to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces how Letchworth connects to public health themes across the period (1900s — direct response to Victorian public health failure; 1940s — inspiration for New Towns Act; present day — Heritage Foundation, preservation). Links to wider themes (role of government, individual vs collective action, continuity of housing as health issue). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Multiple periods with evidence. Developing: Two periods. Emerging: Single period. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Study the following source about post-war Britain. How useful is this source to a historian studying living standards in the 1950s? [Note: for full exam use, insert a source extract here.] In your answer, consider the content, provenance, and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Comments on content only, or makes a simple provenance point without development.
Secure: Comments on content AND makes a developed provenance point, using some contextual knowledge.
Mastering: Integrates content, provenance, and contextual knowledge; makes a substantiated judgement about usefulness for this specific enquiry, acknowledging what the source shows and what it cannot show.

[5 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare Interpretation A [that the 1970s represented a failure of the post-war consensus] with Interpretation B [that the 1970s were a decade of social creativity and change]. Why do these interpretations of the 1970s differ? Use both interpretations and your own knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Describes what each interpretation says; no explanation of why they differ.
Developing: Identifies one reason for difference with limited development.
Secure: Identifies two reasons for difference, ties them to the interpretations with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses multiple reasons for difference (standpoint, evidence, era of writing, purpose), ties each specifically to the interpretations, sustains the argument throughout.

Reasons may include: political standpoint of the author; evidence selected and emphasised; time of writing (proximity to events vs longer hindsight); purpose (academic vs popular history).

[10 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why oral history sources are useful to historians studying the experiences of Caribbean migrants in Britain in the 1950s.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple identification of usefulness, limited development.
Secure: Clear explanation of why oral sources are useful, with specific reference to what they can reveal that official sources cannot.
Mastering: Detailed explanation with specific examples, acknowledgment of limitations, substantiated overall judgement.

Points may include: government and press sources rarely recorded the daily experience of discrimination; oral testimony recovers personal and community experiences invisible in official records; the British Library and National Life Stories project have gathered extensive testimony from Windrush-generation migrants.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant is the Thatcherite interpretation in shaping how the period 1951–1979 is remembered in Britain today? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence.
Developing: Some significance explained, basic evidence.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time addressed, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis, precise evidence, sustained argument.

At the time (1979 onwards): Thatcher used the narrative of 1970s failure to justify her policies; it dominated political discourse through the 1980s.
Over time: revisionist historians (Sandbrook, Beckett) have challenged it; oral history has added voices it ignored; but it remains influential — many people's mental image of the 1970s is still shaped by the Winter of Discontent images.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Historians cannot write objective history of the recent past because they are too close to it politically.' How far do you agree with this view as applied to the period 1951–1979?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation, limited range of evidence.
Secure: Clear evaluation, agreement and disagreement addressed, factual knowledge used.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation, precise evidence, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: Thatcherite historians wrote in a politically charged atmosphere; Sandbrook acknowledged he was writing in the shadow of the Thatcher debate; all historians have political standpoints that shape selection of evidence.

Disagreement: professional historians use evidence systematically; the release of government papers under the thirty-year rule has enabled more detached analysis; revisionist historians (Beckett) have explicitly challenged the politically motivated narrative; oral history adds perspectives that correct politically driven oversimplifications.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of oral history as a method for studying the period 1951–1979.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Oral history gathers spoken testimony from people who lived through events; it recovers voices — migrants, workers, women's liberation activists — not captured in official documents or press coverage.
- Oral history has limitations: memory is fallible, interviewees may retrospectively interpret past experience in the light of later events, and a small sample may not be representative of wider experience.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Marxist interpretation of the Peasants' Revolt.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: The Marxist interpretation sees the revolt as an early example of class struggle [1]; historians such as Rodney Hilton argued in 'Bond Men Made Free' (1973) that it demonstrated the peasantry had developed class consciousness and contributed to the long-term decline of serfdom [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why historians have reached different interpretations of the Peasants' Revolt.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per reason. Reason 1: Historians use different sources [1]; medieval chronicle sources were written by establishment figures hostile to the rebels, while modern social historians use manor court records and economic data that reveal a different picture of peasant conditions and agency [1]. Reason 2: Historians write at different times [1]; a historian writing in 1400 saw an immediately defeated revolt, while Rodney Hilton writing in 1973 could trace the subsequent decline of serfdom and argue for the revolt's long-term significance [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the conservative reading of the Peasants' Revolt might be considered limited.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific limitation (e.g. it relies on hostile chronicle sources; it judges success only by immediate legal change rather than longer-term social and economic shifts; it ignores the significant fact that the Poll Tax was permanently abandoned; it overlooks the long-term decline of serfdom). Explains in depth with precise factual knowledge. Secure: Identifies a limitation with relevant factual support. Developing: States a limitation with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Rodney Hilton's interpretation of the Peasants' Revolt might be considered persuasive.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains why Hilton's argument is convincing — e.g. the evidence that serfdom did decline over the following century supports his claim that the revolt raised the cost of coercion; or the fact that wages did rise by the early fifteenth century supports his economic argument; or the breadth of his evidence base (manor records, economic data) gives his interpretation greater reliability than chronicle-based readings. Secure: Explains persuasiveness with relevant factual support. Developing: States a reason with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the difference between the 'time of writing' and the 'sources used' as factors that explain why interpretations of the Peasants' Revolt differ.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains and distinguishes both factors with precision. Time of writing: a later historian can see long-term consequences unavailable to contemporaries; the intellectual and political context shapes questions asked. Sources: chronicles are hostile and tell a different story from manor records and economic data; different sources produce different evidence bases. Shows how both factors together explain the range of interpretations from conservative to Marxist. Secure: Addresses both factors with some development. Developing: Addresses one factor clearly. Emerging: Vague response; factors not clearly distinguished.

practice_questions.text:
'The Marxist interpretation of the Peasants' Revolt is more convincing than the conservative reading.' How far do you agree with this view?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues for AND against using precise historical knowledge. For: Hilton's evidence of serfdom's decline and rising wages gives the Marxist reading empirical support; it uses wider sources than chronicles; the Poll Tax was abandoned. Against: the revolt failed immediately; the rebels had no coherent ideological programme; the conservative reading's emphasis on continuity (serfdom persisted in law) has some validity. Must explain WHY the interpretations differ (sources, methodology, time of writing), not just what they say. Secure: Makes points for and against with evidence; addresses why they differ. Developing: Describes both interpretations without evaluating them. Emerging: Simple response; no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the first Glastonbury event held in 1970.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with detail: e.g. approximately 1,500 people attended and paid one pound, which included free milk from Worthy Farm / it was organised by Michael Eavis and was called the Pilton Pop, Folk and Blues Festival. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the development of Glastonbury Festival in the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. it became an annual event from 1981, growing in size and ambition (feature + detail); it developed a political character by donating a portion of profits to CND from 1981 (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a security fence was built around Glastonbury Festival in 2002.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking the 1990s rave movement, gatecrashing on a large scale (70,000–80,000 at the 1992 festival beyond licensed capacity), public order concerns, and the threat of closure by local council and police. Secure: Clear cause with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of BBC television coverage of Glastonbury Festival from the late 1990s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Consequence developed, e.g. BBC coverage extended Glastonbury's audience from 200,000 on-site to millions watching at home, transforming a Somerset farm event into a national cultural institution; later streaming extended this globally. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant is Glastonbury Festival as evidence of changes in British popular entertainment since 1970?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses festival as evidence of change at the time (1970s countercultural origins, commercialisation by 2000s) AND over time (links to medieval communal festivity, Victorian music hall, mass broadcasting). Uses specific evidence. Secure: Clear analysis with examples. Developing: Some points. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Glastonbury Festival shows that British popular entertainment has moved from communal and inclusive to commercial and exclusive since the 1970s.' How far do you agree with this view?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees with evidence of commercialisation (fencing 2002, ticket prices, corporate sponsorship). Challenges: BBC and streaming coverage made Glastonbury more accessible than ever to non-ticket holders; community values persist on site; charity donations. Reaches substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Both sides with evidence, overall judgement. Developing: Some argument, limited evidence. Emerging: Simple agree/disagree. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Essex Rebellion of 1601.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with detail, e.g. the Earl of Essex rode through London on 8 February 1601 with around 200 followers calling on citizens to rise against his enemies at court, but the citizens did not respond (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the monopolies crisis of 1601.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: precise feature with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: monopolies were royal licences giving exclusive trading rights; they had raised prices and restricted trade; MPs complained bitterly in the 1601 Parliament; Elizabeth defused the crisis by withdrawing the worst monopolies before Parliament could force a confrontation; the 'Golden Speech' expressed her love for her people. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Earl of Essex's failure in Ireland (1599) for his position at court.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: detailed causal chain with evidence, e.g. Essex's unauthorised truce with Tyrone and return to England without permission led to his loss of offices and his wine licence — his main income; stripped of influence and income, and fearing the growing power of Robert Cecil, Essex turned to rebellion as his only remaining option. Secure: clear consequence with some evidence. Developing: relevant consequence with limited development. Emerging: simple point. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the death of William Cecil, Lord Burghley, in 1598 for the government of Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (loss of his steadying pragmatic influence; intensified court factionalism; power vacuum partly filled by Robert Cecil, but without the same authority) AND over time (the factional tensions contributed directly to the Essex rebellion and the political turbulence of Elizabeth's final years). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation. Emerging: simple points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is the account of a courtier present in London during the Essex Rebellion of 1601 for understanding why it failed so quickly?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (what the courtier describes), provenance (a court insider — may present a loyalist perspective; an eyewitness but with limited view) and contextual knowledge (the citizens did not rise; Essex's support was narrow; he was quickly arrested) to give a substantiated judgement on utility and limitations. Secure: addresses two elements. Developing: mainly describes source. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'Elizabeth I's authority was weaker at the end of her reign (1593–1603) than it had been in her earlier years.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: argues for (Essex Rebellion; monopolies crisis; loss of key advisers; Irish failure; financial strain; no named successor) AND against (Essex rebellion was crushed swiftly; monopolies crisis was defused; Robert Cecil managed succession seamlessly; the settlement survived; no major foreign threat after the Armada) before a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: simple. Maximum 12 marks.

practice_questions.text: A source shows a photograph of a queue of unemployed men outside a soup kitchen in New York in November 1929. What can you learn from this source about the consequences of the Wall Street Crash?
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying what the source shows; one mark for development.
Example: The source shows that the Wall Street Crash had caused mass unemployment within weeks [1], with people who had previously had jobs now relying on charity for food — evidence of the rapid and severe human impact on ordinary Americans. [1]

practice_questions.text:
A source is a cartoon published in a Prohibition campaigners' newspaper in 1925, showing a criminal selling alcohol from a speakeasy while a police officer looks the other way.
How useful is this source for understanding the failure of Prohibition?
Explain your answer, using the source and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Integrates content, provenance and contextual knowledge; makes a specific judgement about usefulness for this enquiry.
Secure: Uses at least two of the three elements with some judgement.
Developing: Mainly describes the source; limited use of provenance or context.
Emerging: Simple points about what the source shows.
Content: shows corruption of law enforcement and operation of speakeasies — useful evidence of failure.
Provenance: produced by Prohibition campaigners — likely to emphasise failures to demand stricter enforcement, so may exaggerate corruption; does not represent the pro-alcohol perspective.
Context: by 1925, approximately 30,000 speakeasies in New York City alone; Prohibition agents only 1,500 nationwide; Al Capone's Chicago Outfit earning $60 million annually — source's content is consistent with this knowledge.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growth of the Ku Klux Klan in the early 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise cause with specific evidence and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Valid cause with supporting detail and a developed link.
Developing: Names a cause without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid causes: fear of immigration and cultural change among white Protestants; 1915 film 'Birth of a Nation' romanticising the Klan; nativist hostility to Catholics, Jews and immigrants; economic competition from Black workers migrating north; weak federal enforcement of civil rights laws; revival by William Joseph Simmons at Stone Mountain, Georgia.

practice_questions.text:
Look at the two interpretations of the 1920s United States below.
Interpretation 1: 'The 1920s was a decade of social liberation, economic dynamism and popular culture that transformed American life.' (Frederick Lewis Allen, 1931)
Interpretation 2: 'The 1920s was characterised as much by cultural anxiety, racial violence and economic inequality as by the prosperity that is usually remembered.' (Lynn Dumenil, 1995)
Why do these two historians offer different interpretations of the 1920s? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Focuses primarily on WHY they differ — time of writing, sources, purpose and standpoint — with specific evidence from both interpretations and contextual knowledge.
Secure: Explains reasons for difference with relevant detail; may occasionally describe what they say.
Developing: Describes what each says with limited explanation of the differences.
Emerging: Simple points.
Reasons: Allen wrote in 1931 as a contemporary urban journalist using personal memory — he naturally emphasised vitality; Dumenil wrote in 1995 with 60+ years of additional social and racial history scholarship, after the civil rights movement had made inequality central to historical consciousness. Sources: Allen used journalism and personal experience; Dumenil used academic social history. Purpose: Allen wrote popular history; Dumenil wrote academic analysis. Contextual knowledge: KKK 4-5 million members, Sacco-Vanzetti, Native American poverty, farm depression — all evidence Dumenil could draw on that Allen underweighted.

practice_questions.text:
'The Wall Street Crash of 1929 was the most important cause of the end of the economic boom in the United States.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Points for and against; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple agreement.
Agreement: Black Thursday 24 October 1929 triggered panic selling; Black Tuesday 29 October; market fell ~40% by mid-November; bank failures followed; 25% unemployment by 1933; psychological shock ended consumer confidence overnight.
Disagreement: structural weaknesses preceded the Crash — overproduction, farm poverty throughout the decade, unequal wealth distribution, buying on margin, weak banking regulation; the Florida land bubble (1926) was an earlier warning; these were the deeper cause — the Crash was the trigger not the root cause.
Judgement: Crash was the decisive trigger but the boom had been fragile for structural reasons throughout the decade — without those weaknesses, the Crash's damage would have been limited.

practice_questions.text:
'The United States in the 1920s was a nation of contrasts, not a nation of prosperity.'
How far do you agree? In your answer you should refer to a range of evidence from across the period.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument drawing on multiple topics across the unit; agrees and disagrees with specific evidence; substantiated overall judgement; clear structure.
Secure: Several relevant points with supporting evidence; judgement present; may not sustain argument consistently.
Developing: Some relevant points; limited range of evidence; judgement underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.
Agreement (contrasts): KKK 4-5 million members alongside jazz and Hollywood; Sacco-Vanzetti execution; Native American reservation poverty; farm depression throughout decade; top 5% receiving one-third of income; Black Americans excluded from prosperity; immigration restriction driven by racism.
Disagreement (genuine prosperity): real GDP growth; 40% of world manufacturing output; car ownership spread down social scale; electrification reached 70% of homes; genuine wage growth for many industrial workers; Nineteenth Amendment; Harlem Renaissance.
Judgement: 'nation of contrasts' is the more accurate description — the prosperity was real but structurally unequal and ultimately fragile; the decade ended with catastrophe precisely because the foundations of the boom were so narrow.

practice_questions.text: Describe one way in which government legislation shaped access to leisure between 1871 and 1949.
practice_questions.marks: One example with detail: e.g. the Bank Holiday Act 1871 created official public holidays / the Holidays with Pay Act 1938 gave workers a legal right to paid leave / the National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949 opened countryside areas to public access. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which wealth and income shaped leisure opportunities in Britain across the period c.500 to 1950.
practice_questions.marks: Two ways each developed: e.g. in the medieval period, jousting, falconry and deer hunting were only available to the wealthy because of expensive equipment and legal restrictions (point + detail); by the early twentieth century, holiday camps such as Butlin's (1936) provided affordable all-inclusive holidays that extended leisure access to working-class families (point + detail). [4 marks: 2 per way]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which religion shaped entertainment and leisure in Britain between c.500 and 1900.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation, e.g. the medieval Church calendar provided feast days as the main leisure occasions for ordinary people; the Reformation ended plainchant and reshaped musical culture; Victorian Evangelical Christianity drove the reform of cruel sports (RSPCA 1824, Cruelty to Animals Act 1835); or the Puritan Parliament closed theatres in 1642 as ungodly. Secure: Clear explanation with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of rising real wages and shorter working hours in post-war Britain (1945–1970) for the leisure industry.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Consequence developed, e.g. mass television ownership; package holiday boom; cinema decline as home entertainment improved; growth of spectator sport; consumer capitalism creating new entertainment industries. Linked to specific evidence. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was technology in changing leisure and entertainment in Britain between 1840 and the present day compared with changes before 1840?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Compares the pace and scale of technology-driven change post-1840 (railway, cinema, radio, TV, streaming) with earlier periods (printing press, but leisure largely face-to-face). Argues technology was more significant after 1840 OR challenges by noting pre-1840 changes (printing press, Elizabethan theatre commercialisation) were also transformative. Uses evidence from both sides. Secure: Clear comparison with examples. Developing: Some points. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Technology was more important than any other factor in changing entertainment and leisure in Britain between c.500 and the present day.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substantiated judgement. Agrees with evidence across all three eras (printing press, railway, cinema, radio, TV, streaming). Challenges with equal or greater evidence for other factors (religion reshaping the medieval calendar; wealth restricting or expanding access; legislation from Bank Holiday Act to Hunting Act). Weighs factors against each other. Overall conclusion with justification. Secure: Evidence from at least two factors and two eras, some weighing. Developing: Some argument, limited range. Emerging: Basic agree/disagree. [16 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: This synthesis lesson is your preparation for the 16-mark thematic change essay. The most common error is treating the essay as a chronological list of changes rather than a structured argument. The examiner wants you to identify the most important factor (or turning point) and argue for it with evidence across all three eras. A strong answer will: name a factor (e.g. technology), explain how it drove change in the medieval, early modern and modern eras with specific examples, weigh it against continuity and against other factors, and reach a substantiated overall conclusion. No factor is the “right” answer — what matters is the quality of argument and evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe one example of continuity in the history of health and medicine in Britain across the period c.500 to the present.
practice_questions.marks: One example with supporting detail. Example: Quarantine — the practice of isolating the sick — was used during the Black Death in 1348, during the Great Plague of 1665, and during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, demonstrating remarkable continuity as a public health tool across 670 years. [2 marks: 1 for identifying an example of continuity, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which war contributed to advances in health and medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: The Crimean War (1853–56) created the conditions for Nightingale's nursing reforms, including her statistical demonstration that sanitation reduced soldier deaths, which transformed hospital care. Feature 2: The Second World War funded US industrial production of penicillin — the first antibiotic in widespread use — enabling it to save millions of lives far sooner than might otherwise have happened. [2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why government action was essential to improving public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of one reason (e.g. individual discoveries or proposals could not reach the whole population without legislation: Chadwick's report needed the 1875 Act to become compulsory; Jenner's vaccine needed the 1853 Compulsory Vaccination Act to reach infants; NHS needed government power and funding to provide universal free care). Embedded evidence. Secure: Clear reason with evidence. Developing: Limited explanation. Emerging: Simple statement. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of religion as a factor in the history of health and medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Religion as driver (monastic infirmaries, preservation of texts, Christian duty of care) AND as brake (Church backing of Galen, restrictions on dissection, opposition to vaccination and anaesthetics). Evaluates relative significance. Secure: Both dimensions with evidence. Developing: One dimension. Emerging: Description only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Science and technology were the most important factors driving change in health and medicine in Britain between c.500 and the present day.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates science/technology against other factors (war, government, religion, chance). Agrees where science was decisive (germ theory, penicillin, DNA). Challenges by showing science alone was insufficient without government, war funding, or public acceptance. Substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: One side. Emerging: Descriptive. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How far did the factors driving change in health and medicine remain the same between the medieval period and the present day? Use evidence from all three eras to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces factors across medieval (religion/Church dominant; limited government action), early modern (science emerging: Vesalius, Harvey; still reactive government), modern (science, war, government all active; religion less dominant). Weighs change in the relative importance of factors over time. Notes continuity (health inequalities, reactive government, quarantine). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Three eras with evidence. Developing: Two eras. Emerging: Single era. [16 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: For the 16-mark thematic change essay, the examiner is looking for two things above all else: coverage of all three eras (medieval, early modern, modern) AND a structured argument about the balance of change and continuity. Don’t just list events in order — organise your answer around one or two key factors (e.g. ‘science was the biggest driver of change, but government action was needed to make discoveries reach the whole population’) and use evidence from all three eras to support your argument. A conclusion that weighs change against continuity and reaches a substantiated judgement is essential for the top band.

practice_questions.text: A chronicle written by a monk at St Albans in 1382 describes the rebel leaders as criminals motivated by greed and pride. What does this source tell you about attitudes to the Peasants' Revolt in 1381?
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for identifying what the source tells us, 2 for developing the point with reference to provenance or context. Example: The source shows that educated churchmen viewed the rebels as dangerous criminals [1]; since monks were part of the same Church establishment whose Archbishop was killed by the rebels in 1381, they had strong reasons to portray the revolt negatively, which helps us understand the establishment response even if it limits the source as evidence for the rebels' own motivations [1].

practice_questions.text: Compare the usefulness of a chronicle written by a hostile monk in 1382 and a manor court record listing peasant labour disputes from the 1370s for an historian studying the causes of the Peasants' Revolt.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per source point. Chronicle: useful for understanding how the establishment perceived the rebels [1]; limited as evidence for rebels' motivations because the author had clear reasons to portray them negatively [1]. Manor court record: useful for showing the specific grievances — unpaid labour dues, prosecutions for leaving manors — that built up over the 1360s and 1370s [1]; less emotionally expressive than the chronicle but more directly relevant to the economic causes of the revolt [1].

practice_questions.text:
How useful is a chronicle source written by a monk in 1382 for an historian studying why the Peasants' Revolt broke out in 1381?
Use the source and your own knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates content (what it tells us), provenance (monk, 1382, establishment perspective, Church targeted in revolt) and integrates own knowledge (rebels had specific political demands; Poll Tax; Statute of Labourers; John Ball's ideas). Judges the source's usefulness for the specific enquiry (causes), not in general. Secure: Addresses content and provenance with some own knowledge. Developing: Addresses one element clearly. Emerging: Describes the source without evaluating its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why an historian writing in 1973 might reach a different interpretation of the Peasants' Revolt from an historian writing in 1400.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific reason (time of writing means different evidence is available; 1973 historian can see long-term decline of serfdom and wage data unavailable in 1400; intellectual context of 1970s social history and labour movement activism shaped questions asked). Explains in depth with precise factual knowledge. Secure: Identifies a reason with relevant factual support. Developing: States a reason with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference without specific factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the chevauchée tactic to England's military strategy in the Hundred Years' War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (undermined French royal prestige; forced battle on English terms; devastating economically; directly contributed to victories at Crécy and Poitiers) and over time (established English tactical approach for decades; the Black Prince's 1356 chevauchée produced Poitiers and ultimately the Treaty of Brétigny). Precise factual knowledge throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes the chevauchée without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The Black Death was more important than the Hundred Years' War in causing the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues both ways with precise factual knowledge. Black Death more important: labour shortages after 1348 created the economic conditions for peasant assertiveness; the Statute of Labourers (1351) was the direct result and a major grievance; the gap between practical freedom and legal serfdom was the Black Death's structural legacy that made 1381 possible. Hundred Years' War important: the cost of failing campaigns produced the Poll Taxes of 1377–1381; the flat-rate 1380 Poll Tax was the immediate trigger; the wars drained resources from communities already struggling. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement weighing the structural vs the immediate. Secure: Makes points on both sides with evidence; judgement present but may lack full development. Developing: Describes both factors without weighing them. Emerging: Simple descriptive response; no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one historical achievement that historians use to support the view that Elizabethan England was a 'Golden Age'.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise achievement with supporting detail, e.g. the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 showed Protestant England resisting the greatest Catholic power in Europe and became a defining symbol of Elizabethan national identity (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two pieces of evidence that historians use to challenge the view that Elizabethan England was a 'Golden Age'.
practice_questions.marks: For each piece of evidence: Mastering: precise evidence with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple point without development (1 mark). Evidence may include: the growth of poverty and vagrancy; harvest failures in the 1590s; the 1601 Poor Law acknowledging the depth of the problem; recusancy never fully suppressed; succession question unresolved; Irish crisis; war with Spain continuing until 1604; court factionalism and the Essex rebellion. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why historians disagree about whether Elizabeth I's reign was a 'Golden Age'.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: detailed explanation, e.g. Whig historians writing in the nineteenth century were shaped by British imperial pride and sought an inspiring national origin story — they emphasised the Armada and Shakespeare. Revisionist historians writing in the late twentieth century used parish records and social history to highlight poverty and religious division, giving a more complex picture. Interpretations differ because of the different questions historians ask and the different sources they prioritise. Secure: clear reason with some evidence. Developing: relevant reason with limited development. Emerging: simple point. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the defeat of the Spanish Armada (1588) in the context of Elizabeth I's whole reign.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (propaganda triumph; reinforced Protestant identity; Elizabeth's Tilbury speech; medals and portraits) AND over time (contributed to the tradition of the English navy; shaped national identity for centuries; but the war with Spain continued until 1604, limiting its immediate strategic impact). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation. Emerging: simple points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a passage from a nineteenth-century history of England praising the Elizabethan era as a 'Golden Age of Protestant triumph' for understanding Elizabeth I's reign?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (praise for Protestant triumph and national achievement), provenance (a nineteenth-century Whig historian — shaped by imperial pride and nationalism; selective use of sources emphasising high politics) and contextual knowledge (revisionist historians have since found more poverty and division than this view allows) to give a substantiated judgement on utility and limitations. Secure: addresses two elements. Developing: mainly describes source. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'Elizabeth I's reign (1558–1603) was a Golden Age for England.' How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use evidence from across the whole period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a thesis-led essay with specific evidence from the whole reign (early: Religious Settlement; middle: Armada, Catholic plots; late: Essex rebellion, monopolies, Poor Law). Argues both for (religious stability, Armada triumph, cultural flourishing, exploration) and against (persistent poverty, recusancy, succession unresolved, Ireland, financial strain, late-reign tensions). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement directly answering 'how far'. Secure: both sides covered, some specific evidence, clear conclusion. Developing: one-sided or limited range of evidence. Emerging: descriptive without judgement. Maximum 16 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe one way in which technology drove change in British warfare between c.500 and the present day.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• The introduction of gunpowder weapons [1] gradually made the armoured knight and the longbow obsolete from the late fifteenth century [1].
• The development of the machine gun in the 1880s [1] changed battlefield tactics by making frontal attacks extremely costly, contributing to trench warfare in 1914 [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which government influenced the development of British warfare.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature:
• Feature 1: The government created the New Model Army in 1645 [1], the first professional standing army, which replaced ad hoc feudal and contract forces [1].
• Feature 2: The government introduced conscription under the Military Service Act in January 1916 [1], a response to the failure of voluntary recruitment to replace the heavy casualties of the Western Front [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which ideology drove change in British warfare.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains how a specific ideological factor drove a specific change: e.g., the religious conviction of Puritan soldiers in the New Model Army shaped the extraordinary discipline that made it more effective than royalist forces; or, Cold War ideology shaped British defence spending, NATO membership and nuclear deterrence for four decades without direct combat. Provides evidence and analysis of mechanism.
Secure: Clear explanation with supporting evidence.
Developing: Identifies ideology as a cause with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of logistics as a continuity in British warfare from c.500 to the present day.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues significance at the time across multiple periods (Viking raids reliant on supply by longship; Wellington in the Peninsula reliant on navy supply; Battle of the Atlantic as an existential logistics battle; Falklands War logistics over 8,000 miles). Explains why logistics is a continuity — regardless of technology, an army without supply cannot function. Reaches a substantiated conclusion on why this is the most persistent factor.
Secure: Significance with evidence from two or more periods.
Developing: One period, limited analysis.
Emerging: Describes logistics without evaluating significance.

practice_questions.text: How far was technology the main factor driving change in British warfare between c.500 and the present day?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues for technology as primary driver with evidence across eras. Argues against: government and ideology also drove significant changes (conscription, nuclear deterrent decision, Cold War posture). Weighs factors against each other. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Arguments for and against with evidence; concludes.
Developing: Some argument, limited evidence.
Emerging: Describes technology without evaluating.

practice_questions.text: How far did the causes of change in British warfare remain the same between c.500 and the present day? In your answer, refer to technology, government and ideology as factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues that all three factors (technology, government, ideology) have always been present but their relative importance has shifted across eras: technology increasingly dominant from industrialisation onwards; ideology strongest in medieval (Crusades) and Cold War eras; government always a shaping factor but more decisive in the modern era (conscription, nuclear deterrent). Identifies continuities (discipline, logistics). Reaches a sophisticated, substantiated overall judgement on whether the causes of change themselves changed.
Secure: Covers all three factors across at least two eras with analysis and conclusion.
Developing: Two factors discussed, limited analysis.
Emerging: One factor, no analytical framework.

practice_questions.text: Describe one area of continuity in American politics between 1929 and 2000.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names area of continuity (the USA remained a two-party democratic republic; the constitutional checks and balances system; the role of the Supreme Court in striking down unconstitutional legislation; or capitalism as the economic system) AND develops it. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two turning points in the development of the USA between 1929 and 2000.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per turning point. Mastering: e.g. (1) 1941 Pearl Harbor attack ended isolationism and made the USA a permanent global power; (2) The New Deal (1933) permanently expanded the federal government's role in the economy. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the role of the federal government in the US economy changed between 1929 and 1941.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (Wall Street Crash and scale of the Depression made Hoover's laissez-faire approach untenable; mass unemployment, Hoovervilles and bank failures demonstrated market failure; Roosevelt's electoral mandate for action) AND develops the chain of reasoning. Secure: Cause with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Second World War for the USA's role in world affairs.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (USA emerged as global superpower; isolationism ended permanently; founding member of UN and NATO; economic dominance with Marshall Plan; possession of nuclear weapons; permanent military presence abroad) AND develops the chain of effects. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of 1941-1945 as a period of change for the development of the USA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies changes (economic: wartime production ended Depression, full employment; social: women in workforce, Black Americans' wartime contribution and changed expectations; foreign policy: from isolationism to global power, UN, NATO) AND explains significance of the changes both at the time and for the longer-term development of the USA. Secure: Changes identified with explanation. Developing: Describes the period without analysing change. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'Economic change was more significant than social change in the development of the USA between 1929 and 2000.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues economic change (Depression, New Deal, wartime boom, post-war prosperity, Reaganomics, 1990s tech boom) against social change (civil rights legislation ending Jim Crow; women's rights; counterculture; Stonewall and gay rights; media transformation) and reaches a substantiated judgement about relative significance. Should acknowledge interaction: economic change shaped social possibilities. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes changes without weighing relative significance. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: A source describes women working in a munitions factory in 1916, written by the factory manager for a government report. How useful is this source for understanding the role of women on the Home Front during the First World War?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4-5): Integrates content, provenance and contextual knowledge. Content: describes women's factory roles and conditions. Provenance: written by a manager for a government report — may understate dangers (TNT exposure, 'canary girls') to satisfy official oversight; written from a management perspective not workers'. Contextual knowledge: by 1918 ~800,000 women were in munitions; this source reflects the scale of women's industrial contribution that underpinned the case for the vote. Limitation: the management perspective means it may not capture women's actual experience of the work. Secure (2-3): addresses two elements. Developing (1): addresses one element only.

practice_questions.text: Compare what two sources about the concentration camps during the Boer War suggest about Britain's conduct of the war. (Assume Source A is an official government report minimising deaths; Source B is Emily Hobhouse's 1901 report.)
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per source comparison. Source A: official government minimisation — useful as evidence of the government's desire to manage public opinion; limited as evidence of actual conditions. Source B: Hobhouse's report — valuable as eyewitness evidence of conditions, with specific data on mortality; provenance: a campaigner with access and no financial interest in exaggerating — gives it credibility; contextual knowledge confirms the Fawcett Commission broadly endorsed her findings. The key comparison: both describe the same events but the difference in purpose (government defence vs humanitarian exposure) explains the divergence. Mastering: precise comparison addressing both provenance and content.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why historians might interpret the importance of the NUWSS differently from the importance of the WSPU in winning women the vote.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6): Historians writing in different eras ask different questions: earlier histories focused on the dramatic militant tactics of the WSPU (Pankhursts, Emily Davison) because they were more visible in the historical record; from the 1970s feminist historians recovering the NUWSS's records emphasised the 20-year constitutional campaign that created the legal and political groundwork; access to NUWSS organisational records (54,000 members, 400+ societies by 1913) changed the evidential basis. The interpretation also depends on which factors the historian weighs most heavily for 1918 — short-term militancy or long-term constitutional pressure. Secure (3-4): clear reason. Developing (1-2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: 'The propaganda techniques used by the government during the First World War successfully maintained public support until the armistice.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Agree and disagree, substantiated, overall judgement. Agree: recruitment posters, censored press, Somme film (~20 million viewers within 6 weeks) maintained public engagement in critical early years; DORA suppressed open dissent; white feather campaigns enforced social conformity; propaganda gave people a narrative of heroism and necessity. Disagree: by 1917 casualty lists contradicted optimistic propaganda; Sassoon's 1917 protest was not suppressed but declared shell shock — showing limits of control; war poetry circulated despite censorship; food shortages and influenza in 1918 created real hardship propaganda could not address. Balanced: propaganda was essential in 1914-16 but was increasingly strained by 1917; public support held partly from genuine patriotism and investment in the lives already lost, not propaganda alone. Secure (7-9). Developing (4-6). Emerging (1-3): one-sided.

practice_questions.text: 'The Liberal reforms of 1906-1911 were the most important development in Britain in the period 1890-1918.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (13-16): Sustained argument, multiple themes, substantiated judgement. Agree: Liberal reforms established the principle of state welfare responsibility; helped hundreds of thousands immediately; created the administrative machinery of national insurance; directly prefigured the 1945 welfare state; driven by overwhelming evidence from Booth and Rowntree. Counter-arguments: Parliament Act 1911 had more immediate constitutional significance; women's suffrage represented a more fundamental change in who could participate in democracy; the First World War's impact (loss of 750,000, changed women's roles, imperial questions) was arguably more transformative in its scale. Judgement: the Liberal reforms were the most important domestic policy development but may be less 'transformative' overall than the constitutional changes or the war's social impact. Secure (9-12): argument covered, some judgement. Developing (5-8): partial. Emerging (1-4): simple listing.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Suffragette campaign for the eventual achievement of women's suffrage in 1918.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): At the time: kept the issue in public debate through militant action; Emily Davison's death brought international attention; Cat and Mouse Act showed government's difficulty managing the campaign; however, the WSPU suspended its campaign in 1914 and did not directly cause the 1918 Act. Over time: Suffragette symbolism (Pankhursts, Davison) became central to how women's suffrage was remembered and celebrated; influenced later feminist movements globally; the WSPU's tactics became a model for civil disobedience movements in the twentieth century. Assessment: significant for publicity and maintaining urgency, but the wartime service and NUWSS constitutional groundwork were arguably more directly causal for 1918. Secure (5-6). Developing (3-4). Emerging (1-2).

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the intentionalist interpretation of Nazi Germany.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific feature with precise detail (e.g. intentionalists argue Hitler had a fixed ideological master plan from the start; point to Mein Kampf as a blueprint; argue all major decisions, including anti-Jewish policy, were planned from the beginning). Secure (1–2): feature with some detail. Developing (1): vague reference to Hitler planning everything. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Ian Kershaw's approach to explaining the Nazi regime.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise detail — e.g. Kershaw's concept of 'working towards the Führer' explains how officials anticipated Hitler's wishes and acted without direct orders; he synthesised intentionalist and functionalist approaches rather than choosing one side; his two-volume biography (1998, 2000) is the most comprehensive modern account. Secure (3): two features with development. Developing (2): two features briefly. Emerging (1): one feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the intentionalist and functionalist interpretations of Nazi Germany differ.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear reason (e.g. intentionalists focus on Hitler's ideology and Mein Kampf as a master plan; functionalists focus on the chaotic structure of the Nazi state and the evidence of improvised rather than planned decision-making; OR: differences in the sources used — functionalists drew on administrative records showing bureaucratic competition rather than Hitler's personal writings) with specific evidence. Secure (3–4): reason identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Daniel Goldhagen's interpretation of ordinary Germans and the Nazi regime was controversial.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear reason (e.g. Goldhagen argued all ordinary German perpetrators were motivated by a specifically German 'eliminationist anti-Semitism' — critics said this ignored evidence of perpetrators from other nations; overstated the uniqueness of German culture; relied on a narrow evidential base; placed collective guilt on an entire nation) with evidence and further implications. Secure (3–4): reason developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the concept of 'working towards the Führer' developed by Ian Kershaw.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): significance for understanding the regime (explains how radical policies could develop without a formal master plan; shows how Nazi bureaucracy radicalised from below; resolves some of the intentionalist-functionalist debate) AND significance for how historians interpret Nazi Germany (bridged two schools; shaped all subsequent scholarship; demonstrated that both Hitler's ideology and structural dynamics mattered). Secure (5–6): both dimensions addressed. Developing (3–4): mainly explains the concept without broader significance. Emerging (1–2): simple description.

practice_questions.text:
Study the following two interpretations of Hitler's role in Nazi Germany and then answer the question.

Interpretation A: 'Hitler was a calculating opportunist who exploited ideology for political advantage. He lacked a detailed programme; his power rested on tactical skill and the ability to exploit situations as they arose.'

Interpretation B: 'Hitler's ideology was consistent from Mein Kampf to the outbreak of war. His aims — reversing Versailles, uniting German speakers, conquering Lebensraum — were always clear, and his policies systematically pursued them.'

Explain why these two historians might have reached different conclusions about Hitler's role.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (9–10): explains WHY the interpretations differ — Interpretation A (similar to Bullock's view) may reflect a focus on Hitler's tactical behaviour and day-to-day decision-making, written in a period (1952) when some archival material was unavailable; Interpretation B (similar to intentionalist view) focuses on ideological continuity and uses Mein Kampf as a primary source. Differences may arise from: sources emphasised; time of writing; theoretical framework (biography vs ideology-focused). Avoids simply describing WHAT each says. Secure (7–8): WHY addressed with evidence but may be uneven. Developing (4–6): partly explains why, partly describes what. Emerging (1–3): mainly describes the two interpretations.

practice_questions.text: Describe one way in which the Soviet economy changed between 1924 and 1953.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: the Soviet Union transformed from a predominantly agricultural economy to the world's second-largest industrial power; the Five Year Plans increased steel, coal and electricity production dramatically; collectivisation merged peasant farms into state-controlled collective farms.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of political continuity in the Soviet Union between 1924 and 1991.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: the Communist Party maintained a monopoly on political power throughout; secret police organisations monitored the population under all leaders (OGPU, NKVD, KGB); there was never a genuine multi-party election; censorship and restrictions on free expression persisted in varying degrees.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the international position of the Soviet Union changed between 1924 and 1965.
practice_questions.marks:
Key changes: the USSR went from diplomatic isolation in 1924 to testing an atomic bomb in 1949 and launching Sputnik in 1957; by the 1960s it was one of only two global superpowers. Strong answers explain why this change occurred: industrialisation produced the economic base for military and scientific development; the Second World War was won largely by the USSR, giving it superpower status by 1945.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise change with causal explanation, specific knowledge.
Secure: change identified and explained.
Developing: change identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point with no analytical development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the period 1924–1991 for understanding continuity in Soviet political structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers weigh significance at the time AND over time. Significance: one-party rule persisted through five leadership transitions (Stalin, Khrushchev, Brezhnev, Andropov, Chernenko, Gorbachev) despite enormous variation in economic conditions and international position.
