This structural continuity shaped what was possible for each leader: Khrushchev could not allow genuine political pluralism; even Gorbachev's reforms ultimately could not save a system where the party's legitimacy had collapsed.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance sustained and nuanced, precise knowledge, comparison across time.
Secure: significance in two ways, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of Soviet history:

“The Soviet Union changed more than it stayed the same between 1924 and 1991.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement (change): economy transformed from agricultural to industrial; living standards and life expectancy improved; urbanisation; women entered workforce; international position rose from isolation to superpower; methods of political control changed from mass terror to selective repression to glasnost.

Disagreement (continuity): one-party rule unbroken; secret police throughout; central planning throughout; consumer goods shortages throughout; political repression in varying degrees throughout; collapse of 1991 ended rather than continued the system.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument across multiple areas, precise evidence, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered in two areas, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: Was economic change the most significant development in the Soviet Union between 1924 and 1991? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement.

For economic change: transformation from agricultural backwater to industrial superpower; Five Year Plans; collectivisation; later stagnation and collapse. Genuine and dramatic.

Alternative developments: political transformation from Stalinist terror to Gorbachev's glasnost; changes in Soviet society (mass literacy, urbanisation, women's work); transformation in international position (isolation to superpower to dissolution); ideological change from revolutionary communist state to a system in legitimacy crisis.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing multiple types of development, clear judgement.
Secure: two or more developments explained and compared, conclusion.
Developing: developments listed, limited weighing.
Emerging: one development or descriptive throughout.

practice_questions.text: Describe one example of change in women's status in Britain between 1919 and 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described example, for example:
• In 1928 the Equal Franchise Act gave all women over 21 the vote on the same terms as men.
• The Equal Pay Act 1970 made it illegal to pay women less than men for the same work.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the change, 1 for developing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the welfare state changed between 1919 and 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described changes, for example:
• The NHS, created in 1948, provided free healthcare at the point of use — a transformation from 1919 when most people paid for medical treatment.
• Thatcher’s privatisation programme from 1979 reversed nationalisation, returning key industries to private ownership.
• The right-to-buy policy (1980) reduced the council housing stock, shifting housing provision towards the private market.
[4 marks: 2 marks per example — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growth of the welfare state in Britain between 1945 and 1951.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. Beveridge Report 1942, Labour’s 1945 election mandate, wartime experience of collective provision) and develops the mechanism in detail — how the cause produced specific welfare reforms.
Secure: Names a clear cause with linked explanation and some development.
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Thatcher's economic reforms for the north of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. deindustrialisation, communities devastated by pit closures and steel plant closures, long-term unemployment) and develops the chain — showing how Thatcher’s policies linked to specific effects in former industrial communities.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the creation of the NHS in 1948 for understanding change in Britain between 1919 and 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains what changed specifically (free healthcare replaced a pay-as-you-go system, the state accepted responsibility for citizens’ health from birth to death), measures the extent of change (enormous — millions who previously had no medical access now could attend a GP), and addresses limits of change (charges introduced 1951, inequalities in provision persisted, but the principle of free access endured through 1990). Weighs how lasting and fundamental the change was.
Secure: Explains the change and addresses extent with some analysis.
Developing: Describes the NHS without fully analysing change.
Emerging: Simple description of what the NHS was.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'There was more continuity than change in the lives of ordinary British people between 1919 and 1990.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument across multiple themes (welfare state, women’s status, economy, class structure, Britain’s world role). Weighs genuine change (NHS, welfare state, women’s rights, shift from manufacturing) against real continuities (north-south divide, class inequality, gender pay gap, Britain’s declining global power). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement on which was more significant.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence for both positions. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one way in which Germany changed between 1933 and 1949.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed point, e.g.:
• In 1933 Germany became a one-party Nazi dictatorship under Hitler. By 1949 — following total defeat in 1945 — the western part of Germany had been reconstituted as a democratic Federal Republic with a Basic Law designed to prevent the return of dictatorship. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Describe two continuities in German politics between 1919 and 1991.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two continuities identified with basic description.
Secure: Each described with context, e.g.:
• Throughout 1919–1991, Germany struggled to achieve lasting democratic governance: democracy failed in 1933 and was replaced by Nazi dictatorship; the GDR represented a second non-democratic system until 1990. [2 marks]
• Germany's central European position made it the pivot of European international relations across the period — whether as a Versailles-humiliated state, a Nazi aggressor, a divided Cold War battleground or a reunified democratic anchor of European integration. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why West German democracy succeeded where Weimar democracy had failed.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses the mechanism in depth, relating it to Weimar's specific structural failures.
Example: The Basic Law (1949) was deliberately designed to prevent Weimar's constitutional weaknesses. The 5% threshold for Bundestag entry prevented the proliferation of small extremist parties that had paralysed Weimar coalitions. The constructive vote of no confidence meant chancellors could only be removed if parliament simultaneously agreed on a replacement — preventing the governmental instability that had made Weimar increasingly dysfunctional after 1930. These mechanisms, combined with economic prosperity and Western integration, created the stable foundation that Weimar had lacked.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of German reunification in 1990 for German society.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores longer-term consequences.
Example: Reunification created sharp economic disparities between East and West. The 1:1 exchange rate between East and West German marks, while politically generous, made East German goods uncompetitive virtually overnight. Many East German factories closed, producing unemployment rates in some eastern regions of 30–40% in the early 1990s. Annual financial transfers of tens of billions of Deutschmarks from West to East became necessary. The psychological consequences — the 'Mauer im Kopf' (wall in the head) — meant that many former East Germans felt their identity and experience had been devalued, creating a sense of alienation that persisted for decades.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the years 1945–1949 as a turning point in German history.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description of what changed.
Developing: Some assessment of the changes.
Secure: Explains what changed and how significant those changes were.
Mastering: Weighs the extent of change against any continuities; considers whether 1945 or 1949 was the more decisive moment.
Changes: Unified Germany ceased to exist; Nazi structures were dismantled; occupation imposed from outside; democratic and communist systems were respectively constructed in West and East.
Continuities: Many institutions (civil service, judiciary) retained personnel from the Nazi era in both zones; German society was not transformed overnight; the economic and psychological traumas of the Nazi period persisted.

practice_questions.text:
'The most significant change in Germany between 1919 and 1991 was the division and reunification of the country.' How far do you agree?
Consider other changes across the period and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, no judgement.
Developing: Some argument on both sides.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence across the period; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Weighs division/reunification against other major changes (collapse of democracy 1933, Holocaust, West German economic miracle, Cold War alliances) using criteria of scale, duration and depth, and argues a nuanced overall position.

For division/reunification: Physically and institutionally divided Germany for 41 years; defined both German states' domestic and foreign policy; reunification is a unique event with no parallel in modern European history.
Against as most significant: The collapse of democracy and the Holocaust (1933–1945) represented a more fundamental moral rupture and had greater global consequences; West Germany's post-war economic and democratic transformation arguably changed German society more deeply than the physical division.

before.exam_tip_html: For 16-mark period essays, use the PEEL paragraph structure for each factor (Point, Evidence, Explain the link to the question, Link to overall argument). But the most important ingredient is a substantiated overall judgement — clearly argued, at the end, after you have weighed both sides. Examiners reward a specific, reasoned conclusion more than a list of balanced points without a decision. Use language like: 'Of these changes, the most significant was... because... whereas the other changes, though important, were...'

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of policing in Liverpool before the establishment of the professional police force in 1836.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Feature may include: the old nightwatch system used poorly paid, elderly watchmen known as 'Charlies'; Liverpool's Police Act of 1787 established a Watch Committee to oversee the watchmen; the system was amateurish and inadequate for a growing port city; watchmen's main function was deterring casual disorder rather than investigating crime. Simple identification (1 mark); developed with context (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the professional police force established in Liverpool in 1836.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: The 1836 force was modelled on the Metropolitan Police — uniformed, paid officers operating on beats and accountable to a civic authority (Watch Committee) rather than individual magistrates. Feature 2: The force faced severe early challenges — Liverpool's dock community attracted sailors, migrants and casual labourers; officer turnover was high as men were dismissed for drunkenness and misconduct in the early years.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which Liverpool's experience of developing a professional police force was typical of the national story between 1829 and 1856.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States Liverpool followed Peel's model. Developing: Notes the timing matched national legislation. Secure: Explains how Liverpool followed the Metropolitan Police model within six years of its creation and was compelled by the 1835 Municipal Corporations Act — the same legislation that drove police reform across English boroughs; the challenges of discipline, pay and community relations were common to all early Victorian forces. Mastering: Sustains analysis of how Liverpool's experience mirrors the national pattern — rapid urbanisation outstripping old watch systems, Municipal Corporations Act forcing reform, 1856 inspection creating national standards — while also showing Liverpool's specific character (dock city, mass immigration) accelerated specialisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the specialist departments established in Liverpool Police between 1844 and 1886.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Lists the departments. Developing: Notes they tackled specific crime types. Secure: Analyses significance at the time: the detective branch (1844) acknowledged that beat policing alone could not address organised and serious crime; the river police (1865) tackled the endemic problem of dock theft; the mounted division (1886) provided crowd control in an expanding city. Each reflected Liverpool's specific character as a port with a large, transient population. Mastering: Evaluates significance over time: Liverpool's early adoption of specialist policing prefigured the national pattern of specialisation that defined twentieth-century policing; it shows how specific local pressures drove innovation, which then spread nationally.

practice_questions.text:
How far does the history of policing in Liverpool between c.1787 and 1900 reflect the wider changes in law enforcement in Britain during this period?
Give reasons for your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments that it reflects wider changes: the shift from Charlies (1787) to professional force (1836) mirrors the national pattern; the 1856 inspection act linked Liverpool to national standards; the development of detective work followed the Metropolitan Police model. Arguments that Liverpool was distinctive: the scale and speed of change in Liverpool was driven by its specific character as a port; mass Irish immigration created policing challenges unique to Liverpool; the river police had no direct equivalent in inland towns; the timing and nature of specialisation was faster than in many forces. Emerging: describes one side only. Developing: notes both sides. Secure: argues a clear position with evidence. Mastering: weighs typical against distinctive features, reaches a justified judgement about how far Liverpool was representative or exceptional.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the challenges facing the Liverpool Police Force in the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Liverpool's docklands were home to a large transient population of sailors, migrants and casual labourers — this community generated high rates of theft, violence and prostitution that required different policing strategies from quieter inland towns. Feature 2: Mass Irish immigration following the Great Famine (1845-1852) brought an impoverished and growing community whose relationship with the predominantly Protestant police force was tense — policing in Irish districts was both politically sensitive and operationally demanding.

practice_questions.text: Study the following statement: 'The Winter of Discontent proved that trade unions had become too powerful in Britain by 1979.' How useful would a newspaper photograph of uncollected rubbish from January 1979 be to a historian studying the causes of Labour's defeat in the May 1979 general election? In your answer, consider the content, provenance, and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Comment on content only, or provenance point without development.
Secure: Content + developed provenance point + some contextual knowledge integrated.
Mastering: Integrates content, provenance, and contextual knowledge; makes substantiated judgement about usefulness for this specific enquiry; acknowledges what the source shows and cannot show.

Content: shows striking visual evidence of disruption during the Winter of Discontent; conveys scale of refuse workers' strike.
Provenance: newspaper photograph — purpose is to inform and persuade; may have been selected to emphasise the most dramatic scene rather than to be representative; reflects press hostility to the Labour government.
Contextual knowledge: the Winter of Discontent directly preceded and contributed to Callaghan's loss of a no-confidence vote (28 March 1979) and Thatcher's election victory (3 May 1979). But the photograph shows effects, not causes — it would need to be combined with other sources to explain why the strikes happened.

[5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: 'The 1970s was a decade of national decline in which Britain's failure to control trade union power and public spending brought the country to its knees.' 
Interpretation B: 'The 1970s was a decade of genuine social change and cultural vitality — the decade of punk, feminism, and gay liberation — whose story has been distorted by the political mythology of the 1980s.'
Compare these two interpretations of Britain in the 1970s. Why do they differ? Use both interpretations and your own knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Describes content of each interpretation; no explanation of divergence.
Developing: One reason for difference identified, limited development.
Secure: Two reasons for difference, tied to both interpretations with evidence.
Mastering: Multiple reasons (standpoint, evidence, era, purpose) tied specifically to each interpretation's wording; sustained analytical argument throughout.

Reasons for divergence: Interpretation A reflects a Thatcherite standpoint emphasising economic failure; likely written closer to 1979 or drawing on that political tradition; selects evidence of union power, IMF, Winter of Discontent. Interpretation B reflects a revisionist cultural history standpoint (cf. Andy Beckett); written with more temporal distance; selects evidence of social movements and cultural creativity the first interpretation ignores.

[10 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the industrial unrest that affected Britain in the 1970s.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple cause, limited explanation.
Secure: Clear cause with explanation and factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation, precise evidence, chain of causation clear.

Causes may include: OPEC oil shock (1973) caused inflation which eroded workers' real wages, triggering wage demands unions would strike to achieve; long-term industrial decline reduced job security and made workers defensive; governments' wage controls were seen as unfair; Heath's anti-union legislation (1971) created confrontational atmosphere.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was the women's liberation movement in changing women's lives in Britain in the period 1951–1979? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence.
Developing: Some significance explained, basic evidence.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time addressed, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis, precise evidence, sustained argument.

At the time: first Women's Liberation Conference (1970) identified four demands; helped pressure for Equal Pay Act (1970) and Sex Discrimination Act (1975); opened public debate about women's equality.
Over time: changed public expectations; laid groundwork for later legislation; established that women's equality was a political issue not a private matter.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Immigration was the most divisive political issue in Britain between 1951 and 1979.' How far do you agree with this view?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence, no sustained argument.
Developing: Some argument, basic evidence, may cover only one side.
Secure: Clear argument, both sides addressed, factual knowledge used, judgement reached.
Mastering: Sophisticated sustained argument, precise evidence throughout, factors weighed against each other, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: Notting Hill riots (1958); Enoch Powell's 'Rivers of Blood' speech (1968) attracted 70%+ public support yet led to his sacking; National Front rise 1970s; Race Relations Acts required by deep societal tensions.

Disagreement: industrial relations / trade union power (miners' strikes 1972/1974, Winter of Discontent 1978-79) caused two governments to fall; nuclear weapons / CND divided parties; Northern Ireland Troubles caused constitutional crisis; economic management (stagflation, IMF 1976) was arguably more immediately divisive at the level of government.

Overall judgement must weigh these factors — immigration divided public and party, but industrial relations divided governments more directly in terms of political consequence.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG marks available on extended responses]

practice_questions.text: 'The welfare state was the greatest achievement of the period 1951–1979.' How far do you agree with this view?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation, limited range of evidence.
Secure: Clear evaluation, agreement and disagreement addressed, factual knowledge used.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation, precise evidence, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: the NHS provided free healthcare for all for the first time; infant mortality fell; life expectancy rose; welfare benefits provided a safety net against unemployment and sickness that had not existed before; represents a fundamental improvement in social justice.

Disagreement: social reforms of the 1960s (Equal Pay Act, Abortion Act, Sexual Offences Act, Race Relations Acts) also transformed society; rising living standards in the 1950s improved material quality of life for millions; cultural achievements (music, fashion, arts) also represent positive transformation.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: What does a thematic change essay question mean when it asks 'How far do you agree'?
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for: it asks you to weigh evidence on both sides (change AND continuity / agreement AND challenge) and reach a substantiated overall conclusion about the degree of change, rather than simply agree or disagree. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of a strong introduction to a 16-mark thematic change essay.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. it immediately engages with the question's claim rather than restating it (feature + detail: names a factor and takes a provisional position); it signals evidence from more than one era (feature + detail: e.g. 'In the medieval period... however, by the modern era...'). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain why examiners penalise thematic change essays that cover only the modern period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation that the question requires analysis across all three eras to access top-band marks; the mark scheme rewards breadth of coverage; an essay covering only the modern era cannot demonstrate change across a long historical sweep; evidence of continuity from earlier eras is needed to weigh against modern change. Secure: Clear explanation with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Technology was the main reason why entertainment changed in Britain between c.500 and the present day.' Write an argued paragraph agreeing with this statement, using evidence from two different eras.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A sustained analytical paragraph that makes a clear point about technology driving change, uses specific evidence from at least two eras (e.g. railway 1840s + cinema 1896 + BBC radio 1922 + streaming 2000s), explains how each piece of evidence shows change, and connects back to the question. Secure: Evidence from at least one era with some explanation. Developing: Some evidence, limited explanation. Emerging: Description only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Write a conclusion to the following essay question: 'Entertainment in Britain became increasingly accessible to ordinary people throughout the period c.500 to the present day.' Your conclusion should state a clear overall judgement, acknowledge a counter-argument, and be supported by specific evidence.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A conclusion that states clearly how far the student agrees, uses specific evidence to support the judgement (e.g. medieval feast days as already communal; railway and Bank Holiday Act widening access; package holidays; streaming), acknowledges the counter-argument (e.g. access was uneven; class still shapes leisure quality; streaming requires a device and broadband), and reaches a fully justified final position. Secure: Clear judgement with some evidence and acknowledgement of counter-argument. Developing: Some judgement, limited evidence. Emerging: Restatement of facts. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Entertainment and leisure in Britain changed more in the period 1850 to the present than in the whole period c.500 to 1850.' How far do you agree? Use evidence from across the full period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substantiated judgement comparing pace and scale of change across both time spans. Agrees: steam railway, cinema, radio, TV, streaming created step-changes in access unparalleled before 1850. Challenges: Elizabethan theatre commercialised entertainment; Norman Forest Laws restricted leisure; Reformation reshaped musical culture; Grand Tour was an eighteenth-century innovation. Weighs the evidence, identifies a turning point, reaches an overall conclusion. Secure: Evidence from at least two eras in each period, some weighing. Developing: Some argument, limited range. Emerging: Basic agree/disagree. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that methods of law enforcement in Britain changed significantly between c.500 and the present day?
In your answer you should consider changes and continuities across different periods.
practice_questions.marks: Change: tithings and hue and cry (Saxon) replaced by parish constable system (medieval-Tudor) replaced by professional policing (1829 Metropolitan Police Act; 1856 County and Borough Police Act); twentieth-century specialisation (fingerprinting 1901, DNA 1984, specialist units). Continuity: policing by consent (Saxon communal responsibility survives in Peelian principle); local rather than national administration; poverty-driven crime requiring the same basic policing response in every era. Turning point: 1829 — most significant single change in the thematic study. Emerging: one-sided, one era only. Developing: covers two eras, some evidence. Secure: covers all three eras, argues a position, uses specific evidence, reaches a conclusion. Mastering: sustained analytical argument across all three eras, weighs change against continuity, evaluates turning points, reaches a justified overall conclusion. SPaG (4 marks): awarded on this question — use specialist vocabulary accurately.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that punishment in Britain changed significantly between c.500 and the present day?
In your answer you should consider changes and continuities across different periods.
practice_questions.marks: Change: wergild/mutilation (Saxon) to stocks/pillory/Bloody Code (early modern) to transportation (eighteenth century) to Victorian imprisonment (Pentonville 1842) to abolition of death penalty (1965) to rehabilitation (borstals, community service, restorative justice). Continuity: the desire to deter crime persists across all eras; poverty as a driver of the crimes being punished is unchanged. Turning point: 1965 abolition of the death penalty is the most dramatic single change in punishment history; the Bloody Code (200+ capital offences) to 1965 (zero) illustrates the scale. Mastering: evaluates whether the change was gradual or had decisive turning points; considers whether rehabilitation has truly replaced deterrence or whether both coexist.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that the nature of crime in Britain changed significantly between c.500 and the present day?
In your answer you should consider changes and continuities across different periods.
practice_questions.marks: Change: new crime types in each era — vagrancy/heresy/witchcraft (Tudor); smuggling/highway robbery (eighteenth century); industrial unrest/urban crime (nineteenth century); car crime/terrorism/cybercrime (twentieth century). Continuity: petty theft driven by poverty is the most common crime in every era; violence persists across all periods; property crime is always the dominant category. Turning point: the Witchcraft Act 1563 created an entirely new crime category; the Industrial Revolution created collective protest crime; the internet created cybercrime on an unprecedented scale. Mastering: evaluates whether new categories represent genuine change or just new forms of the same underlying crimes (poverty-driven property theft).

practice_questions.text:
'The most significant turning point in the history of crime and punishment in Britain was the establishment of the Metropolitan Police in 1829.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation?
Give reasons for your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments agreeing: the 1829 Act ended over 1,000 years of unpaid, amateur law enforcement; it introduced professional policing that became the national model; it reflects a fundamental change in the state's relationship with law and order. Arguments disagreeing: the Bloody Code and its gradual reduction (1820s to 1861) represents a comparable turning point in punishment; the abolition of the death penalty (1965) is arguably more dramatic; the 1856 County and Borough Police Act completed what Peel started. Emerging: accepts the interpretation uncritically or rejects it without evidence. Developing: one side explored. Secure: agrees and disagrees with specific evidence, begins to reach a conclusion. Mastering: sustained evaluation, weighs 1829 against other turning points, reaches a clear justified conclusion about its relative significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one turning point in the history of law enforcement in Britain between c.1750 and the present day.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names a turning point. Developing: Describes what changed. Secure: Explains why 1829 (or another chosen turning point) was a turning point — what came before, what changed, why it happened at that moment; uses specific evidence. Mastering: Evaluates why this was more significant than other changes; analyses the cause of the turning point (urbanisation, crime scale, failure of the old system) not just its content; reaches a judgement about its long-term significance.

practice_questions.text:
'Continuity is more important than change when explaining the history of crime in Britain between c.500 and the present day.'
How far do you agree with this view?
practice_questions.marks: Arguments agreeing with continuity: petty theft has always been the most common crime; poverty has always been the dominant driver; violence between individuals has persisted in every era. Arguments for change: entirely new crime categories (heresy, vagrancy, smuggling, cybercrime) have emerged in each era; the scale and nature of crime has transformed with technology and urbanisation; terrorism and cybercrime are genuinely novel. Emerging: one-sided. Developing: notes both. Secure: argues a clear position with evidence from multiple eras. Mastering: distinguishes between continuity in the type of most common crime (theft) and change in the range and scale of crime; reaches a nuanced justified conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a 'substantiated overall judgement' in a 16-mark essay?
A) Describing events on both sides of an argument without deciding which is more important
B) A clearly argued conclusion that explains which factor was most significant and why
C) A summary of every point made in the body paragraphs
D) A statement of your personal opinion without historical evidence
practice_questions.marks: B) A clearly argued conclusion that explains which factor was most significant and why. [2 marks for B with brief explanation; 1 mark for B alone]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of an effective PEEL paragraph in a 16-mark essay.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two features identified with basic description.
Secure: Each described with explanation, e.g.:
• The Point sentence directly addresses the question and states the paragraph's argument clearly, giving the examiner an immediate sense of what the student is arguing. [2 marks]
• The Link sentence closes the paragraph by connecting it to the overall argument — explaining how this factor compares to others in relation to the question's demands. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The Wall Street Crash (1929) was the main reason why the Weimar Republic collapsed in 1933.' Explain one reason to agree with this interpretation.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement agreeing with the interpretation.
Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with specific evidence.
Mastering: Explains the mechanism of the crash's impact on Germany specifically, with data.
Example: The Wall Street Crash caused American banks to recall their loans to Germany, leading to rapid industrial collapse. Unemployment rose from approximately 1.3 million in 1929 to around 6 million by 1932. This mass unemployment destroyed faith in the Weimar Republic, which was unable to form stable governments capable of tackling the crisis. Nazi support surged from under 3% of the vote in 1928 to 37.4% in July 1932, demonstrating that the Depression directly translated economic despair into political extremism.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason to disagree with the interpretation that 'the Wall Street Crash was the main reason why the Weimar Republic collapsed'.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement disagreeing.
Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with specific evidence.
Mastering: Provides a compelling alternative factor, weighed against the crash.
Example: The structural weaknesses of the Weimar Constitution predated the Depression and were a more fundamental cause of collapse. Proportional representation produced fragmented parliaments; Article 48 provided an emergency bypass to democracy that was increasingly exploited from 1930. These weaknesses meant that Weimar democracy was already precarious before 1929 — the Depression exposed existing fractures rather than creating them from scratch. Without Article 48, the chancellors of 1930–1933 could not have governed by decree, and Hitler's appointment in January 1933 might never have come about.

practice_questions.text: Write a Mastering-level conclusion for the following question: 'How important was the role of Helmut Kohl in bringing about German reunification in 1990?'
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement with no weighing.
Developing: Some assessment but insufficient weighing.
Secure: Acknowledges both sides and reaches a conclusion.
Mastering: Clearly weighs Kohl's role against structural factors and Gorbachev's contribution; specific evidence; explains why Kohl was decisive or less decisive compared to alternatives.
Example Mastering conclusion: 'Of these factors, Kohl's political leadership was essential in determining the speed and terms of reunification — his Ten-Point Plan of November 1989 set the agenda before any other Western leader had responded to the fall of the Wall, and his active campaign in East Germany's March 1990 elections produced the democratic mandate that made formal reunification possible by October. However, without Gorbachev's refusal to use Soviet military force — which made the GDR's collapse possible in the first place — Kohl would have had nothing to work with. Kohl was the decisive actor in the process of reunification; Gorbachev was the necessary precondition for that process to begin.'

practice_questions.text:
'The most important development in Germany between 1919 and 1991 was the rise of Hitler and the Nazi state.' How far do you agree?
In your answer, consider the importance of this development alongside others across the period and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, no judgement.
Developing: Some argument on both sides, limited evidence, weak conclusion.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence across the period; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Sophisticated weighing of the Nazi period against division, the Holocaust, the Wirtschaftswunder and reunification; argues a clear position supported by criteria (scale of impact, duration, legacy).

For Nazi rise and state: Led directly to the Holocaust (murder of ~6 million Jews) and the Second World War (millions dead, Germany physically destroyed); set the conditions for all subsequent German history; permanently defined Germany's international reputation.
Against as single most important: Division (1945–1990) defined Germany's political structure for 45 years and the lives of millions; the democratic success of West Germany was a positive transformation equally significant; the Holocaust's significance arguably transcends 'German history' and becomes world history.
Strongest conclusion: Agree — the Nazi state's consequences (Holocaust, war, division) shaped every subsequent development in German history, making it the pivotal moment without which nothing else can be understood.

practice_questions.text: Describe one technique that helps students structure an extended essay response effectively.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: PEEL structure (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link); planning before writing; including an introduction that states the overall argument; ending with a substantiated conclusion that weighs factors.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear technique with developed explanation of how it helps.
Secure: technique identified with basic explanation.
Developing: technique stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of a strong 16-mark essay conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: it weighs factors explicitly rather than listing them; it gives a clear direct answer to the question; it uses precise historical vocabulary; it briefly acknowledges a counter-argument before reaffirming the judgement; it does not simply summarise paragraphs.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why students who describe events without making an argument fail to reach the top marks on extended-response questions.
practice_questions.marks:
Key reason: extended-response questions reward Analysis (explanation and analysis) as heavily as knowledge (recall and understanding). A narrative retelling of events demonstrates knowledge but not the ability to use that knowledge to construct an argument or reach a judgement. Without analytical framing, even accurate knowledge cannot access the marks reserved for second-order analysis.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: reason explained with reference to assessment objectives or specific analytical requirements.
Secure: reason identified and explained.
Developing: reason identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point, no reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Was Stalin’s use of terror the most important way in which he maintained control of the Soviet Union? Use your knowledge to write a practice 8-mark response.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance in two directions. For terror: show trials eliminated rivals; gulag removed dissidents; mass arrests created a culture of fear; purge of the Red Army removed potential opposition. Against terror as the only method: propaganda and the Cult of Stalin built genuine loyalty; the Five Year Plans delivered real economic achievements that gave Stalin legitimacy; the party structure rewarded those who collaborated.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: terror assessed in context of other methods, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: two methods compared, relevant knowledge.
Developing: one method at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of Soviet history:

“The Soviet Union was fundamentally the same under every leader from Stalin to Gorbachev.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement (continuity): one-party rule throughout; secret police throughout; central planning throughout; consumer goods shortages throughout; no free elections or genuine political pluralism until 1989.

Disagreement (change): Stalin used mass terror; Khrushchev released prisoners and denounced Stalin; Brezhnev used selective rather than mass repression; Gorbachev introduced glasnost, perestroika and competitive elections; the economy transformed from agricultural to industrial and back to stagnation.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence for both sides across multiple leaders, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered with evidence, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: How far did the Soviet Union develop as a superpower between 1924 and 1991? Use your knowledge to produce a full 16-mark essay response.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires sustained argument, precise knowledge, substantiated judgement and good SPaG.

For superpower development: from diplomatic isolation in 1924 to atomic bomb 1949 to Sputnik 1957 to one of two global superpowers by the 1960s; control over Eastern Europe through Warsaw Pact; nuclear parity with USA; space achievements.

Limits and reversal: military power concealed economic weakness; Afghan War exposed limits of military capability; Gorbachev's reforms destabilised the system; by 1991 superpower status had evaporated and the state itself dissolved.

The arc: rise → peak → overstretch → collapse.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument tracing development and decline with precise evidence, clear verdict on 'how far', strong SPaG.
Secure: development and limits both covered, conclusion reached, relevant knowledge.
Developing: chronological or thematic coverage without sustained argument.
Emerging: one aspect only or purely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a 'continuity' in the history of health and medicine?
A) The introduction of anaesthetics in 1847
B) The use of quarantine during both the Black Death (1348) and COVID-19 (2020)
C) The discovery of germ theory by Pasteur in 1861
D) The creation of the NHS in 1948
practice_questions.marks: B — The use of quarantine during both the Black Death (1348) and COVID-19 (2020) [1 mark for correct identification; 1 mark if they can explain why: same method used across 670 years = continuity not change]

practice_questions.text: Describe two common mistakes that students make when answering thematic change essay questions.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: Students cover only one or two eras (typically focusing on the modern period) rather than covering all three — medieval, early modern and modern — which caps the mark at mid-band. Feature 2: Students list events in chronological order without analysis, describing what happened rather than weighing change against continuity or arguing which factors mattered most. [2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain why it is important to cover all three eras (medieval, early modern and modern) in a thematic change essay.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of why three-era coverage is required (the question asks about change across the whole period; single-era answers can't show rate or pattern of change; examiners explicitly cap mid-band for missing eras) with embedded examples of what each era contributes. Secure: Clear explanation with evidence. Developing: Limited explanation. Emerging: Simple statement. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using your knowledge of health and medicine in Britain, write a strong analytical paragraph that identifies a turning point and explains why it was significant across the whole period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a genuine turning point (e.g. germ theory, antiseptics, NHS), explains why it was decisive rather than incremental, links to both what came before and long-term consequences. Secure: Clear turning point with evidence and explanation of significance. Developing: Turning point identified, limited analysis of why it was decisive. Emerging: Description of an event without turning-point analysis. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The most significant changes in health and medicine in Britain took place in the nineteenth century, not the twentieth.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to all three eras.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates 19th-century changes (germ theory, antiseptics, anaesthetics, public health legislation, Nightingale) against 20th-century changes (penicillin, NHS, radiotherapy, DNA, transplants). Considers what 'most significant' means and whether the 19th century's theoretical revolution was a better foundation than the 20th's practical revolution. Substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: One side argued. Emerging: Descriptive. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How far did the treatment and prevention of disease change in Britain between c.500 and the present day? Use evidence from all three eras to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Covers medieval (bloodletting, herbal, barber surgeons; plague prevention by prayer/flagellants/quarantine), early modern (Simpson anaesthetics 1847, Lister antiseptics 1865; Jenner vaccination 1796), modern (penicillin 1944, NHS 1948, cancer treatments, COVID vaccines 2020). Weighs change against continuity (quarantine throughout; alternative medicine persisting; health inequalities persistent). Substantiated judgement about rate and nature of change across the period. Secure: Three eras with evidence and clear argument. Developing: Two eras. Emerging: Single era. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Write an opening thesis (2-3 sentences) for the following question: 'How far was Roosevelt's New Deal the most important turning point in the development of the USA between 1929 and 2000?'
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks awarded for a clear argument stated in first sentence; 2 additional marks for identifying at least one counter-factor and indicating the direction of the answer. Mastering: 'The New Deal was a significant turning point in expanding federal power, but the Second World War, the 1954 civil rights ruling and the 1981 Reagan revolution were all arguably more transformative depending on the theme considered — on balance, Pearl Harbor and its consequences represent the greatest turning point because they permanently changed America's global role.' Developing: A thesis that agrees entirely with the question without identifying any counter-factor.

practice_questions.text: Identify and explain two factors that caused political change in the USA between 1960 and 2000.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed factors, each with: clear identification of the factor; precise evidence; explanation of how it caused political change. e.g. (1) Watergate (1972-74) — Nixon's resignation damaged public trust in government and led to congressional reforms limiting executive power; (2) Reagan's 1980 election — a decisive ideological shift from New Deal liberalism to conservatism, reducing federal spending and cutting taxes. Secure: Two factors identified with development. Developing: One factor only or limited development. Emerging: Vague or narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'Civil rights was the most significant social change in the USA between 1929 and 2000.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs civil rights (Brown v Board 1954; Civil Rights Act 1964; Voting Rights Act 1965; end of Jim Crow) against other social changes (women's rights — Equal Pay Act 1963, Roe v Wade 1973; media transformation — TV to internet; counterculture and generational change). Must acknowledge: civil rights was profound in law but economic racial inequality persisted; therefore 'most significant' requires definition. Substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes civil rights without weighing against other changes. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which change in the USA's foreign policy between 1929 and 1945 was significant for the rest of the period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (Pearl Harbor ended isolationism permanently; USA became founding member of UN and NATO; Cold War defined foreign policy 1947-1991; nuclear deterrence became central to global security) AND develops the chain of effects from 1941 forward. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Using this question structure as your guide, write a full concluding paragraph (5-8 sentences) for the following: 'How far was economic change the main driver of political change in the USA between 1929 and 2000?'
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A conclusion that: directly answers the question; weighs at least two factors; uses precise evidence from the period; reaches a qualified judgement that addresses the 'how far' element. Should argue something like: 'Economic crises (1929 Depression, 1970s stagflation, 1990s boom) were often catalysts for political change — the Depression enabled the New Deal, stagflation enabled Reagan. However, political change also occurred independently of economics — civil rights legislation was driven by social protest rather than economic forces, and Watergate's impact on public trust had no economic cause. Overall, economics was the most consistent driver of political change but not the only one.' Secure: Answers the question with evidence but judgement less precisely balanced. Developing: Summarises arguments without reaching a clear judgement. Emerging: Describes rather than concludes.

practice_questions.text: A student argues: 'The 16-mark essay should always agree with the statement in the question because examiners set questions about the most important factors.' Do you agree with this strategy? Explain your reasoning.
practice_questions.marks: This question tests exam technique understanding. Mastering: Explains that top marks require weighing factors, not agreeing with the question's claim; that 'how far do you agree' invites a qualified response; that examiners specifically reward substantiated judgement including awareness of counter-arguments; uses examples of how counter-arguments improve rather than weaken a response. Secure: Identifies that both agreement and counter-argument are needed. Developing: Suggests agreement is fine without explanation. Emerging: Agrees with the student's flawed strategy.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the structure recommended for a strong 16-mark Period Essay.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• The essay should open with a clear thesis that states the overall judgement immediately.
• Body paragraphs should follow a Point-Evidence-Explanation structure, using specific dated evidence.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of a 'substantiated overall judgement' in a 16-mark Period Essay.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• A substantiated overall judgement commits to a clear verdict rather than saying 'there are arguments on both sides'.
• It weighs the counter-argument explicitly before explaining why the main thesis is more convincing.
• It links back to the specific wording and concept of the question.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why telling the story of events in chronological order is not an effective approach to the 16-mark essay.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the problem (chronological narrative is description, not analysis) and develops it — the essay tests explanation and analysis (analysis) and interpretation analysis (organised argument), both of which require grouping evidence by argument rather than by date; a chronological story cannot reach the top band because it does not weigh or compare factors.
Secure: Clear explanation of why chronological narrative is insufficient, with some development.
Developing: Identifies the problem with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of writing a 'see-saw' essay without a clear overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the consequence (the essay cannot access the top band because it lacks a substantiated overall judgement — the defining feature of Mastering) and develops the chain — without a clear verdict, the examiner cannot credit analytical weighing of arguments, which is what explanation and analysis and interpretation analysis reward.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation of the consequence.
Developing: Names the consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The welfare state was the most significant development in Britain between 1919 and 1990.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge of the period to support or challenge this view.
[This question asks you to apply the essay technique practised in this lesson.]
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Opens with a clear thesis. Two or three analytically focused paragraphs with dated evidence (NHS 1948, Beveridge 1942, Thatcher’s challenges post-1979, right-to-buy 1980). Counter-argument acknowledges alternative significant developments (women’s rights, economic transformation, Britain’s global role). Conclusion delivers a substantiated overall judgement on whether the welfare state was the most significant development. Argument is sustained and coherent throughout.
Secure: Clear thesis, two body paragraphs with evidence, one counter-argument, weighted conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account of the welfare state without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Thatcher's economic reforms changed Britain more than any other development between 1919 and 1990.' How far do you agree? Apply the four-part essay structure in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Opens with a clear thesis. Analytically focused paragraphs address Thatcherite change (privatisation, unemployment, deindustrialisation, right-to-buy, Big Bang) with dated evidence. Counter-argument addresses alternative transformations (Attlee’s welfare state, women’s emancipation, or Britain’s post-imperial decline). Conclusion delivers a substantiated overall judgement weighing Thatcher’s reforms against other major changes.
Secure: Clear thesis, two body paragraphs, counter-argument, weighted conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Study this source.

Source A: A photograph taken by a Nazi Party photographer in 1933 showing the burning of books outside Berlin's Humboldt University, with crowds watching and SA men carrying armfuls of books to the fire.

How useful is Source A for an enquiry into how the Nazi regime controlled information and cultural life in Germany?

Use the source and your own knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4–5): evaluates content (book burning visible, SA involved, public setting shows regime was open about cultural control), provenance (Nazi photographer, 1933, serves propaganda function — designed to show strength rather than hide it; still useful because it is evidence of the regime's actions as well as its self-image), and own contextual knowledge (book burnings were organised by Goebbels' ministry in May 1933; works by Jewish authors, Marxists and pacifists targeted; part of the wider Gleichschaltung of culture). Secure (3): two strands addressed. Developing (2): one strand with some development. Emerging (1): simple comment on bias or content.

practice_questions.text:
Study these two interpretations about the nature of Hitler's power.

Interpretation A: 'Hitler was an all-powerful dictator who dominated every aspect of Nazi Germany's government. His personal ideology drove every major decision, and no significant policy was made without his direct approval or initiation.'

Interpretation B: 'Hitler's power was more limited and chaotic than it appeared. He rarely involved himself in day-to-day administration, leaving competing agencies to battle for influence. Policy often emerged from below, with officials guessing what the Führer wanted.'

Explain why these two interpretations reach different conclusions about Hitler's power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (9–10): explains WHY — Interpretation A reflects an intentionalist approach (may emphasise Mein Kampf, Hitler's speeches, direct ideological statements; written when full administrative record was not available); Interpretation B reflects a functionalist/structuralist approach (emphasises administrative chaos, Broszat and Mommsen's research using bureaucratic records). Differences in: sources used, time written, scholarly framework, what counts as evidence. Does NOT simply describe how they differ. Secure (7–8): WHY addressed with evidence. Developing (4–6): partly WHY, partly HOW. Emerging (1–3): only describes what each says.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way you would evaluate the usefulness of a Nazi propaganda source for an enquiry into how the Nazi regime maintained popular support.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): identifies a specific evaluative approach (e.g. provenance evaluation: a propaganda source was designed to create support, so it is very useful for showing WHAT the regime wanted people to believe, even if it doesn't reveal what people actually thought; OR: content evaluation: specific elements of the source — images, slogans, claims — can be tested against contextual knowledge about whether the regime's promises were real). Secure (3–4): approach identified and developed. Developing (2): brief point. Emerging (1): simple mention.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the intentionalist-functionalist debate for how historians understand the Nazi regime.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): significance for historiography (the debate reshaped the entire field; led to new research into administrative structure; Kershaw's synthesis in 'working towards the Führer' emerged from it) AND significance for our understanding of the regime (whether Hitler had a master plan or policy emerged from chaos affects how we judge both Hitler's responsibility and ordinary Germans' agency). Secure (5–6): both dimensions. Developing (3–4): mainly describes the debate. Emerging (1–2): simple points.

practice_questions.text: 'Nazi propaganda was the most important method by which the regime maintained control over Germany in the years 1933 to 1939.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): agreement (Goebbels' media control reached 70% of households by radio by 1939; rallies created sense of invincibility; effective because it mixed entertainment with ideology; economic successes gave propaganda genuine truth) AND disagreement (terror was also crucial — Gestapo, concentration camps, self-censorship; economic benefits (falling unemployment, KdF) were equally important in generating support; propaganda alone could not have maintained control without real benefits and real threats). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both sides; judgement. Developing (4–6): one side stronger. Emerging (1–3): mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: 'The failure of the Weimar Republic was more important than Hitler's own actions in explaining his rise to power.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (13–16): agreement (structural weaknesses of Weimar — proportional representation, Article 48, hostile judiciary; economic crises of 1923 and 1929–1932 created conditions; Papen and Hindenburg's miscalculation completed the process) AND disagreement (Hitler's own qualities — propaganda skills, ability to appeal to different groups, tactical shift to legal strategy after 1923; Nazi Party organisation; SA street pressure). Sustained analysis that weighs the factors. Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (9–12): both sides developed; judgement. Developing (5–8): one side stronger. Emerging (1–4): mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the 16-mark thematic change essay question.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• It requires evidence from all three eras (medieval, early modern, modern) [1], unlike shorter questions which may focus on a single period [1].
• It asks ‘how far’, which means students must reach a substantiated judgement weighing change against continuity [1+1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between description and analysis in a thematic change essay.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per difference:
• Description states what changed (e.g., ‘armies used longbows in the medieval period and machine guns in the twentieth century’) [1]; analysis explains what the change meant and why it mattered (e.g., the shift changed the relationship between training and firepower) [1].
• Description narrates events [1]; analysis weighs significance, considers causation, and reaches a judgement about extent of change [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why covering all three eras is important in a thematic change essay.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the question asks how far change occurred across the whole thematic period (c.500 to present); covering only the modern era cannot demonstrate whether change was gradual or sudden, early or late. Examiners award marks for breadth of era coverage because a genuine thematic argument requires comparison across time, not just description of one period.
Secure: Clear explanation with reference to mark allocation and analytical requirement.
Developing: Identifies the need for all eras with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the PEEL paragraph structure for thematic change essays.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains how each element of PEEL serves the essay’s analytical purpose — Point ensures the paragraph has a clear argument; Evidence grounds it in specific historical knowledge; Explain connects evidence to the argument; Link ensures the paragraph directly addresses the question’s change/continuity focus. The structure prevents the common problem of description without analysis.
Secure: Explains at least two elements with clear reasoning.
Developing: Describes PEEL with limited analysis of why it is useful.
Emerging: Simple statement about essay structure.

practice_questions.text: How far did tactics change in British warfare between c.500 and the present day? Use your knowledge to write a plan (introduction argument, one evidence point per era, one continuity observation, outline conclusion).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Introduction argues a clear position (tactics changed significantly, primarily driven by technology, but discipline remained constant). Medieval evidence: shield wall → longbow at Crécy (1346). Early modern evidence: linear tactics → New Model Army (1645). Modern evidence: trench warfare 1914–18 → combined arms 1918 → guerrilla from 1899. Continuity: discipline as constant. Conclusion: most significant change came with industrialisation from c.1850; fundamentals of disciplined combined arms warfare persistent.
Secure: Arguments for and against with evidence from at least two eras; concludes.
Developing: Some argument, one or two eras covered.
Emerging: Describes events without evaluating.

practice_questions.text: How far did the recruitment of British soldiers change between c.500 and the present day? In your answer, cover all three eras and weigh change against continuity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Medieval: feudal levy and chivalric codes — obligation-based. Early modern: Tudor militia, New Model Army (1645) — beginning of professional army; press gangs for navy. Modern: Kitchener volunteers (1914), Pals Battalions, conscription (1916), National Service (1947–60), all-volunteer professional (1960–present). Continuity: training and discipline always central; voluntary ethos recurring even alongside compulsion. Conclusion: most significant single change was the Military Service Act (1916) — first compulsory service in British history — but the overall direction of change has been towards professionalism and voluntarism. Substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Covers all three eras with evidence and some analysis of change/continuity; concludes.
Developing: Two eras, limited analysis.
Emerging: One era, no analytical framework.
